Implementing an Interactive Theorem Prover from Scratch

A guided tour of MiniLean4, a small Lean 4-style proof kernel written in Rust.

Hideaki Takahashi

Chapter 1

Propositions as Types

A theorem prover has to decide whether a proof is correct. A proof written in English cannot be checked by a computer, so we need a representation of proofs that a program can inspect. This chapter introduces the idea that makes everything else possible: a proof is a program, a proposition is its type, and checking a proof is type checking.

Proofs as programs

Here is a proof, in ordinary mathematical prose, of the proposition "AAA implies BBB":

Assume AAA. Then ... (some argument) ... so BBB holds.

The shape of this proof is a function. It takes something, a reason to believe AAA, and produces something else, a reason to believe BBB. If we take this literally and treat "a reason to believe AAA" as a value of type AAA, then a proof of A→BA \to BA→B is a function from AAA to BBB, and the proposition A→BA \to BA→B is the type of that function.

This observation is the Curry-Howard correspondence. It says that

  • a proposition is a type,
  • a proof of the proposition is a term of that type, and
  • the proposition AAA is true exactly when some term ttt of type AAA exists, written t:At : At:A.

Three examples show how far this already goes. On the left is a proposition, in the middle a proof of it written as a function, and on the right the idea of the proof in words. Here λx. e\lambda x.\,eλx.e denotes the function that takes xxx and returns eee.

Proposition Proof In words
P→PP \to PP→P λp. p\lambda p.\,pλp.p Return the assumption.
A→B→AA \to B \to AA→B→A λa. λb. a\lambda a.\,\lambda b.\,aλa.λb.a Ignore the second assumption.
(A→B)→(B→C)→A→C(A \to B) \to (B \to C) \to A \to C(A→B)→(B→C)→A→C λf. λg. λa. g (f a)\lambda f.\,\lambda g.\,\lambda a.\,g\,(f\,a)λf.λg.λa.g(fa) Compose the two implications.

The third row deserves a second look. To prove that implication is transitive, you assume A→BA \to BA→B and B→CB \to CB→C, and then, given AAA, you apply the first assumption to get BBB and the second to get CCC. The proof term says exactly that: fff and ggg are the assumptions, aaa is the proof of AAA, and g (f a)g\,(f\,a)g(fa) applies them in order. Using an assumption is applying a function; this is the step that distinguishes real reasoning from merely restating hypotheses, and we will return to it in Chapter 3.

Think of a type as a specification and of a term as something that meets it. "There is a term of type AAA" means "the specification AAA can be met". When AAA is a proposition, meeting it is proving it. A type with no terms is an unprovable proposition, which is precisely the role that False\mathsf{False}False will play later.

Quantifiers become dependent functions

The same idea extends to "for all". To prove that B(x)B(x)B(x) holds for every x:Ax : Ax:A, we give a method that, handed any particular xxx, produces a proof of B(x)B(x)B(x). That is again a function, with one twist: its return type depends on the argument. For x=3x = 3x=3 it returns a proof of B(3)B(3)B(3), for x=7x = 7x=7 a proof of B(7)B(7)B(7). A function type whose result type may mention the argument is called a dependent function type, or a Π\PiΠ-type, and is written

Π(x:A). B(x).\Pi(x : A).\,B(x).Π(x:A).B(x).

The ordinary function type A→BA \to BA→B is the special case in which BBB does not mention xxx.

For example, "every proposition implies itself" quantifies over propositions. If Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 is the type of propositions, the statement is

Π(P:Sort 0). P→P,\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P},Π(P:Sort0).P→P,

and its proof is the function that takes a proposition PPP, then a proof ppp of PPP, and returns ppp:

λ(P:Sort 0). λ(p:P). p.\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{p}}.λ(P:Sort0).λ(p:P).p.

Notice that the binders now carry types: λ(P:Sort 0)\lambda(P : \Sort{0})λ(P:Sort0) says that PPP ranges over propositions, and λ(p:P)\lambda(p : P)λ(p:P) says that ppp is a proof of the particular PPP that was passed in. A type checker will need these annotations.

What the kernel does

This gives us the central idea behind a theorem prover.

Proving a theorem means constructing a term of the required type, and verifying a proof means type checking that term.

The kernel does not reason about truth. It implements typing rules, which say when a term has a type, and it mechanically checks that a given term has a given type under those rules. Whether that counts as proof checking depends on whether the typing rules faithfully implement a logic, which is the subject of Chapter 4. Whether the rules are sound, so that no term inhabits the type of a false proposition, is the subject of Chapter 13 and Chapter 14.

This division of labour has a consequence that shapes the design of every serious prover. Everything that finds proofs (tactics, automation, decision procedures, a large language model) can be arbitrarily clever and arbitrarily buggy, because its output is just a term, and the kernel checks the term. The kernel is the only part that must be right. Keeping it small is the whole game, and the kernel in this book is under fifteen hundred lines of Rust, comments included.

Lean 4 works the same way. The theorem command elaborates your statement into a type, tactics build a term of that type, and the kernel checks the term before the theorem is added to the environment. Lean's kernel is larger than ours because it supports universe polymorphism, mutual and nested inductive types, definitional proof irrelevance, and performance features such as caching and lazy unfolding, but its job is the same: decide Γ⊢t:A\Gamma \vdash t : AΓ⊢t:A.

The plan

The chapters of Part I build the kernel for a type theory that is just large enough to serve as a logic.

  1. Chapter 2 fixes the language: universes, variables, Π\PiΠ-types, λ\lambdaλ-abstractions, and application.
  2. Chapter 3 gives the typing rules, one per kind of term plus one that lets computation happen inside types.
  3. Chapter 4 shows that these rules are the rules of a logic, and defines consistency.
  4. Chapter 5 turns the rules into an algorithm and matches it against the Rust implementation.
  5. Chapter 6 runs the algorithm by hand on correct proofs, incorrect proofs, and proofs that need computation.

Two operations are deliberately treated as black boxes until Part III: substitution and definitional equality. Both are easy to state and surprisingly easy to get wrong, and the kernel's correctness depends on them.

What to remember

  • Propositions are types; proofs are terms; t:At : At:A means that ttt proves AAA.
  • Implication is the function type. Using a hypothesis is applying a function.
  • Universal quantification is the dependent function type Π(x:A). B(x)\Pi(x : A).\,B(x)Π(x:A).B(x).
  • A theorem prover's kernel is a type checker. Everything else only produces terms for it to check.

Chapter 2

The Language of Terms

Before a kernel can check anything, it needs a precise language of terms. Ours has five kinds of term, and that is enough to express propositional logic with quantification over propositions. This chapter fixes the grammar, the notational conventions used for the rest of the book, and the Rust type that represents terms.

Five kinds of terms

The core language is a small dependent type theory. Its terms are generated by the grammar

t,A,B  ::=  Sort u  ∣  x  ∣  Π(x:A). B  ∣  λ(x:A). t  ∣  t  st, A, B \;::=\; \Sort{u} \;\mid\; x \;\mid\; \tPi{x}{A}{B} \;\mid\; \tLam{x}{A}{t} \;\mid\; t\;st,A,B::=Sortu∣x∣Π(x:A).B∣λ(x:A).t∣ts

where uuu is a natural number and xxx is a variable name. Each form has a role.

  • Sort u\Sort{u}Sortu is a universe: a type whose elements are themselves types. The number uuu is its level. Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 is the universe of propositions. Chapter 13 explains why there is a whole hierarchy rather than a single universe.
  • xxx is a variable. Its meaning comes from the context in which it appears, either a λ\lambdaλ or Π\PiΠ binder enclosing it or an assumption in the typing context.
  • Π(x:A). B\tPi{x}{A}{B}Π(x:A).B is a Π\PiΠ-type, the dependent function type from Chapter 1. It is the type of functions that take an x:Ax : Ax:A and return something of type BBB, where BBB may mention xxx.
  • λ(x:A). t\tLam{x}{A}{t}λ(x:A).t is a λ\lambdaλ-abstraction, a function that takes an argument xxx of type AAA and returns ttt.
  • t  st\;sts is application of ttt to sss.

The grammar makes no distinction between types and terms. The proposition Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P and its proof λ(P:Sort 0). λ(p:P). p\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{p}}λ(P:Sort0).λ(p:P).p are both terms built from the same five constructors:

λ(P:Sort 0). λ(p:P). p⏟proof:Π(P:Sort 0). P→P⏟proposition, the type of the proof.\underbrace{\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{p}}}_{\text{proof}} \quad : \quad \underbrace{\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}_{\text{proposition, the type of the proof}}.proofλ(P:Sort0).λ(p:P).p​​:proposition, the type of the proofΠ(P:Sort0).P→P​​.

The same two terms, seen as trees, make the shared grammar visible. Every node is one of the five constructors; the name on a Π\PiΠ or λ\lambdaλ node is the variable it binds. Click a node to see the subterm it stands for, or type another term.

Whether a term is a valid type is not a syntactic property. It is decided by the type checker: a term is a type exactly when its own type is a universe (Chapter 5).

Part II adds one more form, the constant ccc, which names something declared in the kernel's signature, such as Nat\mathsf{Nat}Nat or Nat.succ\mathsf{Nat.succ}Nat.succ. Constants behave like free variables whose types come from a global table, and they are never bound. Everything in Part I works without them, so they are introduced when needed, in Chapter 7. The Rust type below already includes them.

Conventions

The book uses the following letters consistently.

Letters Stand for
s,t,a,b,fs, t, a, b, fs,t,a,b,f and A,B,C,TA, B, C, TA,B,C,T (possibly primed or subscripted) terms
x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z and any name bound by Π\PiΠ or λ\lambdaλ variable names
u,v,wu, v, wu,v,w universe levels
Γ\GammaΓ typing contexts (Chapter 3)
Σ\SigmaΣ the signature of constants (Chapter 7)

Three abbreviations keep terms readable.

Arrows. When BBB does not mention xxx, we write A→BA \to BA→B for Π(x:A). B\tPi{x}{A}{B}Π(x:A).B. Ordinary function types are thus a special case of dependent function types, and implication is a special case of universal quantification. In the implementation the binder of an arrow is the reserved name _.

Associativity. Application associates to the left and arrows to the right:

f  a  b  =  (f  a)  b,A→B→C  =  A→(B→C).f\;a\;b \;=\; (f\;a)\;b, \qquad A \to B \to C \;=\; A \to (B \to C).fab=(fa)b,A→B→C=A→(B→C).

Currying. A function of two arguments is a function that takes the first argument and returns a function waiting for the second. For example, λ(a:A). λ(b:B). a\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}}λ(a:A).λ(b:B).a has type A→B→AA \to B \to AA→B→A, and applying it to x:Ax : Ax:A and y:By : By:B is written

(λ(a:A). λ(b:B). a)  x  y  =  ((λ(a:A). λ(b:B). a)  x)  y.(\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}})\;x\;y \;=\; ((\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}})\;x)\;y.(λ(a:A).λ(b:B).a)xy=((λ(a:A).λ(b:B).a)x)y.

The two associativity conventions are designed to fit together: a curried function of type A→B→CA \to B \to CA→B→C applied as f  a  bf\;a\;bfab needs no parentheses on either side.

Currying is why the whole language needs only one-argument functions. A proof of A→B→CA \to B \to CA→B→C is a function that, given a proof of AAA, returns a proof of B→CB \to CB→C, which is itself a function. "Assume AAA and BBB" becomes two nested assumptions, and the two λ\lambdaλs in the proof term mirror them.

Binding and scope

In λ(x:A). t\tLam{x}{A}{t}λ(x:A).t and Π(x:A). B\tPi{x}{A}{B}Π(x:A).B, the variable xxx is bound, and its scope is the body ttt or BBB. The annotation AAA is outside the scope: in λ(x:x). x\tLam{x}{x}{x}λ(x:x).x the xxx in the annotation refers to something outside the term, while the xxx in the body refers to the argument. A variable occurrence that is not inside the scope of a binder for it is free. For example, in λ(x:P). f  x  y\tLam{x}{P}{f\;x\;y}λ(x:P).fxy the variables PPP, fff, and yyy are free and xxx is bound.

Two facts about bound variables matter throughout the book, and both are formalized in Chapter 11.

  1. The name of a bound variable carries no meaning: λ(x:A). x\tLam{x}{A}{x}λ(x:A).x and λ(y:A). y\tLam{y}{A}{y}λ(y:A).y are the same function. Terms that differ only in the names of bound variables are called alpha-equivalent, and a kernel must treat them as equal.
  2. Replacing a variable by a term, which the typing rules and computation both require, must not accidentally bring a free variable under a binder of the same name. Getting this right is called capture-avoiding substitution.

Both facts are easy to state and both have caused real bugs in real proof checkers, which is why they get their own chapter.

In the code

Terms are the Rust enum Term in src/term.rs. There is one variant per kind of term, plus the constants of Part II.

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Term {
    Sort(u64),                          // Sort u
    Var(String),                        // x        (local, bound or in the context)
    Const(String),                      // c        (global, from the signature)
    Pi(String, Box<Term>, Box<Term>),   // Pi (x : A). B
    Lam(String, Box<Term>, Box<Term>),  // fun (x : A). b
    App(Box<Term>, Box<Term>),          // f a
}

Variables are represented by their names as strings, and binders store the bound name. This is the most direct representation and the easiest to read; it is also the one that makes the naming problems of Chapter 11 unavoidable, which is deliberate, because the point of the book is to see those problems and solve them.

The same file provides small constructor functions so that terms can be written without nested Box::new calls: var("x"), const_term("Nat"), app(f, a), pi("x", a, b), lam("x", a, b), and arrow(a, b), which builds pi("_", a, b). Three helpers encode the conventions of this chapter directly.

/// f a_1 ... a_n   (left-associated application)
pub fn apps(f: Term, args: impl IntoIterator<Item = Term>) -> Term {
    args.into_iter().fold(f, app)
}

/// Pi (x_1 : A_1) ... Pi (x_k : A_k). tail   (a telescope of binders)
pub fn telescope(binders: &[(String, Term)], tail: Term) -> Term {
    binders.iter().rev().fold(tail, |body, (name, ty)| pi(name, ty.clone(), body))
}

/// Decomposes t into its spine: a head that is not an application, and its arguments.
/// f a b  becomes  (f, [a, b]);  a non-application becomes  (t, []).
pub fn spine(t: &Term) -> (Term, Vec<Term>) {
    match t {
        Term::App(f, a) => {
            let (head, mut args) = spine(f);
            args.push((**a).clone());
            (head, args)
        }
        _ => (t.clone(), vec![]),
    }
}

apps and spine are inverses of each other: apps(h, args) builds the left-nested application h  a1⋯anh\;a_1 \cdots a_nha1​⋯an​, and spine takes it apart again. The spine view is how the reduction engine of Chapter 12 looks at a term, so it is worth being comfortable with it now. The nested term ((f  a)  b)  c((f\;a)\;b)\;c((fa)b)c has head fff and arguments [a,b,c][a, b, c][a,b,c]; walking down the function side of each application reaches the head, and the arguments collected on the way, read from the inside out, are in the right order.

The surface syntax of the .leanmini scripts used throughout the book writes the same terms as Sort 0, forall (x : A), B, A -> B, fun (x : A) => b, and juxtaposition for application. Appendix E gives the full grammar.

Exercises

Write the proposition "for all propositions PPP and QQQ, PPP implies QQQ implies PPP" as a term, and give a proof term for it.

Solution

The proposition is Π(P:Sort 0). Π(Q:Sort 0). P→Q→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{P \to Q \to P}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(Q:Sort0).P→Q→P, which unfolds to Π(P:Sort 0). Π(Q:Sort 0). Π(_:P). Π(_:Q). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{\_}{P}{\tPi{\_}{Q}{P}}}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(Q:Sort0).Π(_:P).Π(_:Q).P. A proof is λ(P:Sort 0). λ(Q:Sort 0). λ(p:P). λ(q:Q). p\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{\tLam{q}{Q}{p}}}}λ(P:Sort0).λ(Q:Sort0).λ(p:P).λ(q:Q).p. In leanmini syntax:

goal forall (P : Sort 0), forall (Q : Sort 0), P -> Q -> P
exact fun (P : Sort 0) => fun (Q : Sort 0) => fun (p : P) => fun (q : Q) => p
qed

Fully parenthesize f  a  (g  b)  cf\;a\;(g\;b)\;cfa(gb)c and A→(B→C)→DA \to (B \to C) \to DA→(B→C)→D, then give the spine of the first term.

Solution

f  a  (g  b)  c=((f  a)  (g  b))  cf\;a\;(g\;b)\;c = ((f\;a)\;(g\;b))\;cfa(gb)c=((fa)(gb))c, with head fff and arguments [a,  g  b,  c][a,\; g\;b,\; c][a,gb,c]. Note that g  bg\;bgb stays a single argument because of the parentheses. A→(B→C)→D=A→((B→C)→D)A \to (B \to C) \to D = A \to ((B \to C) \to D)A→(B→C)→D=A→((B→C)→D), which is Π(_:A). Π(_:(Π(_:B). C)). D\tPi{\_}{A}{\tPi{\_}{(\tPi{\_}{B}{C})}{D}}Π(_:A).Π(_:(Π(_:B).C)).D.

In λ(x:A). λ(y:x). λ(x:Sort 0). y\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{y}{x}{\tLam{x}{\Sort{0}}{y}}}λ(x:A).λ(y:x).λ(x:Sort0).y, which occurrences of xxx refer to which binder? Which variables are free?

Solution

The xxx in the annotation of yyy refers to the outer binder λ(x:A)\lambda(x : A)λ(x:A), because the inner λ(x:Sort 0)\lambda(x : \Sort{0})λ(x:Sort0) has not been entered yet. The innermost xxx is bound by the inner binder but never used. The only free variable is AAA. This term reappears in Chapter 11, where it breaks a type checker that handles shadowing carelessly.

What to remember

  • Terms are universes Sort u\Sort{u}Sortu, variables, Π\PiΠ-types, λ\lambdaλ-abstractions, and applications. Types and terms share one grammar.
  • A→BA \to BA→B abbreviates a Π\PiΠ-type whose body ignores its variable. Application is left-associative, arrows are right-associative, and functions are curried.
  • Bound variable names are arbitrary, and substitution must avoid capture. Both are handled in Chapter 11.
  • In Rust, Term is an enum with one variant per form, and spine/apps convert between nested applications and a head with an argument list.

Chapter 3

Typing Rules

The kernel's job is to decide the judgment "term ttt has type AAA". This chapter defines that judgment by a small set of inference rules, one for each kind of term and one extra rule that lets computation happen inside types. Reading each rule bottom-up turns it into a recipe for checking a term, and that recipe becomes the algorithm of Chapter 5.

Contexts and judgments

A term such as f  pf\;pfp cannot be checked in isolation: its type depends on what fff and ppp are. A context Γ\GammaΓ records that information. It is an ordered list of assumptions

Γ  =  x1:A1,  x2:A2,  …,  xn:An,\Gamma \;=\; x_1 : A_1,\; x_2 : A_2,\; \ldots,\; x_n : A_n,Γ=x1​:A1​,x2​:A2​,…,xn​:An​,

giving the type of each variable in scope, and dom(Γ)\dom(\Gamma)dom(Γ) denotes the set of names {x1,…,xn}\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}{x1​,…,xn​}. The empty context is written ⋅\cdot⋅.

Order matters. A later type may mention an earlier variable, as in P:Sort 0,  h:PP : \Sort{0},\; h : PP:Sort0,h:P: the assumption h:Ph : Ph:P only makes sense once PPP is known to be a proposition. Names in a context will be required to be distinct, so a context can be used like a dictionary from names to types; but it is a dictionary whose entries depend on each other in sequence.

Two judgments are defined together.

  • ⊢Γ;ok\ctxok{\Gamma}⊢Γ;ok means that the context Γ\GammaΓ is well formed: each assumed type is a genuine type in the context before it.
  • Γ⊢t:A\Gamma \vdash t : AΓ⊢t:A means that under the assumptions in Γ\GammaΓ, the term ttt has type AAA.

Through the Curry-Howard lens, Γ⊢t:A\Gamma \vdash t : AΓ⊢t:A says that ttt is a proof of AAA from the hypotheses Γ\GammaΓ.

The rules

Figure 3.1 lists all the rules. Each rule has premises above the line and a conclusion below it; the conclusion holds whenever every premise does. The rule names on the right are used throughout the book.

Two of the rules use operations on terms that the next chapters treat as black boxes.

Substitution. T-App writes B[x↦a]\subst{B}{x}{a}B[x↦a] for the result of replacing every free occurrence of xxx in BBB by aaa. For example, (P→P)[P↦Q]=Q→Q\subst{(P \to P)}{P}{Q} = Q \to Q(P→P)[P↦Q]=Q→Q. Replacing names inside binders needs care, which Chapter 11 explains; until then the intuitive meaning is enough.

Definitional equality. T-Conv writes A≡BA \conv BA≡B when AAA and BBB are "the same type" in a sense the kernel can decide mechanically. Two kinds of difference are ignored.

  • The names of bound variables. Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P and Π(Q:Sort 0). Q→Q\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{Q \to Q}Π(Q:Sort0).Q→Q state the same proposition. Terms that differ only in this way are alpha-equivalent, written A=αBA \alphaeq BA=α​B.
  • Computation. If Id=λ(X:Sort 0). X\mathit{Id} = \tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}Id=λ(X:Sort0).X, then Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP computes to PPP by plugging PPP in for XXX, so a proof of Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP should count as a proof of PPP. The computation step (λ(x:A). t)  s→βt[x↦s](\tLam{x}{A}{t})\;s \betared \subst{t}{x}{s}(λ(x:A).t)s→β​t[x↦s] is called beta-reduction.

The kernel decides A≡BA \conv BA≡B by computing both sides as far as possible and then checking whether the results are alpha-equivalent. Chapter 12 defines this precisely.

Reading the rules

The rules are best read from the bottom up, as a recipe: to establish the conclusion, establish the premises.

C-Empty and C-Ext. A context is built one assumption at a time, and each new assumption must have a type as its type. The side condition x∉dom(Γ)x \notin \dom(\Gamma)x∈/dom(Γ) forbids two assumptions with the same name. Since the names of bound variables do not matter, this restricts nothing: a binder that would clash can always be renamed first. Chapter 11 shows what goes wrong in a kernel that skips this condition.

T-Sort. Every universe lives in the next one: Sort 0:Sort 1\Sort{0} : \Sort{1}Sort0:Sort1, Sort 1:Sort 2\Sort{1} : \Sort{2}Sort1:Sort2, and so on. Chapter 13 explains why a universe cannot be its own type.

T-Var. A variable has the type the context assigns to it. Logically: use a hypothesis.

T-Pi. Π(x:A). B\tPi{x}{A}{B}Π(x:A).B is a type if AAA is a type and BBB is a type once x:Ax : Ax:A is assumed. The resulting universe is imax(u,v)\imax(u, v)imax(u,v), which is 000 if v=0v = 0v=0 and max⁡(u,v)\max(u, v)max(u,v) otherwise. In words: a Π\PiΠ-type is a proposition whenever its body is a proposition, no matter what it quantifies over; otherwise it lives in the larger of the two universes. Logically, this rule says when A→BA \to BA→B and ∀x:A. B\forall x{:}A.\,B∀x:A.B are well-formed statements.

T-Lam. To build a function from AAA to BBB, assume x:Ax : Ax:A and build a term ttt of type BBB. The body's type BBB may mention xxx, and it is kept as is in the resulting Π\PiΠ-type, which is where dependency enters. Logically, this is the introduction rule for implication and for the universal quantifier: to prove A→BA \to BA→B, assume AAA and prove BBB.

T-App. If fff maps each x:Ax : Ax:A to an element of BBB, and a:Aa : Aa:A, then f  af\;afa has type BBB with xxx replaced by aaa. When BBB does not mention xxx this is modus ponens: from A→BA \to BA→B and AAA, conclude BBB. When it does, it is instantiation of a universal statement. For example, if f:Π(n:Nat). n+0=nf : \tPi{n}{\Nat}{n + 0 = n}f:Π(n:Nat).n+0=n, then f  3:3+0=3f\;3 : 3 + 0 = 3f3:3+0=3 (natural numbers arrive in Chapter 7).

T-Conv. Types that are equal up to computation are interchangeable: from h:Id  Ph : \mathit{Id}\;Ph:IdP we may conclude h:Ph : Ph:P. The premise Γ⊢B:Sort u\Gamma \vdash B : \Sort{u}Γ⊢B:Sortu ensures that the new type is itself a type. This is the only rule whose use is not determined by the shape of ttt, a fact that matters for the algorithm in Chapter 5.

Each rule is a small piece of common sense about functions. T-Lam says how to make a function; T-App says how to use one; T-Pi says when a function type makes sense; T-Var and T-Sort say what the basic things are; and T-Conv says that computing inside a type does not change what it means. There is nothing specifically "logical" in the rules. The logic is a consequence of reading them through Curry-Howard, which Chapter 4 makes precise.

Why application matters

It is tempting to think that the interesting rules are the ones that build things (T-Lam, T-Pi) and that T-App is bookkeeping. The opposite is closer to the truth. Without T-App a hypothesis can be returned but never used. Roughly, the provable propositions would then be only those whose conclusion is literally one of the hypotheses, such as P→Q→PP \to Q \to PP→Q→P. Composition,

(P→Q)→(Q→R)→P→R,(P \to Q) \to (Q \to R) \to P \to R,(P→Q)→(Q→R)→P→R,

has the proof λ(f:P→Q). λ(g:Q→R). λ(p:P). g (f p)\tLam{f}{P \to Q}{\tLam{g}{Q \to R}{\tLam{p}{P}{g\,(f\,p)}}}λ(f:P→Q).λ(g:Q→R).λ(p:P).g(fp), which applies fff and then ggg. Every proof that does more than restate an assumption goes through T-App, and in a dependent type theory T-App is also where substitution, and therefore most of the subtlety, lives.

A first derivation

A derivation is a tree of rule instances whose root is the judgment being established. Here is the derivation that λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:P). h\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:P).h proves Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P. Write Γ1=P:Sort 0\Gamma_1 = P : \Sort{0}Γ1​=P:Sort0 and Γ2=Γ1,h:P\Gamma_2 = \Gamma_1, h : PΓ2​=Γ1​,h:P, and omit the well-formedness premises ⊢Γ;ok\ctxok{\Gamma}⊢Γ;ok, which are routine.

⋅⊢Sort 0:Sort 1;(T-Sort)Γ1⊢P:Sort 0;(T-Var)Γ2⊢h:P;(T-Var)Γ1⊢λ(h:P). h:Π(h:P). P;(T-Lam)⋅⊢λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:P). h:Π(P:Sort 0). Π(h:P). P;(T-Lam)\dfrac{ \dfrac{}{\cdot \vdash \Sort{0} : \Sort{1}}\rulename{T-Sort} \qquad \dfrac{ \dfrac{}{\Gamma_1 \vdash P : \Sort{0}}\rulename{T-Var} \qquad \dfrac{}{\Gamma_2 \vdash h : P}\rulename{T-Var} }{\Gamma_1 \vdash \tLam{h}{P}{h} : \tPi{h}{P}{P}}\rulename{T-Lam} }{\cdot \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}}\rulename{T-Lam}⋅⊢λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:P).h:Π(P:Sort0).Π(h:P).P⋅⊢Sort0:Sort1​;(T-Sort)Γ1​⊢λ(h:P).h:Π(h:P).PΓ1​⊢P:Sort0​;(T-Var)Γ2​⊢h:P​;(T-Var)​;(T-Lam)​;(T-Lam)

The kernel builds exactly this tree. Below, each node is one application of a rule, with the judgment it establishes; switch to the call view to read it top-down as the recursion that produces it. Replace the term with your own to see which rules fire.

Two observations. First, the shape of the tree follows the shape of the term: a λ\lambdaλ at the root, a λ\lambdaλ below it, variables at the leaves. Second, the type at the root is Π(P:Sort 0). Π(h:P). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(h:P).P, whereas the stated proposition was Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P. These differ only in the name of a bound variable (hhh versus the anonymous _ of the arrow), so they are alpha-equivalent, and T-Conv bridges the gap. Chapter 6 revisits this example with the algorithm.

The rules of this chapter are implemented by Kernel::infer and Kernel::check in src/typecheck.rs, which Chapter 5 reads line by line. Contexts are the Rust type Context = Vec<(String, Term)> in src/declaration.rs: a vector of name-type pairs, searched from the end so that the most recent assumption for a name wins.

Exercises

Which rule, applied bottom-up, handles each of the following judgments, and what premises does it produce? (a) Γ⊢λ(x:A). x:A→A\Gamma \vdash \tLam{x}{A}{x} : A \to AΓ⊢λ(x:A).x:A→A. (b) Γ⊢Sort 2:Sort 3\Gamma \vdash \Sort{2} : \Sort{3}Γ⊢Sort2:Sort3. (c) Γ⊢f  a:B\Gamma \vdash f\;a : BΓ⊢fa:B where f:A→Bf : A \to Bf:A→B.

Solution

(a) T-Lam, with premises Γ⊢A:Sort u\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u}Γ⊢A:Sortu for some uuu and Γ,x:A⊢x:A\Gamma, x : A \vdash x : AΓ,x:A⊢x:A; the latter is T-Var. The resulting type is Π(x:A). A\tPi{x}{A}{A}Π(x:A).A, which is A→AA \to AA→A up to the binder name. (b) T-Sort, with the single premise ⊢Γ;ok\ctxok{\Gamma}⊢Γ;ok. (c) T-App, with premises Γ⊢f:Π(_:A). B\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{\_}{A}{B}Γ⊢f:Π(_:A).B and Γ⊢a:A\Gamma \vdash a : AΓ⊢a:A. The conclusion is B[_↦a]=B\subst{B}{\_}{a} = BB[_↦a]=B, since _ does not occur in BBB.

Using T-Pi, compute the universe of Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P and of Π(A:Sort 1). A→A\tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{A \to A}Π(A:Sort1).A→A.

Solution

For the first, Sort 0:Sort 1\Sort{0} : \Sort{1}Sort0:Sort1 so u=1u = 1u=1, and P→P:Sort 0P \to P : \Sort{0}P→P:Sort0 (by T-Pi again with u=v=0u = v = 0u=v=0) so v=0v = 0v=0. Hence the universe is Sort imax(1,0)=Sort 0\Sort{\imax(1, 0)} = \Sort{0}Sortimax(1,0)=Sort0: a statement quantifying over all propositions is itself a proposition. For the second, u=2u = 2u=2 and A→A:Sort 1A \to A : \Sort{1}A→A:Sort1 so v=1v = 1v=1, giving Sort imax(2,1)=Sort 2\Sort{\imax(2,1)} = \Sort{2}Sortimax(2,1)=Sort2. Chapter 13 explains the asymmetry.

What to remember

  • A context is an ordered list of distinct assumptions x:Ax : Ax:A; the judgment Γ⊢t:A\Gamma \vdash t : AΓ⊢t:A says that ttt has type AAA under those assumptions.
  • There is one rule per kind of term, plus T-Conv, which identifies types up to computation and bound-variable renaming.
  • T-App is where hypotheses are used and where substitution happens; T-Conv is the only rule not triggered by the shape of the term.
  • Substitution and definitional equality are treated as black boxes until Part III.

Chapter 4

The Typing Rules as a Logic

Chapter 3 presented eight typing rules and promised that they are rules of logic. This chapter keeps that promise. It picks a concrete logic, translates its formulas into types, and shows that every proof in the logic becomes a term that the kernel accepts. It then identifies the property, consistency, that a kernel must have before it can be trusted at all.

A logic to compare against

The logic has formulas built from proposition variables P,Q,…P, Q, \ldotsP,Q,… by implication and by quantification over propositions:

φ,ψ  ::=  P  ∣  φ→ψ  ∣  ∀P. φ\varphi, \psi \;::=\; P \;\mid\; \varphi \to \psi \;\mid\; \forall P.\,\varphiφ,ψ::=P∣φ→ψ∣∀P.φ

This is second-order propositional logic: "second-order" because ∀\forall∀ ranges over propositions rather than over individuals. It is small, but far from trivial. Conjunction, disjunction, negation, and falsity can all be defined inside it, for example ⊥=∀P. P\bot = \forall P.\,P⊥=∀P.P and φ∧ψ=∀R. (φ→ψ→R)→R\varphi \wedge \psi = \forall R.\,(\varphi \to \psi \to R) \to Rφ∧ψ=∀R.(φ→ψ→R)→R.

Proofs in this logic are natural-deduction derivations of judgments Δ⊢φ\Delta \vdash \varphiΔ⊢φ, where Δ\DeltaΔ is a list of hypotheses. The rules are the ones in the left column of Figure 4.1 below: use a hypothesis, introduce and eliminate implication, introduce and eliminate the quantifier.

Translating formulas into types

Each formula translates to a type, written φ∗\varphi^\astφ∗:

P∗=P,(φ→ψ)∗=φ∗→ψ∗,(∀P. φ)∗=Π(P:Sort 0). φ∗.P^\ast = P, \qquad (\varphi \to \psi)^\ast = \varphi^\ast \to \psi^\ast, \qquad (\forall P.\,\varphi)^\ast = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}.P∗=P,(φ→ψ)∗=φ∗→ψ∗,(∀P.φ)∗=Π(P:Sort0).φ∗.

A proposition variable becomes a type variable, implication becomes the function type, and quantification over propositions becomes a Π\PiΠ-type over Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0.

A list of hypotheses translates to a context. Besides one assumption hi:φi∗h_i : \varphi_i^\asthi​:φi∗​ per hypothesis, the context must declare the proposition variables that occur anywhere in the judgment:

(φ1,…,φn)∗  =  P1:Sort 0,…,Pk:Sort 0,  h1:φ1∗,…,hn:φn∗,(\varphi_1, \ldots, \varphi_n)^\ast \;=\; P_1 : \Sort{0}, \ldots, P_k : \Sort{0},\; h_1 : \varphi_1^\ast, \ldots, h_n : \varphi_n^\ast,(φ1​,…,φn​)∗=P1​:Sort0,…,Pk​:Sort0,h1​:φ1∗​,…,hn​:φn∗​,

where P1,…,PkP_1, \ldots, P_kP1​,…,Pk​ are the proposition variables free in Δ\DeltaΔ or in the conclusion φ\varphiφ of the judgment Δ⊢φ\Delta \vdash \varphiΔ⊢φ being translated, and h1,…,hnh_1, \ldots, h_nh1​,…,hn​ are fresh names. The conclusion must be included because a variable may occur only there, as PPP does in ⋅⊢P→P\cdot \vdash P \to P⋅⊢P→P.

Figure 4.1 places each logical rule next to the typing rule that implements it. The premises that merely check that a type is well formed are omitted.

In the ∀\forall∀-intro row, the logic's side condition P∉FV(Δ)P \notin \FV(\Delta)P∈/FV(Δ) guarantees that no hypothesis mentions PPP, so the typing rule may add P:Sort 0P : \Sort{0}P:Sort0 after the hypotheses without breaking the dependency order of the context.

In the ∀\forall∀-elim row, the premise ψ∗:Sort 0\psi^\ast : \Sort{0}ψ∗:Sort0 holds for every formula ψ\psiψ, even one that contains ∀\forall∀, because T-Pi places every translated formula in Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0. (The imax\imaximax in T-Pi is responsible: Π(P:Sort 0). φ∗\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}Π(P:Sort0).φ∗ lands in Sort imax(1,0)=Sort 0\Sort{\imax(1, 0)} = \Sort{0}Sortimax(1,0)=Sort0.) So a universal statement can be instantiated with any formula, as it can in the logic. Chapter 13 returns to this point, which is called impredicativity.

Proofs are terms

Theorem 4.1 (Proofs are terms). If Δ⊢φ\Delta \vdash \varphiΔ⊢φ is provable in the logic, then Δ∗⊢t:φ∗\Delta^\ast \vdash t : \varphi^\astΔ∗⊢t:φ∗ for some term ttt.

Figure 4.1 turns each step of a logical proof into a step of a typing derivation, so every proof becomes a term by induction on the proof. Appendix A states the theorem with the scoping of proposition variables made explicit and gives the full proof.

The theorem says that the type checker can check every proof of the logic. For the kernel to be trustworthy, we also need the opposite guarantee: it must not accept a term for a proposition that the logic refutes.

Consistency

Define ⊥=∀P. P\bot = \forall P.\,P⊥=∀P.P, "everything holds". No proof of ⊥\bot⊥ exists in the logic: if each proposition variable is read as true or false, every rule preserves truth under every reading, but ∀P. P\forall P.\,P∀P.P is false under the reading that makes some PPP false.

The type theory should agree. That is, no closed term should have the type

⊥∗  =  Π(P:Sort 0). P.\bot^\ast \;=\; \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}.⊥∗=Π(P:Sort0).P.

A closed term ttt of this type would be a disaster: for every proposition C:Sort 0C : \Sort{0}C:Sort0, the application t  Ct\;CtC would have type CCC, so every proposition would be provable and the kernel would be worthless.

Definition 4.2 (Consistency). A type system is consistent if no closed term has type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P.

Consistency is the property that every design decision in this book must preserve. In particular, a design for universes is acceptable only if the system remains consistent; Chapter 13 shows a natural-looking design that fails this test, and Chapter 14 states consistency for our system as Theorem 14.5.

One might hope for the full converse of Theorem 4.1: every term of type φ∗\varphi^\astφ∗ comes from a proof of φ\varphiφ. That stronger property is called conservativity, and it is harder to establish here, because Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 also contains types that are not translations of formulas, such as Π(F:Sort 0→Sort 0). F  P→F  P\tPi{F}{\Sort{0} \to \Sort{0}}{F\;P \to F\;P}Π(F:Sort0→Sort0).FP→FP, and a term may pass through them on its way to φ∗\varphi^\astφ∗. We do not need conservativity. Consistency is what makes the kernel's "yes" worth something, and it is enough.

Why single out Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P rather than, say, 0=10 = 10=1? Because it is the universal counterfeit: any proof of it can be converted into a proof of anything else by a single application. If some other absurd statement had a proof, that proof could be used to build a proof of Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P as well, so ruling out this one type rules out all of them.

Exercises

Translate the formula ∀P. ∀Q. (P→Q)→P→Q\forall P.\,\forall Q.\,(P \to Q) \to P \to Q∀P.∀Q.(P→Q)→P→Q to a type, and write the proof term that Figure 4.1 produces for the natural-deduction proof "assume P→QP \to QP→Q and PPP; apply the first to the second".

Solution

The type is Π(P:Sort 0). Π(Q:Sort 0). (P→Q)→P→Q\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{(P \to Q) \to P \to Q}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(Q:Sort0).(P→Q)→P→Q. Two ∀\forall∀-intros give two outer λ\lambdaλs over Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0, two →\to→-intros give λ(f:P→Q)\lambda(f : P \to Q)λ(f:P→Q) and λ(p:P)\lambda(p : P)λ(p:P), and →\to→-elim gives the body f  pf\;pfp: λ(P:Sort 0). λ(Q:Sort 0). λ(f:P→Q). λ(p:P). f  p\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{f}{P \to Q}{\tLam{p}{P}{f\;p}}}}λ(P:Sort0).λ(Q:Sort0).λ(f:P→Q).λ(p:P).fp.

Show that from t:Π(P:Sort 0). Pt : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}t:Π(P:Sort0).P one can build a term of type Π(P:Sort 0). Π(Q:Sort 0). P→Q\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{P \to Q}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(Q:Sort0).P→Q, "every proposition implies every other".

Solution

λ(P:Sort 0). λ(Q:Sort 0). λ(p:P). t  Q\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{t\;Q}}}λ(P:Sort0).λ(Q:Sort0).λ(p:P).tQ. The hypothesis ppp is ignored and t  Q:Qt\;Q : QtQ:Q by T-App. This is the sense in which a proof of ⊥∗\bot^\ast⊥∗ proves everything.

What to remember

  • Second-order propositional logic translates into the type theory: →\to→ becomes the function type, ∀P\forall P∀P becomes Π(P:Sort 0)\Pi(P : \Sort{0})Π(P:Sort0), hypotheses become context entries.
  • Theorem 4.1: every proof in the logic becomes a well-typed term. The translation is rule by rule (Figure 4.1).
  • The kernel is trustworthy only if it is consistent: no closed term of type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P.
  • Impredicativity, via imax\imaximax, is what lets a universal statement be instantiated by any formula, including itself.

Chapter 5

A Type Checking Algorithm

The typing rules say which judgments hold; they do not say how to find out. This chapter turns them into an algorithm. The standard trick is to split the work into two mutually recursive functions, one that computes the type of a term and one that compares a computed type with an expected one, and to use definitional equality only in the second. The result is a few dozen lines of Rust.

From rules to an algorithm

Seven of the eight rules of Figure 3.1 are syntax-directed: looking at the term tells you which rule applies. A universe triggers T-Sort, a variable T-Var, a Π\PiΠ T-Pi, a λ\lambdaλ T-Lam, an application T-App. T-Conv is the exception. It can be applied to any term at any point, so a program cannot tell from the term when to use it, and a naive search for a derivation would have to guess.

The standard solution [Barendregt 1992] is to split type checking into two functions:

  • Infer(Γ,t)\Infer(\Gamma, t)Infer(Γ,t) computes the type of ttt in Γ\GammaΓ, following the syntax-directed rules, or fails.
  • Check(Γ,t,T)\Check(\Gamma, t, T)Check(Γ,t,T) verifies that ttt has the expected type TTT: it infers a type and compares it with TTT using definitional equality.

T-Conv is applied in exactly one place, inside Check\CheckCheck. There are two further places where a type must have a particular shape, a Π\PiΠ in T-App and a universe in the premises of T-Pi and T-Lam. There the algorithm computes the inferred type just far enough to see its outermost form.

The algorithm uses two functions on terms whose definitions are postponed to Chapter 12:

  • Whnf(T)\Whnf(T)Whnf(T) computes TTT until its outermost shape is visible. For example, Whnf(Id  (P→P))=P→P\Whnf(\mathit{Id}\;(P \to P)) = P \to PWhnf(Id(P→P))=P→P, which is a Π\PiΠ.
  • IsDefEq(A,B)\IsDefEq(A, B)IsDefEq(A,B) decides A≡BA \conv BA≡B.

The algorithm

Algorithm 5.1 is written in pseudocode close to the Rust. Each case of Infer\InferInfer is annotated with the rule it implements.

Algorithm 5.1. Type inference and checking.

Infer(Γ, t):
  if t = Sort u:                                        -- T-Sort
      return Sort (u + 1)
  if t = x:                                             -- T-Var
      if (x : A) ∈ Γ: return A  else fail "unbound variable"
  if t = Π(x : A). B:                                   -- T-Pi
      u ← InferSort(Γ, A)
      (x', B') ← Freshen(Γ, x, B)
      v ← InferSort((Γ, x' : A), B')
      return Sort (imax(u, v))
  if t = λ(x : A). s:                                   -- T-Lam
      InferSort(Γ, A)
      (x', s') ← Freshen(Γ, x, s)
      B ← Infer((Γ, x' : A), s')
      return Π(x' : A). B
  if t = f a:                                           -- T-App
      T ← Whnf(Infer(Γ, f))
      if T = Π(x : A). B:
          Check(Γ, a, A)
          return B[x ↦ a]
      else fail "not a function"

Check(Γ, t, T):                                         -- T-Conv
  T' ← Infer(Γ, t)
  if IsDefEq(T', T): return  else fail "type mismatch"

InferSort(Γ, A):
  T ← Whnf(Infer(Γ, A))
  if T = Sort u: return u  else fail "expected a type"

Freshen(Γ, x, b):
  if x ∈ dom(Γ):
      choose x' ∉ dom(Γ) ∪ FV(b)
      return (x', b[x ↦ x'])
  else return (x, b)

The algorithm has the following properties.

  • Syntax-directed. Each case of Infer\InferInfer corresponds to exactly one rule of Figure 3.1. Finding a proof may be hard, but checking a given proof is mechanical: there is never a choice to make.
  • T-Conv is never applied on its own. It happens inside Check\CheckCheck, the only place where an inferred type meets an expected one.
  • InferSort\InferSortInferSort is how the kernel decides whether a term is a type. A term AAA is a type exactly when its type computes to a universe. A λ\lambdaλ-abstraction, for instance, is never a type, because its inferred type is always a Π\PiΠ.
  • Freshen\FreshenFreshen implements the side condition of C-Ext. It renames a binder whose name is already in the context. Chapter 11 shows a term that makes the kernel unsound without this step.
  • Contexts stay well formed. Starting from the empty context, every context the algorithm builds is well formed, because an assumption is added only after InferSort\InferSortInferSort has succeeded on its type. A caller that starts from a non-empty context must check that context separately.
  • Termination depends on Whnf\WhnfWhnf and IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq terminating, which holds for well-typed terms by strong normalization (Chapter 14).

The division into Infer\InferInfer and Check\CheckCheck is sometimes called bidirectional type checking. The intuition is that information flows in two directions. Inference flows up from the leaves: a variable knows its type, an application computes its type from its parts. Checking flows down from an expectation: the user says "this term should have this type", and the comparison happens at the root. In our kernel, every term can be inferred, so checking is just inference plus one comparison; in richer systems some terms can only be checked, not inferred.

In the code

Algorithm 5.1 is Kernel::infer, Kernel::check, and Kernel::infer_sort in src/typecheck.rs; Freshen is the helper rename_binder_if_needed in the same file. The complete infer follows, with the constants case of Part II included; unfold it when you want to compare line by line.

the complete infer function (about fifty lines) 
pub fn infer(&self, ctx: &Context, t: &Term) -> Result<Term> {
    match t {
        // T-Sort
        Term::Sort(u) => Ok(Term::Sort(u.checked_add(1).ok_or("universe overflow")?)),
        // T-Var
        Term::Var(x) => ctx
            .iter()
            .rev()
            .find(|(name, _)| name == x)
            .map(|(_, ty)| ty.clone())
            .ok_or_else(|| format!("unbound local: {x}")),
        // T-Const (Chapter 7)
        Term::Const(c) => self
            .decls
            .get(c)
            .map(|decl| decl.ty.clone())
            .ok_or_else(|| format!("unknown constant: {c}")),
        // T-Pi: Sort 0 is impredicative.
        Term::Pi(x, domain, body) => {
            let domain_level = self.infer_sort(ctx, domain)?;
            let (x, body) = rename_binder_if_needed(ctx, x, body);
            let mut extended = ctx.clone();
            extended.push((x, (**domain).clone()));
            let body_level = self.infer_sort(&extended, &body)?;
            Ok(Term::Sort(if body_level == 0 {
                0
            } else {
                domain_level.max(body_level)
            }))
        }
        // T-Lam
        Term::Lam(x, domain, body) => {
            self.infer_sort(ctx, domain)?;
            let (x, body) = rename_binder_if_needed(ctx, x, body);
            let mut extended = ctx.clone();
            extended.push((x.clone(), (**domain).clone()));
            let body_type = self.infer(&extended, &body)?;
            Ok(Term::Pi(x, domain.clone(), Box::new(body_type)))
        }
        // T-App
        Term::App(f, a) => match self.whnf(&self.infer(ctx, f)?)? {
            Term::Pi(x, domain, codomain) => {
                self.check(ctx, a, &domain)?;
                Ok(subst(&codomain, &x, a))
            }
            ty => Err(format!("application of non-function: {ty:?}")),
        },
    }
}

A few details are worth noticing against the pseudocode.

  • The context lookup in the variable case searches from the end (.rev()). Because rename_binder_if_needed keeps names distinct, there is never more than one match, but searching from the end is the right behaviour if a caller passes a context with repeated names.
  • The imax\imaximax of T-Pi is the if body_level == 0 expression: a Π\PiΠ whose body is a proposition is a proposition, otherwise it lives in the maximum of the two levels.
  • The universe level is a u64 and checked_add guards against overflow. No real proof comes anywhere near level 2642^{64}264, but a kernel should not have undefined behaviour on any input.
  • The application case calls whnf on the inferred type of f before matching on it, exactly as the pseudocode does. Without this, a function whose type is written as Id  (A→B)\mathit{Id}\;(A \to B)Id(A→B) could not be applied.

The remaining two functions are short.

/// Gamma |- t : expected, using T-Conv to compare the inferred type.
pub fn check(&self, ctx: &Context, t: &Term, expected: &Term) -> Result<()> {
    self.infer_sort(ctx, expected)?;
    let actual = self.infer(ctx, t)?;
    if self.is_def_eq(&actual, expected)? {
        Ok(())
    } else {
        Err(format!("type mismatch: actual {actual:?}, expected {expected:?}"))
    }
}

/// Infers the type of t and requires it to be a universe Sort u. Returns u.
pub fn infer_sort(&self, ctx: &Context, t: &Term) -> Result<u64> {
    match self.whnf(&self.infer(ctx, t)?)? {
        Term::Sort(u) => Ok(u),
        other => Err(format!("expected a type, got {other:?}")),
    }
}

check begins with infer_sort(ctx, expected). That is the premise Γ⊢B:Sort u\Gamma \vdash B : \Sort{u}Γ⊢B:Sortu of T-Conv: the expected type must itself be a type. The pseudocode omits it because callers inside the algorithm always pass types that have already been checked, but the public check is also called with user-supplied statements, so the Rust version verifies it.

Finally, Freshen:

fn rename_binder_if_needed(ctx: &Context, x: &str, body: &Term) -> (String, Term) {
    if !ctx.iter().any(|(name, _)| name == x) {
        return (x.into(), body.clone());
    }
    let mut used = all_names(body);
    for (name, ty) in ctx {
        used.insert(name.clone());
        used.extend(all_names(ty));
    }
    let renamed = fresh(x, &used);
    let renamed_body = subst(body, x, &var(&renamed));
    (renamed, renamed_body)
}

The set of names to avoid is larger than the pseudocode's dom(Γ)∪FV(b)\dom(\Gamma) \cup \FV(b)dom(Γ)∪FV(b): it includes every name appearing anywhere in the body and in the context's types, bound or free. Avoiding more names than necessary is always safe, and it keeps the renamed term readable. fresh appends primes until the name is unused, so a clash on x produces x'.

Watching Infer run

The explorer below runs the algorithm on a term and records every recursive call: which case of Infer\InferInfer it entered, in which context, and what it returned. The notes report the hidden work, such as Whnf\WhnfWhnf exposing a Π\PiΠ or Freshen\FreshenFreshen renaming a binder. The context field accepts assumptions such as Q : Sort 0; q : Q, separated by semicolons.

How a proof is checked

To verify that a term ttt proves a theorem TTT, the kernel runs Check(⋅,t,T)\Check(\cdot, t, T)Check(⋅,t,T) in the empty context. In the script language this is what qed does: the tactics of Chapter 10 assemble a term, and qed hands it to check together with the statement given by goal. Everything between is untrusted.

The next chapter runs Infer\InferInfer and Check\CheckCheck by hand on several terms, including one that is well typed but does not prove what it claims to.

Exercises

Trace Infer(⋅,λ(A:Sort 1). λ(a:A). a)\Infer(\cdot, \tLam{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tLam{a}{A}{a}})Infer(⋅,λ(A:Sort1).λ(a:A).a) and give the result and its universe.

Solution

InferSort(⋅,Sort 1)\InferSort(\cdot, \Sort{1})InferSort(⋅,Sort1) returns 222. The context becomes A:Sort 1A : \Sort{1}A:Sort1. For the inner λ\lambdaλ, InferSort(A:Sort 1,A)\InferSort(A : \Sort{1}, A)InferSort(A:Sort1,A) returns 111, the context becomes A:Sort 1,a:AA : \Sort{1}, a : AA:Sort1,a:A, and Infer\InferInfer returns AAA for the body. So the inner result is Π(a:A). A\tPi{a}{A}{A}Π(a:A).A and the outer result is Π(A:Sort 1). Π(a:A). A\tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tPi{a}{A}{A}}Π(A:Sort1).Π(a:A).A. Running InferSort\InferSortInferSort on that type gives imax(2,imax(1,1))=2\imax(2, \imax(1, 1)) = 2imax(2,imax(1,1))=2, so the type lives in Sort 2\Sort{2}Sort2.

Why does the Π\PiΠ case of Infer\InferInfer call Freshen\FreshenFreshen even though a Π\PiΠ-type is "just a type"? Give a term where skipping it would change the result.

Solution

The body of a Π\PiΠ is checked in an extended context, so the same shadowing problem arises as for λ\lambdaλ. For Γ=x:Sort 0,y:x\Gamma = x : \Sort{0}, y : xΓ=x:Sort0,y:x, the type Π(x:Sort 1). y\tPi{x}{\Sort{1}}{y}Π(x:Sort1).y should fail, because y:xy : xy:x where xxx is the outer proposition and a proposition is not a universe. Without renaming, the inner x:Sort 1x : \Sort{1}x:Sort1 would be found first by the reversed lookup, making yyy's type appear to be Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1-valued, and the result would be wrong. With renaming the inner binder becomes x′x'x′ and the body still refers to the outer xxx.

What to remember

  • Infer\InferInfer follows the shape of the term; Check\CheckCheck infers and then compares with IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq. T-Conv lives only inside Check\CheckCheck.
  • Whnf\WhnfWhnf exposes the outermost shape of a type where a Π\PiΠ or a universe is required.
  • InferSort\InferSortInferSort is the test "is this term a type?": its type must compute to a universe.
  • Freshen\FreshenFreshen renames binders that would shadow a context entry. It is a correctness requirement, not a convenience.
  • src/typecheck.rs is a direct transcription, about one hundred lines.

Chapter 6

Worked Examples

This chapter runs Algorithm 5.1 by hand on a handful of small terms and relates each run to the typing rules. The examples are chosen to show the algorithm doing each of its jobs: building a derivation, catching a wrong proof, using a hypothesis, instantiating a universal statement, and computing inside a type. Every trace below can be reproduced in the kernel with the playgrounds.

To verify a proof ttt of a theorem TTT, the kernel calls Check(⋅,t,T)\Check(\cdot, t, T)Check(⋅,t,T), which calls Infer(⋅,t)\Infer(\cdot, t)Infer(⋅,t) and compares the result with TTT. The traces show the recursive calls that Infer\InferInfer makes, with the typing rule each call corresponds to. Expand or collapse the nodes to follow the recursion.

A wrong proof

Suppose a user claims that t=λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:P). Pt = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{P}}t=λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:P).P proves Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P. The body returns the proposition PPP instead of the proof hhh. The kernel calls Check(⋅,t,Π(P:Sort 0). P→P)\Check(\cdot, t, \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P})Check(⋅,t,Π(P:Sort0).P→P), which first calls Infer\InferInfer. The calls are the same as above, except that the last one, Infer(Γ2,P)\Infer(\Gamma_2, P)Infer(Γ2​,P), returns Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0. So Infer\InferInfer succeeds, with

Infer(⋅,t)  =  Π(P:Sort 0). Π(h:P). Sort 0.\Infer(\cdot, t) \;=\; \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}}}.Infer(⋅,t)=Π(P:Sort0).Π(h:P).Sort0.

The term ttt is perfectly well typed; it is just not a proof of the claimed proposition. Check\CheckCheck then compares the two types. Neither can compute any further, and no renaming of bound variables makes them equal: the innermost body is Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 on one side and PPP on the other. So IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq fails and Check\CheckCheck reports a type mismatch. (Chapter 11 replays this comparison step by step with the algorithm that IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq uses.)

The error is found only because the user stated the proposition to be proved. A kernel that only ran Infer\InferInfer would accept ttt and silently assign it a different type. This is why goal comes first in every script, and why qed checks against it.

goal forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P
exact fun (P : Sort 0) => fun (h : P) => P
qed

"Well typed" and "proves the theorem" are different properties. Every closed term that passes Infer\InferInfer proves something, namely its inferred type. The kernel's job is to confirm that the something is what was claimed. Tactics (Chapter 10) are designed so that the claim is fixed before any term is built.

Using a hypothesis: modus ponens

The examples so far never apply a function. Consider checking

t=λ(P:Sort 0). λ(Q:Sort 0). λ(f:P→Q). λ(p:P). f  pagainstΠ(P:Sort 0). Π(Q:Sort 0). (P→Q)→P→Q,t = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{f}{P \to Q}{\tLam{p}{P}{f\;p}}}} \quad\text{against}\quad \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{(P \to Q) \to P \to Q}},t=λ(P:Sort0).λ(Q:Sort0).λ(f:P→Q).λ(p:P).fpagainstΠ(P:Sort0).Π(Q:Sort0).(P→Q)→P→Q,

which says "if PPP implies QQQ and PPP holds, then QQQ holds". The four λ\lambdaλs extend the context to Γ=P:Sort 0,  Q:Sort 0,  f:P→Q,  p:P\Gamma = P : \Sort{0},\; Q : \Sort{0},\; f : P \to Q,\; p : PΓ=P:Sort0,Q:Sort0,f:P→Q,p:P exactly as before.
