Instantiating a universal statement

In a dependent application the substitution in T-App does real work. Let id=λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:P). h\mathit{id} = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}id=λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:P).h be the proof from the first example, and let Γ=Q:Sort 0\Gamma = Q : \Sort{0}Γ=Q:Sort0. Then Infer(Γ,id  Q)\Infer(\Gamma, \mathit{id}\;Q)Infer(Γ,idQ):

  • Infer(Γ,  id  Q)\Infer(\Gamma,\; \mathit{id}\;Q)Infer(Γ,idQ) T-App
    • Infer(Γ,  id)\Infer(\Gamma,\; \mathit{id})Infer(Γ,id) returns Π(P:Sort 0). Π(h:P). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(h:P).P, already a Π\PiΠ T-Lam
    • Check(Γ,  Q,  Sort 0)\Check(\Gamma,\; Q,\; \Sort{0})Check(Γ,Q,Sort0) succeeds T-Var
    • returns (Π(h:P). P)[P↦Q]=Π(h:Q). Q\subst{(\tPi{h}{P}{P})}{P}{Q} = \tPi{h}{Q}{Q}(Π(h:P).P)[P↦Q]=Π(h:Q).Q, that is, Q→QQ \to QQ→Q

Logically, this is ∀\forall∀-elimination: from "every proposition implies itself" we obtain "QQQ implies QQQ". The type of the result depends on the value of the argument QQQ, which is exactly what the dependent Π\PiΠ-type expresses and exactly why T-App substitutes. In the explorer, id\mathit{id}id is a defined constant and QQQ comes from the context; the note on the T-App node records the substitution.

def id : forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P := fun (P : Sort 0) => fun (h : P) => h

Conversion

Recall Id=λ(X:Sort 0). X\mathit{Id} = \tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}Id=λ(X:Sort0).X from Chapter 3. The core system has no definitions, so Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP is shorthand for the term (λ(X:Sort 0). X)  P(\tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X})\;P(λ(X:Sort0).X)P. Consider checking

t=λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:Id  P). hagainstΠ(P:Sort 0). P→P.t = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{h}} \quad\text{against}\quad \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}.t=λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:IdP).hagainstΠ(P:Sort0).P→P.

Infer\InferInfer first checks that the annotation Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP is a type. InferSort(Γ1,Id  P)\InferSort(\Gamma_1, \mathit{Id}\;P)InferSort(Γ1​,IdP) reaches the application case of Infer\InferInfer: the function λ(X:Sort 0). X\tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}λ(X:Sort0).X has type Π(X:Sort 0). Sort 0\tPi{X}{\Sort{0}}{\Sort{0}}Π(X:Sort0).Sort0, the argument PPP passes Check(Γ1,P,Sort 0)\Check(\Gamma_1, P, \Sort{0})Check(Γ1​,P,Sort0), and the result is Sort 0[X↦P]=Sort 0\subst{\Sort{0}}{X}{P} = \Sort{0}Sort0[X↦P]=Sort0. So Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP is a type (a proposition, in fact). The body hhh then has type Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP, so

Infer(⋅,t)  =  Π(P:Sort 0). Π(h:Id  P). Id  P.\Infer(\cdot, t) \;=\; \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{\mathit{Id}\;P}}.Infer(⋅,t)=Π(P:Sort0).Π(h:IdP).IdP.

Renaming bound variables alone does not turn this into Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P. But IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq computes both sides before comparing them, and Id  P→βP\mathit{Id}\;P \betared PIdP→β​P, so the inferred type becomes Π(P:Sort 0). Π(h:P). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{P}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(h:P).P and the comparison succeeds as in the first example. In the typing rules, this step is a single use of T-Conv at the root of the derivation:

⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort 0). Id  P→Id  P⋅⊢Π(P:Sort 0). P→P:Sort 0Π(P:Sort 0). Id  P→Id  P≡Π(P:Sort 0). P→P⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort 0). P→P;(T-Conv)\dfrac{ \cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\mathit{Id}\;P \to \mathit{Id}\;P} \qquad \cdot \vdash \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} : \Sort{0} \qquad \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\mathit{Id}\;P \to \mathit{Id}\;P} \conv \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} }{\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}}\rulename{T-Conv}⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort0).P→P⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort0).IdP→IdP⋅⊢Π(P:Sort0).P→P:Sort0Π(P:Sort0).IdP→IdP≡Π(P:Sort0).P→P​;(T-Conv)

The algorithm never decides where to apply T-Conv. As described in Chapter 5, conversion is hidden in the call to IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq, which runs only where two types are compared.

The live derivation shows where the computation happens: the annotation Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP is checked by T-App, and the inferred type still contains Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP until Check\CheckCheck compares it with the goal.

# The annotation of h is (fun (X : Sort 0) => X) P, which computes to P.
goal forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P
exact fun (P : Sort 0) => fun (h : (fun (X : Sort 0) => X) P) => h
qed

Exercises

Running Infer\InferInfer on these by hand, as in the examples above, is a good check of one's understanding of the algorithm. Each can also be tried in a playground.

Prove Π(P:Sort 0). Π(Q:Sort 0). P→Q→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{P \to Q \to P}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(Q:Sort0).P→Q→P.

Solution

One answer is λ(P:Sort 0). λ(Q:Sort 0). λ(p:P). λ(q:Q). p\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{p}{P}{\tLam{q}{Q}{p}}}}λ(P:Sort0).λ(Q:Sort0).λ(p:P).λ(q:Q).p. The proof never uses qqq: the system allows hypotheses to go unused.

Prove that implication is transitive: Π(P:Sort 0). Π(Q:Sort 0). Π(R:Sort 0). (P→Q)→(Q→R)→P→R\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{R}{\Sort{0}}{(P \to Q) \to (Q \to R) \to P \to R}}}Π(P:Sort0).Π(Q:Sort0).Π(R:Sort0).(P→Q)→(Q→R)→P→R.

Solution

One answer ends in λ(f:P→Q). λ(g:Q→R). λ(p:P). g  (f  p)\tLam{f}{P \to Q}{\tLam{g}{Q \to R}{\tLam{p}{P}{g\;(f\;p)}}}λ(f:P→Q).λ(g:Q→R).λ(p:P).g(fp); it uses the application case twice, first for f  p:Qf\;p : Qfp:Q and then for g  (f  p):Rg\;(f\;p) : Rg(fp):R.

goal forall (P : Sort 0), forall (Q : Sort 0), forall (R : Sort 0), (P -> Q) -> (Q -> R) -> P -> R
exact fun (P : Sort 0) => fun (Q : Sort 0) => fun (R : Sort 0) => fun (f : P -> Q) => fun (g : Q -> R) => fun (p : P) => g (f p)
qed

Explain why λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:P). h  h\tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h\;h}}λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:P).hh is rejected, and at which line of Algorithm 5.1.

Solution

In the context P:Sort 0,h:PP : \Sort{0}, h : PP:Sort0,h:P, the body h  hh\;hhh reaches the application case. Infer\InferInfer returns PPP for the function hhh, and Whnf(P)=P\Whnf(P) = PWhnf(P)=P is a variable, not a Π\PiΠ. The algorithm fails at the line else fail "not a function": a proof of PPP is not something that can be applied. In Rust the message is application of non-function.

What to remember

  • A run of Infer\InferInfer mirrors a derivation tree; each returning call is one node.
  • Infer\InferInfer can succeed on a term that does not prove the stated theorem. Check\CheckCheck against the stated type is what catches it.
  • T-App is where hypotheses are used (modus ponens) and where universal statements are instantiated (substitution into the body of a Π\PiΠ).
  • Computation inside types is handled entirely by IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq; the algorithm never chooses where to apply T-Conv.

Chapter 7

Inductive Types I: Natural Numbers

So far the only types are universes and Π\PiΠ-types. That is enough for propositional logic, but not for mathematics: there are no numbers to reason about and no way to state that two things are equal. Lean provides both through a single mechanism, inductive types. This chapter adds constants to the kernel, declares the natural numbers, and discovers that computing with numbers and proving things about them are the same operation.

Constants and definitions

First we need a way to add named objects to the kernel. Terms gain constants ccc:

t,A,B  ::=  ⋯  ∣  ct, A, B \;::=\; \cdots \;\mid\; ct,A,B::=⋯∣c

A signature Σ\SigmaΣ lists the constants. Each entry either declares a constant with its type, written c:Cc : Cc:C, or also gives it a body, written c:C:=tc : C \mathrel{:=} tc:C:=t. Entries with a body are definitions. For example, Nat:Sort 1\Nat : \Sort{1}Nat:Sort1 below is a declaration, and add\addadd later in this chapter is a definition. Before an entry is added, its type is checked to be a type in the empty context, and its body, if any, is checked against that type, exactly as Lean does for each def.

The signature is used in two ways. First, a constant has the type the signature gives it:

⊢Γ;ok(c:C)∈ΣΓ⊢c:C;(T-Const)\dfrac{\ctxok{\Gamma} \qquad (c : C) \in \Sigma}{\Gamma \vdash c : C}\rulename{T-Const}Γ⊢c:C⊢Γ;ok(c:C)∈Σ​;(T-Const)

where (c:C)∈Σ(c : C) \in \Sigma(c:C)∈Σ covers both declarations and definitions. Second, a definition can be unfolded: the constant is replaced by its body. This computation step is called delta-reduction:

c  →δ  tif (c:C:=t)∈Σ.c \;\deltared\; t \qquad \text{if } (c : C \mathrel{:=} t) \in \Sigma.c→δ​tif (c:C:=t)∈Σ.

For example, add  2  1→δ(λ(m:Nat). λ(n:Nat). ⋯ )  2  1\add\;2\;1 \deltared (\tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\cdots}})\;2\;1add21→δ​(λ(m:Nat).λ(n:Nat).⋯)21, after which beta-reduction continues. A declared constant without a body, such as Nat\NatNat or zero\zerozero, never delta-reduces. Like beta, the step may be applied to any subterm.

Constants are not variables: they are never bound, so FV(c)=∅\FV(c) = \emptysetFV(c)=∅ and substitution leaves them unchanged. Reduction now consists of beta, delta, and the iota-rules introduced below, and definitional equality (Chapter 12) is taken with respect to all three.

The signature is the field decls: HashMap<String, Decl> of Kernel in src/kernel.rs. A Decl pairs a type with a DeclKind, which records whether the constant is an Axiom (declared, no body), a Definition(body), or one of the three kinds generated by an inductive declaration (Inductive, Constructor, Recursor). Kernel::axiom and Kernel::define add entries after the checks described above; infer handles T-Const by looking up the type; and whnf handles delta by unfolding a Definition.

Natural numbers

In Lean, the natural numbers are declared as

inductive Nat where
  | zero : Nat
  | succ (n : Nat) : Nat

The declaration says that every natural number is built in one of two ways: it is zero\zerozero, or it is succ  n\suc\;nsuccn, the successor of a natural number nnn. For example, 222 is succ  (succ  zero)\suc\;(\suc\;\zero)succ(succzero). In our kernel the declaration adds three constants without bodies:

Nat:Sort 1,zero:Nat,succ:Nat→Nat.\Nat : \Sort{1}, \qquad \zero : \Nat, \qquad \suc : \Nat \to \Nat.Nat:Sort1,zero:Nat,succ:Nat→Nat.

zero\zerozero and succ\sucsucc are called constructors. They build values but never compute: succ  (succ  zero)\suc\;(\suc\;\zero)succ(succzero) is already in normal form, and it is the number 222. We write 0,1,2,…0, 1, 2, \ldots0,1,2,… for zero\zerozero, succ  zero\suc\;\zerosucczero, succ  (succ  zero)\suc\;(\suc\;\zero)succ(succzero), and so on.

This gives us numbers, but nothing to do with them. A function such as addition must look at a number and act differently on zero\zerozero and on succ  n\suc\;nsuccn, and our terms have no way to do that yet. A λ\lambdaλ can only pass its argument along; it cannot inspect it.

Computing: addition

How should addition be defined? By recursion on the second argument:

add  m  zero=m,add  m  (succ  k)=succ  (add  m  k).\add\;m\;\zero = m, \qquad \add\;m\;(\suc\;k) = \suc\;(\add\;m\;k).addmzero=m,addm(succk)=succ(addmk).

Look at the shape of this definition. For a fixed mmm, the function add  m\add\;maddm is determined by two pieces of data: its value on zero\zerozero, which is mmm, and a way to turn its value rrr on kkk into its value on succ  k\suc\;ksucck, which is succ  r\suc\;rsuccr. Every function f:Nat→Cf : \Nat \to Cf:Nat→C defined by recursion of this kind, called structural recursion, has the same shape:

f  zero=z,f  (succ  k)=s  k  (f  k),f\;\zero = z, \qquad f\;(\suc\;k) = s\;k\;(f\;k),fzero=z,f(succk)=sk(fk),

for some z:Cz : Cz:C and s:Nat→C→Cs : \Nat \to C \to Cs:Nat→C→C. The step function sss receives both kkk and the result f  kf\;kfk of the recursive call. So we add one constant that builds fff from zzz and sss, once and for all:

recC:C→(Nat→C→C)→Nat→C,\mathsf{rec}_C : C \to (\Nat \to C \to C) \to \Nat \to C,recC​:C→(Nat→C→C)→Nat→C,

together with two computation rules, called iota-rules, which are exactly the equations above:

recC  z  s  zero  →ι  z,recC  z  s  (succ  n)  →ι  s  n  (recC  z  s  n).\mathsf{rec}_C\;z\;s\;\zero \;\iotared\; z, \qquad \mathsf{rec}_C\;z\;s\;(\suc\;n) \;\iotared\; s\;n\;(\mathsf{rec}_C\;z\;s\;n).recC​zszero→ι​z,recC​zs(succn)→ι​sn(recC​zsn).

Addition is now an ordinary, non-recursive definition:

add:Nat→Nat→Nat:=λ(m:Nat). λ(n:Nat). recNat  m  s  n,s=λ(k:Nat). λ(r:Nat). succ  r.\add : \Nat \to \Nat \to \Nat \mathrel{:=} \tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\mathsf{rec}_{\Nat}\;m\;s\;n}}, \qquad s = \tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\suc\;r}}.add:Nat→Nat→Nat:=λ(m:Nat).λ(n:Nat).recNat​msn,s=λ(k:Nat).λ(r:Nat).succr.

We write m+nm + nm+n for add  m  n\add\;m\;naddmn. The kernel computes 2+12 + 12+1 with delta, beta, and iota steps only. The explorer below is the kernel doing exactly that, one head step at a time, with the add\addadd definition loaded.

def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n

Each row is one head step: the highlighted part is the redex, and the next row shows what it became. Change the numerals, or try add Nat.zero n with the context n : Nat to see the recursor get stuck.

Other functions follow the same pattern. Doubling, with double  (succ  k)=succ  (succ  (double  k))\mathit{double}\;(\suc\;k) = \suc\;(\suc\;(\mathit{double}\;k))double(succk)=succ(succ(doublek)), is

double:=λ(n:Nat). recNat  zero  (λ(k:Nat). λ(r:Nat). succ  (succ  r))  n,\mathit{double} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{n}{\Nat}{\mathsf{rec}_{\Nat}\;\zero\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\suc\;(\suc\;r)}})\;n},double:=λ(n:Nat).recNat​zero(λ(k:Nat).λ(r:Nat).succ(succr))n,

and double  2→succ  (succ  (double  1))→succ4  (double  0)→succ4  zero=4\mathit{double}\;2 \to \suc\;(\suc\;(\mathit{double}\;1)) \to \suc^4\;(\mathit{double}\;0) \to \suc^4\;\zero = 4double2→succ(succ(double1))→succ4(double0)→succ4zero=4.

The interesting point is that no new recursion mechanism is needed. The constants of the inductive type, together with recC\mathsf{rec}_CrecC​ and its two rules, are enough to express every structurally recursive function on Nat\NatNat. And unlike general recursion, this one always terminates: each iota-step removes one succ\sucsucc from the argument.

Programmers know recC\mathsf{rec}_CrecC​ by another name: it is a fold over the natural numbers, in the same way that fold over a list replaces nil by a value and cons by a function. A fold cannot loop forever because it consumes its argument one constructor at a time. That is the price and the reward of structural recursion: less expressive than a while loop, but every program terminates, which a logic needs.

Proving: induction

Now consider proofs. To prove that a property P  nP\;nPn holds for every nnn, where P:Nat→Sort 0P : \Nat \to \Sort{0}P:Nat→Sort0, mathematics uses induction: prove the base case P  zeroP\;\zeroPzero, and the step Π(k:Nat). P  k→P  (succ  k)\tPi{k}{\Nat}{P\;k \to P\;(\suc\;k)}Π(k:Nat).Pk→P(succk), whose argument P  kP\;kPk is the induction hypothesis.

Through Curry-Howard, a proof of Π(n:Nat). P  n\tPi{n}{\Nat}{P\;n}Π(n:Nat).Pn is a function fff that takes nnn and returns a proof of P  nP\;nPn. How do we build such an fff from base:P  zero\mathit{base} : P\;\zerobase:Pzero and step\mathit{step}step? For 333, the proof is step  2  (step  1  (step  0  base))\mathit{step}\;2\;(\mathit{step}\;1\;(\mathit{step}\;0\;\mathit{base}))step2(step1(step0base)), and in general

f  zero=base,f  (succ  k)=step  k  (f  k).f\;\zero = \mathit{base}, \qquad f\;(\suc\;k) = \mathit{step}\;k\;(f\;k).fzero=base,f(succk)=stepk(fk).

This is a structurally recursive function again, with exactly the shape of add\addadd above: z=basez = \mathit{base}z=base and s=steps = \mathit{step}s=step. Induction is recursion that returns proofs.

There is one difference. For add\addadd, the result type CCC was the same for every nnn. Here it depends on nnn: f  zero:P  zerof\;\zero : P\;\zerofzero:Pzero, f  1:P  1f\;1 : P\;1f1:P1, and so on. So recC\mathsf{rec}_CrecC​, whose type mentions a fixed CCC, cannot express induction as it stands.

One recursor for both

Putting the two cases side by side shows what to generalize.

Recursion Induction
result for nnn CCC P  nP\;nPn
case zero\zerozero z:Cz : Cz:C base:P  zero\mathit{base} : P\;\zerobase:Pzero
case succ\sucsucc s:Π(k:Nat). C→Cs : \tPi{k}{\Nat}{C \to C}s:Π(k:Nat).C→C step:Π(k:Nat). P  k→P  (succ  k)\mathit{step} : \tPi{k}{\Nat}{P\;k \to P\;(\suc\;k)}step:Π(k:Nat).Pk→P(succk)
result Nat→C\Nat \to CNat→C Π(n:Nat). P  n\tPi{n}{\Nat}{P\;n}Π(n:Nat).Pn

The left column is the special case of the right column in which P  nP\;nPn is the same type CCC for every nnn. So we take the right column, with PPP replaced by an arbitrary function M:Nat→Sort uM : \Nat \to \Sort{u}M:Nat→Sortu that gives the type of the result for each nnn. This function is called the motive. The result is the recursor Nat.recu\NatRec{u}Nat.recu​ of Figure 7.1. Its arguments are the motive, one minor premise for each constructor, and finally the number nnn to recurse on, called the major premise. Its iota-rules are those of recC\mathsf{rec}_CrecC​. As in Lean, where the recursor is Nat.rec.{u}, there is one recursor for each universe level; since we have no universe polymorphism, the level is a subscript.

Figure 7.1. The constants for natural numbers and the iota-rules of the recursor.

Nat:Sort 1Lean: Natzero:NatNat.zerosucc:Nat→NatNat.succNat.recu:Π(M:Nat→Sort u).   M  zero→(Π(n:Nat). M  n→M  (succ  n))→Π(n:Nat). M  nNat.rec\begin{array}{lcll} \Nat &:& \Sort{1} & \text{Lean: } \texttt{Nat} \\[2pt] \zero &:& \Nat & \texttt{Nat.zero} \\[2pt] \suc &:& \Nat \to \Nat & \texttt{Nat.succ} \\[2pt] \NatRec{u} &:& \tPi{M}{\Nat \to \Sort{u}}{\;M\;\zero \to (\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n \to M\;(\suc\;n)}) \to \tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n}} & \texttt{Nat.rec} \end{array}NatzerosuccNat.recu​​::::​Sort1NatNat→NatΠ(M:Nat→Sortu).Mzero→(Π(n:Nat).Mn→M(succn))→Π(n:Nat).Mn​Lean: NatNat.zeroNat.succNat.rec​
Nat.recu  M  z  s  zero→ιzNat.recu  M  z  s  (succ  n)→ιs  n  (Nat.recu  M  z  s  n)\begin{array}{rcl} \NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;\zero &\iotared& z \\[2pt] \NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;(\suc\;n) &\iotared& s\;n\;(\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;n) \end{array}Nat.recu​MzszeroNat.recu​Mzs(succn)​→ι​→ι​​zsn(Nat.recu​Mzsn)​

The one recursor does both jobs, depending on the motive.

Recursion. With the constant motive λ(_:Nat). C\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{C}λ(_:Nat).C at level 111, the type of Nat.rec1  (λ(_:Nat). C)\NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{C})Nat.rec1​(λ(_:Nat).C) is convertible to the type of recC\mathsf{rec}_CrecC​. So recC\mathsf{rec}_CrecC​ is just Nat.rec1  (λ(_:Nat). C)\NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{C})Nat.rec1​(λ(_:Nat).C), and from now on

add:=λ(m:Nat). λ(n:Nat). Nat.rec1  (λ(_:Nat). Nat)  m  (λ(k:Nat). λ(r:Nat). succ  r)  n,\add \mathrel{:=} \tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{\Nat})\;m\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\suc\;r}})\;n}},add:=λ(m:Nat).λ(n:Nat).Nat.rec1​(λ(_:Nat).Nat)m(λ(k:Nat).λ(r:Nat).succr)n,

which is the definition in examples/zero-add.leanmini.

Induction. With a predicate M:Nat→Sort 0M : \Nat \to \Sort{0}M:Nat→Sort0 at level 000, the type of Nat.rec0\NatRec{0}Nat.rec0​ is the induction principle

M  zero→(∀n.  M  n→M  (succ  n))→∀n.  M  n.M\;\zero \to (\forall n.\; M\;n \to M\;(\suc\;n)) \to \forall n.\; M\;n.Mzero→(∀n.Mn→M(succn))→∀n.Mn.

Here the choice of imax\imaximax in T-Pi is essential. The conclusion Π(n:Nat). M  n\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n}Π(n:Nat).Mn has type Sort imax(1,0)=Sort 0\Sort{\imax(1, 0)} = \Sort{0}Sortimax(1,0)=Sort0, so "M  nM\;nMn for every nnn" is a proposition although Nat\NatNat lives in Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1. With max⁡\maxmax instead, it would live in Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1, and statements about numbers would not be propositions at all.

The type of Nat.recu\NatRec{u}Nat.recu​ is not arbitrary: it can be read off the declaration of Nat\NatNat. There is one minor premise per constructor. Each minor premise takes the constructor's arguments, plus one induction hypothesis for each argument whose type is Nat\NatNat itself (a recursive argument), and returns the motive applied to the constructor. zero\zerozero has no arguments, so its case is just M  zeroM\;\zeroMzero; succ\sucsucc has one recursive argument nnn, so its case is Π(n:Nat). M  n→M  (succ  n)\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;n \to M\;(\suc\;n)}Π(n:Nat).Mn→M(succn). Chapter 8 applies this recipe to more and more general declarations.

Try it

The kernel starts with Nat\NatNat and its recursors already declared (Kernel::standard in src/kernel.rs). The script below defines addition and asks the kernel to confirm that 2+12 + 12+1 and 333 are definitionally equal, which rfl does by computing both sides. Try changing three to Nat.succ three and see the kernel refuse.

def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n
def one : Nat := Nat.succ Nat.zero
def two : Nat := Nat.succ one
def three : Nat := Nat.succ two
# Both sides compute to succ (succ (succ zero)), so refl proves this.
goal Eq Nat (add two one) three
rfl
qed

The Eq in the goal is the equality type, declared in Chapter 9. For now, read Eq Nat a b as "a=ba = ba=b" and rfl as "both sides compute to the same thing".

Lean generates Nat.rec from the inductive declaration exactly as described here, and its type agrees with Figure 7.1 up to the names of bound variables and implicit arguments. Lean's compiler then replaces the recursor by efficient machine arithmetic for execution, and its elaborator lets users write recursive functions by pattern matching, compiling them to recursors behind the scenes. The kernel, however, only ever sees recursors.

Exercises

Define multiplication mul  m  n\mathit{mul}\;m\;nmulmn by recursion on nnn, using add\addadd, in the style of add\addadd above.

Solution

mul  m  zero=zero\mathit{mul}\;m\;\zero = \zeromulmzero=zero and mul  m  (succ  k)=add  m  (mul  m  k)\mathit{mul}\;m\;(\suc\;k) = \add\;m\;(\mathit{mul}\;m\;k)mulm(succk)=addm(mulmk), so mul:=λ(m:Nat). λ(n:Nat). Nat.rec1  (λ(_:Nat). Nat)  zero  (λ(k:Nat). λ(r:Nat). add  m  r)  n\mathit{mul} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{m}{\Nat}{\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{\Nat})\;\zero\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\add\;m\;r}})\;n}}mul:=λ(m:Nat).λ(n:Nat).Nat.rec1​(λ(_:Nat).Nat)zero(λ(k:Nat).λ(r:Nat).addmr)n.

def mul : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) Nat.zero (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => add m r) n

Why can the kernel not accept a general fixed-point combinator fix:(C→C)→C\mathsf{fix} : (C \to C) \to Cfix:(C→C)→C with the rule fix  g→g  (fix  g)\mathsf{fix}\;g \to g\;(\mathsf{fix}\;g)fixg→g(fixg), which would make every recursive function definable?

Solution

With C=Π(P:Sort 0). PC = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}C=Π(P:Sort0).P and g=λ(x:C). xg = \tLam{x}{C}{x}g=λ(x:C).x, the term fix  g\mathsf{fix}\;gfixg would have type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P, a proof of everything, and the system would be inconsistent. It also reduces to itself forever, so IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq would not terminate. Structural recursion avoids both problems because every iota-step consumes a constructor.

What to remember

  • Constants come from a signature Σ\SigmaΣ; definitions unfold by delta-reduction, declarations never do.
  • An inductive type adds a type former and constructors, which build values and do not compute.
  • Structural recursion on Nat\NatNat is captured by one constant, the recursor, with one iota-rule per constructor.
  • Induction is the same recursor with a dependent motive M:Nat→Sort 0M : \Nat \to \Sort{0}M:Nat→Sort0. Recursion and induction are one operation.
  • The imax\imaximax rule is what makes "for all nnn, M  nM\;nMn" a proposition.

Chapter 8

Inductive Types II: The General Recipe

Chapter 7 built the recursor for the natural numbers by hand. In Lean, a user never does that: they write an inductive declaration, and the kernel checks it and generates the type former, the constructors, the recursor, and its computation rules. This chapter develops that procedure in three steps, from more constructors to parameters to indices, and then states it in general. The kernel's own code for it is about five hundred lines.

More constructors: trees

Nat\NatNat has two constructors, and only one of them has a recursive argument. Consider a type with three:

inductive Tree where
  | leaf   : Tree
  | node   : Tree -> Tree
  | branch : Tree -> Tree -> Tree

For example, branch  (node  leaf)  leaf\mathsf{branch}\;(\mathsf{node}\;\mathsf{leaf})\;\mathsf{leaf}branch(nodeleaf)leaf is a tree built from four constructors. To build M  tM\;tMt for every tree ttt, where M:Tree→Sort vM : \mathsf{Tree} \to \Sort{v}M:Tree→Sortv, the recipe of Chapter 7 asks for one case per constructor, and each argument of type Tree\mathsf{Tree}Tree contributes one induction hypothesis:

mleaf:M  leafmnode:Π(t:Tree). M  t→M  (node  t)mbranch:Π(l:Tree). Π(r:Tree). M  l→M  r→M  (branch  l  r)\begin{array}{lcl} m_{\mathsf{leaf}} &:& M\;\mathsf{leaf} \\[2pt] m_{\mathsf{node}} &:& \tPi{t}{\mathsf{Tree}}{M\;t \to M\;(\mathsf{node}\;t)} \\[2pt] m_{\mathsf{branch}} &:& \tPi{l}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\tPi{r}{\mathsf{Tree}}{M\;l \to M\;r \to M\;(\mathsf{branch}\;l\;r)}} \end{array}mleaf​mnode​mbranch​​:::​MleafΠ(t:Tree).Mt→M(nodet)Π(l:Tree).Π(r:Tree).Ml→Mr→M(branchlr)​

The recursor takes the motive, the three cases, and a tree:

Tree.recv:Π(M:Tree→Sort v).   M  leaf→(⋯node)→(⋯branch)→Π(t:Tree). M  t,\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v : \tPi{M}{\mathsf{Tree} \to \Sort{v}}{\; M\;\mathsf{leaf} \to (\cdots_{\mathsf{node}}) \to (\cdots_{\mathsf{branch}}) \to \tPi{t}{\mathsf{Tree}}{M\;t}},Tree.recv​:Π(M:Tree→Sortv).Mleaf→(⋯node​)→(⋯branch​)→Π(t:Tree).Mt,

where the dots stand for the types of mnodem_{\mathsf{node}}mnode​ and mbranchm_{\mathsf{branch}}mbranch​. Compared with Nat.recv\NatRec{v}Nat.recv​, only the number of cases and the number of hypotheses per case have changed. Writing RRR for the partial application Tree.recv  M  mleaf  mnode  mbranch\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v\;M\;m_{\mathsf{leaf}}\;m_{\mathsf{node}}\;m_{\mathsf{branch}}Tree.recv​Mmleaf​mnode​mbranch​, the iota-rules are

R  leaf→ιmleafR  (node  t)→ιmnode  t  (R  t)R  (branch  l  r)→ιmbranch  l  r  (R  l)  (R  r).\begin{array}{rcl} R\;\mathsf{leaf} &\iotared& m_{\mathsf{leaf}} \\[2pt] R\;(\mathsf{node}\;t) &\iotared& m_{\mathsf{node}}\;t\;(R\;t) \\[2pt] R\;(\mathsf{branch}\;l\;r) &\iotared& m_{\mathsf{branch}}\;l\;r\;(R\;l)\;(R\;r). \end{array}RleafR(nodet)R(branchlr)​→ι​→ι​→ι​​mleaf​mnode​t(Rt)mbranch​lr(Rl)(Rr).​

Each rule selects the case for the constructor at the head of the major premise, and fills each hypothesis with a recursive call on the corresponding subtree. For example, with M=λ(_:Tree). NatM = \tLam{\_}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\Nat}M=λ(_:Tree).Nat and the cases

mleaf=1,mnode=λ(t:Tree). λ(i:Nat). 1+i,mbranch=λ(l:Tree). λ(r:Tree). λ(i:Nat). λ(j:Nat). 1+i+j,m_{\mathsf{leaf}} = 1, \qquad m_{\mathsf{node}} = \tLam{t}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\tLam{i}{\Nat}{1 + i}}, \qquad m_{\mathsf{branch}} = \tLam{l}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\tLam{r}{\mathsf{Tree}}{\tLam{i}{\Nat}{\tLam{j}{\Nat}{1 + i + j}}}},mleaf​=1,mnode​=λ(t:Tree).λ(i:Nat).1+i,mbranch​=λ(l:Tree).λ(r:Tree).λ(i:Nat).λ(j:Nat).1+i+j,

RRR counts the constructors of a tree:

R  (branch  (node  leaf)  leaf)→1+R  (node  leaf)+R  leaf→1+(1+R  leaf)+1→1+(1+1)+1=4.R\;(\mathsf{branch}\;(\mathsf{node}\;\mathsf{leaf})\;\mathsf{leaf}) \to 1 + R\;(\mathsf{node}\;\mathsf{leaf}) + R\;\mathsf{leaf} \to 1 + (1 + R\;\mathsf{leaf}) + 1 \to 1 + (1 + 1) + 1 = 4.R(branch(nodeleaf)leaf)→1+R(nodeleaf)+Rleaf→1+(1+Rleaf)+1→1+(1+1)+1=4.

With MMM a predicate (v=0v = 0v=0), the same recursor is structural induction on trees. In general, a type with nnn constructors gets a recursor with nnn minor premises m1,…,mnm_1, \ldots, m_nm1​,…,mn​, and the kernel needs no code specific to the type: it only needs to know, for each constructor, which case to pick and which arguments to recurse on.

Here is that tree as the kernel sees it. Each box is a constructor application; the recursive fields hang below it, and the line at the bottom of each box is the recursor case that handles it, with (R  l)(R\;l)(Rl) and (R  r)(R\;r)(Rr) the induction hypotheses computed by recursive calls. Type another tree to see its cases.

inductive Tree : Sort 1 where
  | leaf
  | node (t : Tree)
  | branch (l : Tree) (r : Tree)
inductive Tree : Sort 1 where
  | leaf
  | node (t : Tree)
  | branch (l : Tree) (r : Tree)

def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n
def one : Nat := Nat.succ Nat.zero
def four : Nat := Nat.succ (Nat.succ (Nat.succ one))

# The minor premise for branch takes l, r, then the two induction hypotheses.
def count : Tree -> Nat := fun (t : Tree) => Tree.rec1 (fun (_t : Tree) => Nat) one (fun (t : Tree) => fun (i : Nat) => Nat.succ i) (fun (l : Tree) => fun (r : Tree) => fun (i : Nat) => fun (j : Nat) => Nat.succ (add i j)) t

goal Eq Nat (count (Tree.branch (Tree.node Tree.leaf) Tree.leaf)) four
rfl
qed

Parameters: lists

A list of numbers is either empty or a number in front of a list of numbers, so we could declare a type ListNat\mathsf{ListNat}ListNat with constructors nil\mathsf{nil}nil and cons:Nat→ListNat→ListNat\mathsf{cons} : \Nat \to \mathsf{ListNat} \to \mathsf{ListNat}cons:Nat→ListNat→ListNat. But then lists of trees would need another declaration, ListTree\mathsf{ListTree}ListTree, with the same constructors and a separate recursor, and so on for every element type. It is better to make the element type an argument of the type itself:

inductive List (A : Sort 1) where
  | nil  : List A
  | cons : A -> List A -> List A

Now List  Nat\mathsf{List}\;\NatListNat and List  Tree\mathsf{List}\;\mathsf{Tree}ListTree are two instances of one declaration. The declaration adds

List:Sort 1→Sort 1,nil:Π(A:Sort 1). List  A,cons:Π(A:Sort 1). A→List  A→List  A.\mathsf{List} : \Sort{1} \to \Sort{1}, \qquad \mathsf{nil} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\mathsf{List}\;A}, \qquad \mathsf{cons} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{A \to \mathsf{List}\;A \to \mathsf{List}\;A}.List:Sort1→Sort1,nil:Π(A:Sort1).ListA,cons:Π(A:Sort1).A→ListA→ListA.

The constructors take AAA as an explicit first argument. For example, the one-element list [5][5][5] is cons  Nat  5  (nil  Nat)\mathsf{cons}\;\Nat\;5\;(\mathsf{nil}\;\Nat)consNat5(nilNat). Within one list, AAA never changes: the tail of cons  A  a  as\mathsf{cons}\;A\;a\;\mathit{as}consAaas is again a List  A\mathsf{List}\;AListA. An argument of the type that stays the same in every constructor and every recursive argument is called a parameter. Because it never changes, the recursor can take it once, before the motive, and treat it as fixed:

List.recv:Π(A:Sort 1). Π(M:List  A→Sort v).   M  (nil  A)→(Π(a:A). Π(as:List  A). M  as→M  (cons  A  a  as))→Π(x:List  A). M  xList.recv  A  M  m1  m2  (nil  A′)  →ι  m1List.recv  A  M  m1  m2  (cons  A′  a  as)  →ι  m2  a  as  (List.recv  A  M  m1  m2  as)\begin{array}{l} \mathsf{List.rec}_v : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tPi{M}{\mathsf{List}\;A \to \Sort{v}}{\;M\;(\mathsf{nil}\;A) \to {}}} \\[2pt] \qquad (\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{\mathit{as}}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{M\;\mathit{as} \to M\;(\mathsf{cons}\;A\;a\;\mathit{as})}}) \to \tPi{x}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{M\;x} \\[8pt] \mathsf{List.rec}_v\;A\;M\;m_1\;m_2\;(\mathsf{nil}\;A') \;\iotared\; m_1 \\[2pt] \mathsf{List.rec}_v\;A\;M\;m_1\;m_2\;(\mathsf{cons}\;A'\;a\;\mathit{as}) \;\iotared\; m_2\;a\;\mathit{as}\;(\mathsf{List.rec}_v\;A\;M\;m_1\;m_2\;\mathit{as}) \end{array}List.recv​:Π(A:Sort1).Π(M:ListA→Sortv).M(nilA)→(Π(a:A).Π(as:ListA).Mas→M(consAaas))→Π(x:ListA).MxList.recv​AMm1​m2​(nilA′)→ι​m1​List.recv​AMm1​m2​(consA′aas)→ι​m2​aas(List.recv​AMm1​m2​as)​

Apart from the leading AAA, this is the recipe of Chapter 7 once more: cons\mathsf{cons}cons has two arguments, of which only as\mathit{as}as is recursive, so its case gets one induction hypothesis. The rules ignore the parameter A′A'A′ stored in the constructor; in a well-typed term it is convertible to AAA. For example, the length of a list is

length:=λ(A:Sort 1). λ(x:List  A). List.rec1  A  (λ(_:List  A). Nat)  zero  (λ(a:A). λ(as:List  A). λ(r:Nat). succ  r)  x.\mathit{length} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tLam{x}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{ \mathsf{List.rec}_1\;A\;(\tLam{\_}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{\Nat})\;\zero\;(\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{\mathit{as}}{\mathsf{List}\;A}{\tLam{r}{\Nat}{\suc\;r}}})\;x}}.length:=λ(A:Sort1).λ(x:ListA).List.rec1​A(λ(_:ListA).Nat)zero(λ(a:A).λ(as:ListA).λ(r:Nat).succr)x.

A list value carries the parameter AAA in every constructor, which the tree below shows next to each box: the parameter is repeated, the fields differ.

inductive List (A : Sort 1) : Sort 1 where
  | nil
  | cons (head : A) (tail : List A)
inductive List (A : Sort 1) : Sort 1 where
  | nil
  | cons (head : A) (tail : List A)

def length : forall (A : Sort 1), List A -> Nat := fun (A : Sort 1) => fun (xs : List A) => List.rec1 A (fun (_xs : List A) => Nat) Nat.zero (fun (head : A) => fun (tail : List A) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) xs

# length [0, 0] = 2
goal Eq Nat (length Nat (List.cons Nat Nat.zero (List.cons Nat Nat.zero (List.nil Nat)))) (Nat.succ (Nat.succ Nat.zero))
rfl
qed

Indices: vectors

A List  Nat\mathsf{List}\;\NatListNat may have any length. What if we want the length to be part of the type, so that Vec  Nat  0\mathsf{Vec}\;\Nat\;0VecNat0 and Vec  Nat  2\mathsf{Vec}\;\Nat\;2VecNat2 are different types?

inductive Vec (A : Sort 1) : Nat -> Sort 1 where
  | vnil  : Vec A 0
  | vcons : (n : Nat) -> A -> Vec A n -> Vec A (succ n)

The element type AAA is still a parameter. The length is not: vnil\mathsf{vnil}vnil has length 000, and vcons\mathsf{vcons}vcons takes a vector of length nnn and returns one of length succ  n\suc\;nsuccn. An argument of the type that may differ between constructors, and between a constructor and its recursive arguments, is called an index. The constructors are

vnil:Π(A:Sort 1). Vec  A  zero,vcons:Π(A:Sort 1). Π(n:Nat). A→Vec  A  n→Vec  A  (succ  n).\mathsf{vnil} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\mathsf{Vec}\;A\;\zero}, \qquad \mathsf{vcons} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tPi{n}{\Nat}{A \to \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n \to \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;(\suc\;n)}}.vnil:Π(A:Sort1).VecAzero,vcons:Π(A:Sort1).Π(n:Nat).A→VecAn→VecA(succn).

Because an index varies, the recursor cannot fix it in advance. Instead, the motive takes it as an argument, M:Π(n:Nat). Vec  A  n→Sort vM : \tPi{n}{\Nat}{\mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n \to \Sort{v}}M:Π(n:Nat).VecAn→Sortv, and the case for vcons\mathsf{vcons}vcons is

Π(n:Nat). Π(a:A). Π(xs:Vec  A  n). M  n  xs→M  (succ  n)  (vcons  A  n  a  xs).\tPi{n}{\Nat}{\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{\mathit{xs}}{\mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n}{M\;n\;\mathit{xs} \to M\;(\suc\;n)\;(\mathsf{vcons}\;A\;n\;a\;\mathit{xs})}}}.Π(n:Nat).Π(a:A).Π(xs:VecAn).Mnxs→M(succn)(vconsAnaxs).

The induction hypothesis is about a vector of length nnn, read off the type Vec  A  n\mathsf{Vec}\;A\;nVecAn of the recursive argument, and the conclusion is about one of length succ  n\suc\;nsuccn, read off the result type of the constructor. The script examples/generic-vec.leanmini (Appendix E) declares this type and checks a small term that uses it.

The general recipe

This section states the procedure for a single inductive type with parameters and indices. Mutual and nested inductive types, which Lean also supports, are out of scope.

The procedure also answers a question that T-Const leaves open. A constant without a body is an assumption: T-Const would accept c:Π(P:Sort 0). Pc : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}c:Π(P:Sort0).P just as readily as zero:Nat\zero : \Natzero:Nat, and with it the system would be inconsistent. The constants generated below are not arbitrary assumptions. They are instances of a fixed schema, the inductive types of the Calculus of Inductive Constructions, whose consistency is known [Werner 1994].

Telescopes. We write (x⃗:A⃗)(\vec{x} : \vec{A})(x:A) for a sequence of bindings (x1:A1)⋯(xk:Ak)(x_1 : A_1) \cdots (x_k : A_k)(x1​:A1​)⋯(xk​:Ak​) in which each AiA_iAi​ may mention x1,…,xi−1x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}x1​,…,xi−1​; Π(x⃗:A⃗). B\tPi{\vec{x}}{\vec{A}}{B}Π(x:A).B for Π(x1:A1). ⋯ Π(xk:Ak). B\tPi{x_1}{A_1}{\cdots\,\tPi{x_k}{A_k}{B}}Π(x1​:A1​).⋯Π(xk​:Ak​).B; and f  x⃗f\;\vec{x}fx for f  x1⋯xkf\;x_1 \cdots x_kfx1​⋯xk​. The length of x⃗\vec{x}x is ∣x⃗∣|\vec{x}|∣x∣. In the code, a telescope is a Context, and telescope(binders, tail) in src/term.rs builds the nested Π\PiΠ.

Declarations. A declaration introduces a type former III and constructors c1,…,cnc_1, \ldots, c_nc1​,…,cn​:

I:Π(p⃗:P⃗). Π(ı⃗:J⃗). Sort ucj:Π(p⃗:P⃗). Π(a⃗:A⃗j). I  p⃗  t⃗j(j=1,…,n)\begin{array}{rcll} I &:& \tPi{\vec{p}}{\vec{P}}{\tPi{\vec{\imath}}{\vec{J}}{\Sort{u}}} & \\[2pt] c_j &:& \tPi{\vec{p}}{\vec{P}}{\tPi{\vec{a}}{\vec{A}_j}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{t}_j}} & (j = 1, \ldots, n) \end{array}Icj​​::​Π(p​:P).Π(:J).SortuΠ(p​:P).Π(a:Aj​).Ip​tj​​(j=1,…,n)​

The parameters p⃗\vec{p}p​ are shared by all constructors and appear unchanged in every result type. The indices ı⃗\vec{\imath} may differ between constructors: the index terms t⃗j\vec{t}_jtj​ may mention p⃗\vec{p}p​ and the constructor's own arguments a⃗\vec{a}a, which are called its fields. For the examples so far, with the leading Π\PiΠ over the parameters omitted from the constructor types:

Type former Parameters Indices Constructors
Nat:Sort 1\Nat : \Sort{1}Nat:Sort1 none none zero:Nat\zero : \Natzero:Nat,   succ:Nat→Nat\;\suc : \Nat \to \Natsucc:Nat→Nat
Tree:Sort 1\mathsf{Tree} : \Sort{1}Tree:Sort1 none none leaf\mathsf{leaf}leaf, node\mathsf{node}node, branch\mathsf{branch}branch
List:Sort 1→Sort 1\mathsf{List} : \Sort{1} \to \Sort{1}List:Sort1→Sort1 (A:Sort 1)(A : \Sort{1})(A:Sort1) none nil:List  A\mathsf{nil} : \mathsf{List}\;Anil:ListA,   cons:A→List  A→List  A\;\mathsf{cons} : A \to \mathsf{List}\;A \to \mathsf{List}\;Acons:A→ListA→ListA
Vec:Sort 1→Nat→Sort 1\mathsf{Vec} : \Sort{1} \to \Nat \to \Sort{1}Vec:Sort1→Nat→Sort1 (A:Sort 1)(A : \Sort{1})(A:Sort1) (n:Nat)(n : \Nat)(n:Nat) vnil:Vec  A  zero\mathsf{vnil} : \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;\zerovnil:VecAzero,   vcons:Π(n:Nat). A→Vec  A  n→Vec  A  (succ  n)\;\mathsf{vcons} : \tPi{n}{\Nat}{A \to \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;n \to \mathsf{Vec}\;A\;(\suc\;n)}vcons:Π(n:Nat).A→VecAn→VecA(succn)

Acceptance. The kernel accepts a declaration only if the following four conditions hold.

  1. The type of III is a type in the current signature.
  2. With III added to the signature, each constructor type is a type, and it ends in I  p⃗  t⃗jI\;\vec{p}\;\vec{t}_jIp​tj​, where p⃗\vec{p}p​ are exactly the parameters in order and III does not occur in t⃗j\vec{t}_jtj​.
  3. Strict positivity. Each field type either does not mention III, or has the form Π(y⃗:B⃗). I  p⃗  s⃗\tPi{\vec{y}}{\vec{B}}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{s}}Π(y​:B).Ip​s where III occurs neither in B⃗\vec{B}B nor in s⃗\vec{s}s. A field of the second form is recursive.
  4. Universes. If u≥1u \ge 1u≥1, each field type lies in some Sort w\Sort{w}Sortw with w≤uw \le uw≤u. If u=0u = 0u=0, there is no condition.

Condition 2 lets the recursor treat the parameters uniformly. Condition 3 rules out declarations such as

inductive Bad where
  | mk : (Bad -> False) -> Bad

whose field mentions Bad to the left of an arrow. Case analysis on Bad would let one define f:Bad→Falsef : \mathsf{Bad} \to \mathsf{False}f:Bad→False by f  (mk  g)=g  (mk  g)f\;(\mathsf{mk}\;g) = g\;(\mathsf{mk}\;g)f(mkg)=g(mkg). Then f  (mk  f)f\;(\mathsf{mk}\;f)f(mkf) is a closed term of type False\mathsf{False}False, and it reduces to itself, so it has no normal form. For a type Tree\mathsf{Tree}Tree under declaration, some field types and their status are:

Field type Status Reason
Nat\NatNat accepted, not recursive does not mention Tree\mathsf{Tree}Tree
Tree\mathsf{Tree}Tree accepted, recursive induction hypothesis M  akM\;a_kMak​
Nat→Tree\Nat \to \mathsf{Tree}Nat→Tree accepted, recursive produces trees; hypothesis Π(n:Nat). M  (ak  n)\tPi{n}{\Nat}{M\;(a_k\;n)}Π(n:Nat).M(ak​n)
Tree→Nat\mathsf{Tree} \to \NatTree→Nat rejected Tree\mathsf{Tree}Tree to the left of an arrow
List  Tree\mathsf{List}\;\mathsf{Tree}ListTree rejected here nested occurrence; Lean accepts it, but it is out of scope

A field of type Nat→Tree\Nat \to \mathsf{Tree}Nat→Tree is a tree with infinitely many children, one for each number; the recursor can still recurse into each child ak  na_k\;nak​n. A field of type Tree→Nat\mathsf{Tree} \to \NatTree→Nat consumes trees instead of containing them, and it is the shape that makes Bad paradoxical.

Condition 4 prevents a type from containing a larger universe. Without it, a declaration T:Sort 1T : \Sort{1}T:Sort1 with a constructor mk:Sort 1→T\mathsf{mk} : \Sort{1} \to Tmk:Sort1→T would place a copy of all of Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1 inside Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1, which is the self-containment that Chapter 13 shows to be inconsistent. For u=0u = 0u=0 no condition is needed, because Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 is impredicative.

The recursor. For an accepted declaration, the kernel generates a recursor I.recvI.\mathsf{rec}_vI.recv​ for each admissible level vvv (see below):

I.recv:Π(p⃗:P⃗).   Π(M:(Π(ı⃗:J⃗). I  p⃗  ı⃗→Sort v)).   Π(m1:C1). ⋯ Π(mn:Cn).   Π(ı⃗:J⃗). Π(x:I  p⃗  ı⃗). M  ı⃗  x.I.\mathsf{rec}_v : \tPi{\vec{p}}{\vec{P}}{\; \tPi{M}{(\tPi{\vec{\imath}}{\vec{J}}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{\imath} \to \Sort{v}})}{\; \tPi{m_1}{C_1}{\cdots\,\tPi{m_n}{C_n}{\; \tPi{\vec{\imath}}{\vec{J}}{\tPi{x}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{\imath}}{M\;\vec{\imath}\;x}}}}}}.I.recv​:Π(p​:P).Π(M:(Π(:J).Ip​→Sortv)).Π(m1​:C1​).⋯Π(mn​:Cn​).Π(:J).Π(x:Ip​).Mx.

The parameters come first and stay fixed, as for lists; the motive takes the indices and the element, as for vectors. The minor premise CjC_jCj​ asks for the case of constructor cjc_jcj​: given its fields and an induction hypothesis for each recursive field, build MMM for cjc_jcj​ applied to those fields:

Cj=Π(a⃗:A⃗j).   Π(h⃗:H⃗j).   M  t⃗j  (cj  p⃗  a⃗),Hj,k=Π(y⃗:B⃗). M  s⃗  (ak  y⃗)for each recursive field ak:Π(y⃗:B⃗). I  p⃗  s⃗.\begin{array}{l} C_j = \tPi{\vec{a}}{\vec{A}_j}{\;\tPi{\vec{h}}{\vec{H}_j}{\;M\;\vec{t}_j\;(c_j\;\vec{p}\;\vec{a})}}, \\[4pt] H_{j,k} = \tPi{\vec{y}}{\vec{B}}{M\;\vec{s}\;(a_k\;\vec{y})} \quad\text{for each recursive field } a_k : \tPi{\vec{y}}{\vec{B}}{I\;\vec{p}\;\vec{s}}. \end{array}Cj​=Π(a:Aj​).Π(h:Hj​).Mtj​(cj​p​a),Hj,k​=Π(y​:B).Ms(ak​y​)for each recursive field ak​:Π(y​:B).Ip​s.​

The final arguments are the indices and the element xxx itself, the major premise.

The rules. For each constructor, the kernel generates one iota-rule, which applies the minor premise to the fields and to the induction hypotheses, computed by recursive calls:

I.recv  p⃗  M  m⃗  ı⃗  (cj  p⃗ ′  a⃗)  →ι  mj  a⃗  h⃗,hk=λ(y⃗:B⃗). I.recv  p⃗  M  m⃗  s⃗  (ak  y⃗).I.\mathsf{rec}_v\;\vec{p}\;M\;\vec{m}\;\vec{\imath}\;(c_j\;\vec{p}\,'\;\vec{a}) \;\iotared\; m_j\;\vec{a}\;\vec{h}, \qquad h_k = \tLam{\vec{y}}{\vec{B}}{I.\mathsf{rec}_v\;\vec{p}\;M\;\vec{m}\;\vec{s}\;(a_k\;\vec{y})}.I.recv​p​Mm(cj​p​′a)→ι​mj​ah,hk​=λ(y​:B).I.recv​p​Mms(ak​y​).

The major premise is at position ∣p⃗∣+1+n+∣ı⃗∣|\vec{p}| + 1 + n + |\vec{\imath}|∣p​∣+1+n+∣∣ (counting from zero), the constructor has ∣p⃗∣|\vec{p}|∣p​∣ parameters and ∣a⃗∣|\vec{a}|∣a∣ fields, and in a well-typed redex p⃗ ′\vec{p}\,'p​′ is convertible to p⃗\vec{p}p​, so the rule ignores it, as the rules for lists ignore A′A'A′. For Nat\NatNat, Tree\mathsf{Tree}Tree, List\mathsf{List}List, and Vec\mathsf{Vec}Vec the procedure produces exactly the recursors and rules of this chapter and the last, and the recursor types agree with the ones Lean 4 generates, up to the names of bound variables and implicit arguments.

Eliminating from propositions. If u≥1u \ge 1u≥1, the recursor is generated for every level vvv. If u=0u = 0u=0, so that III is a proposition, the recursor is generated only for v=0v = 0v=0, unless III is a subsingleton: it has at most one constructor, and each field either is a proof (its type lies in Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0) or occurs among the index terms t⃗j\vec{t}_jtj​. The restriction keeps data from depending on which proof of a proposition was given. For example, P∨QP \vee QP∨Q has two constructors, so a function from proofs of P∨QP \vee QP∨Q into Nat\NatNat could return 000 for one and 111 for the other, and a proof would carry computational information. Lean's Or.rec and Exists.rec therefore eliminate only into Prop, while And.rec and Eq.rec eliminate into every universe: And has one constructor whose fields are proofs, and Eq (Chapter 9) has one constructor with no fields.

So the kernel's rules stay fixed while the signature grows: one generic procedure turns each declaration into signature entries, and a single reduction function runs their rules (Chapter 12).

In the code

The procedure lives in src/inductive/. The input is an InductiveSpec (src/declaration.rs): the name, the parameter and index telescopes, the universe level uuu, and one ConstructorSpec per constructor giving its fields and its index terms t⃗j\vec{t}_jtj​. The script parser builds this from an inductive block.

  • Kernel::add_inductive in src/inductive/mod.rs runs the four acceptance conditions in order (check_inductive_type is condition 1, check_constructor_fields checks that fields are types and enforces condition 4, check_constructor_result is condition 2) and, if all pass, registers the type former and constructors and records an InductiveInfo. On failure the signature is left unchanged.
  • src/inductive/positivity.rs is condition 3. check_recursive_field peels the leading Π\PiΠs of a field type, rejecting any whose domain mentions III, and requires the target to be III applied to exactly the parameter variables followed by index terms that do not mention III. It returns a RecursiveFieldInfo recording y⃗:B⃗\vec{y} : \vec{B}y​:B and s⃗\vec{s}s, which is all the recursor generator needs.
  • src/inductive/recursor.rs builds the recursor type from the formula above. recursor_type assembles the telescope p⃗\vec{p}p​, the motive, the minor premises, the indices, and the major premise; minor_premise_type builds each CjC_jCj​; induction_hypothesis_type builds each Hj,kH_{j,k}Hj,k​. The generated binder names (__motive, __minor_j, __ih_j_k, __major) start with two underscores, which user declarations may not use, so they can never clash with fields.
  • allows_large_elimination in mod.rs implements the subsingleton test. add_inductive registers I.rec0 always and I.rec1 when large elimination is allowed; register_recursor generates higher levels on demand.

The iota-rules are not generated as terms. whnf applies them directly from the stored InductiveInfo, which Chapter 12 explains.

The heart of the generator is short enough to read in full. Compare it with the formula for CjC_jCj​.

/// C_j = Pi (as : As_j). Pi (hs : Hs_j). M ts_j (c_j ps as)
fn minor_premise_type(info: &InductiveInfo, j: usize, constructor: &ConstructorInfo) -> Term {
    // c_j ps as
    let constructor_application = apps(
        const_term(&constructor.name),
        info.params.iter().chain(constructor.fields.iter()).map(|(name, _)| var(name)),
    );
    // (as : As_j) followed by (hs : Hs_j)
    let mut minor_premise_binders = constructor.fields.clone();
    for (k, recursive_field) in constructor.recursive_fields.iter().enumerate() {
        minor_premise_binders.push((
            format!("{INDUCTION_HYPOTHESIS_PREFIX}{j}_{k}"),
            induction_hypothesis_type(constructor, recursive_field),
        ));
    }
    telescope(&minor_premise_binders, apply_motive(&constructor.result_indices, constructor_application))
}

The kernel never special-cases Nat\NatNat. Kernel::standard in src/kernel.rs declares Nat\NatNat and Eq\mathsf{Eq}Eq by calling add_inductive with the same InductiveSpec a user script would produce, so Figure 7.1 is generated, not hard-coded, and the tests in src/inductive/tests.rs check that the generated types agree with the hand-written ones.

The positivity check is a soundness requirement, not a convenience. Lean, Coq, and Agda have each had bugs over the years in exactly this part of the kernel, because the general case (nested and mutual inductives, universe constraints, indices mentioning other inductives) is intricate. Our restricted schema keeps the check to eighty lines. When extending it, the question to ask of every new feature is: can a value of the type be built from a function that consumes the type?

Exercises

Write the recursor type Bool.recv\mathsf{Bool.rec}_vBool.recv​ for inductive Bool where | true | false, and define negation with it.

Solution

Bool.recv:Π(M:Bool→Sort v). M  true→M  false→Π(b:Bool). M  b\mathsf{Bool.rec}_v : \tPi{M}{\mathsf{Bool} \to \Sort{v}}{M\;\mathsf{true} \to M\;\mathsf{false} \to \tPi{b}{\mathsf{Bool}}{M\;b}}Bool.recv​:Π(M:Bool→Sortv).Mtrue→Mfalse→Π(b:Bool).Mb, with no induction hypotheses since neither constructor has fields. Negation is λ(b:Bool). Bool.rec1  (λ(_:Bool). Bool)  false  true  b\tLam{b}{\mathsf{Bool}}{\mathsf{Bool.rec}_1\;(\tLam{\_}{\mathsf{Bool}}{\mathsf{Bool}})\;\mathsf{false}\;\mathsf{true}\;b}λ(b:Bool).Bool.rec1​(λ(_:Bool).Bool)falsetrueb. The recursor of a type without recursive fields is just case analysis.

Which of the four acceptance conditions rejects each of the following, if any? (a) inductive T : Sort 1 where | mk (f : Sort 1). (b) inductive T : Sort 1 where | mk (f : T -> T). (c) inductive T : Sort 0 where | mk (f : Sort 1).

Solution

(a) Condition 4: the field Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1 has type Sort 2\Sort{2}Sort2, which exceeds u=1u = 1u=1. (b) Condition 3: TTT occurs to the left of an arrow in a field type. (c) Accepted: for u=0u = 0u=0 condition 4 imposes nothing, and the type is a proposition that packs up a type; this is the impredicativity of Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 at work, and it is harmless because TTT eliminates only into Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 (it is not a subsingleton, since its field is neither a proof nor an index).

What to remember

  • A declaration gives a type former with parameters and indices, and constructors with fields. Parameters are fixed throughout; indices vary and become arguments of the motive.
  • The recursor has one minor premise per constructor, with one induction hypothesis per recursive field, and one iota-rule per constructor.
  • Acceptance requires well-formedness, uniform parameters, strict positivity, and a universe bound. Positivity is what keeps recursion terminating and the logic consistent.
  • Propositions eliminate only into Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 unless they are subsingletons.
  • The kernel generates all of this from data; it contains no code specific to Nat\NatNat.

Chapter 9

Equality Is an Inductive Type Too

To state facts about numbers, such as 0+n=n0 + n = n0+n=n, we need a way to say that two things are equal. One might expect equality to be a primitive of the kernel, wired in with its own rules. It is not. Equality is just another inductive type, generated by the recipe of Chapter 8, and its recursor is the principle that lets a fact about aaa be turned into a fact about bbb. This chapter declares it, explains the two notions of equality that now coexist, and proves the first real theorem of the book.

The declaration

In Lean, equality is declared as

inductive Eq {A : Sort u} (a : A) : A -> Prop where
  | refl : Eq a a

For a,b:Aa, b : Aa,b:A, the type Equ  A  a  b\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;bEqu​Aab is the proposition that aaa and bbb are equal; when AAA is Nat\NatNat we write it a=ba = ba=b. In the terms of Chapter 8, AAA and aaa are parameters and bbb is an index:

Equ:Π(A:Sort u). A→A→Sort 0,reflu:Π(A:Sort u). Π(a:A). Equ  A  a  a.\Eq{u} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{A \to A \to \Sort{0}}, \qquad \refl{u} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;a}}.Equ​:Π(A:Sortu).A→A→Sort0,reflu​:Π(A:Sortu).Π(a:A).Equ​Aaa.

The only constructor reflu\refl{u}reflu​ has no fields, and its index term is aaa: it can only prove equations whose two sides are the same aaa. So Eq\Eq{}Eq​ is an inductive family like Vec\mathsf{Vec}Vec, not a single type. The left side is fixed by the parameter; the right side varies, and the constructor pins it to the left side.

Why is one constructor enough? Because the declaration does not define when two things are equal; it says how proofs of equality can be built, and the only way is to observe that something equals itself. Everything else, such as symmetry, transitivity, and substitution, is derived from the recursor, which says what can be done with such a proof once one has it.

The recursor: transport

Informally, the recursor of Eq\Eq{}Eq​ says: if a=ba = ba=b, then whatever holds of aaa holds of bbb. This is Leibniz's principle, and in its most common form it reads

Eq.ndrecu,v:Π(A:Sort u). Π(a:A). Π(M:A→Sort v). M  a→Π(b:A). Equ  A  a  b→M  b.\EqRec{u,v} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{M}{A \to \Sort{v}}{M\;a \to \tPi{b}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b \to M\;b}}}}.Eq.ndrecu,v​:Π(A:Sortu).Π(a:A).Π(M:A→Sortv).Ma→Π(b:A).Equ​Aab→Mb.

Given a property MMM of elements of AAA, evidence m:M  am : M\;am:Ma, and a proof hhh that a=ba = ba=b, it returns evidence of M  bM\;bMb. We say that it transports mmm along hhh. Its computation rule says that transporting along refl\refl{}refl​ does nothing:

Eq.ndrecu,v  A  a  M  m  b  (reflu  A  c)  →  m.\EqRec{u,v}\;A\;a\;M\;m\;b\;(\refl{u}\;A\;c) \;\to\; m.Eq.ndrecu,v​AaMmb(reflu​Ac)→m.

That is the whole idea. The version the general recipe of Chapter 8 actually generates is slightly more general, and Eq.ndrec\EqRec{}Eq.ndrec​ is a definition built from it.

the full dependent recursor, as generated by the recipe

Because bbb is an index, the motive takes bbb and the proof h:Equ  A  a  bh : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;bh:Equ​Aab, and there is one minor premise, for reflu\refl{u}reflu​, with no fields and no hypotheses:

Eq.recu,v:Π(A:Sort u). Π(a:A). Π(M:(Π(b:A). Equ  A  a  b→Sort v)). M  a  (reflu  A  a)→Π(b:A). Π(h:Equ  A  a  b). M  b  hEq.recu,v  A  a  M  m  b  (reflu  A′  c)  →ι  m.\begin{array}{l} \EqRecDep{u,v} : \tPi{A}{\Sort{u}}{\tPi{a}{A}{\tPi{M}{(\tPi{b}{A}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b \to \Sort{v}})}{{}}}} \\[2pt] \qquad\qquad M\;a\;(\refl{u}\;A\;a) \to \tPi{b}{A}{\tPi{h}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b}{M\;b\;h}} \\[8pt] \EqRecDep{u,v}\;A\;a\;M\;m\;b\;(\refl{u}\;A'\;c) \;\iotared\; m. \end{array}Eq.recu,v​:Π(A:Sortu).Π(a:A).Π(M:(Π(b:A).Equ​Aab→Sortv)).Ma(reflu​Aa)→Π(b:A).Π(h:Equ​Aab).MbhEq.recu,v​AaMmb(reflu​A′c)→ι​m.​

Eq\Eq{}Eq​ is a subsingleton (one constructor, no fields), so vvv is arbitrary: equality proofs can be used to build data, not only proofs. The non-dependent Eq.ndrecu,v\EqRec{u,v}Eq.ndrecu,v​ is the special case whose motive ignores the proof:
