For example, suppose P:Nat→Sort 0P : \Nat \to \Sort{0}P:Nat→Sort0, a,b:Nata, b : \Nata,b:Nat, h:a=bh : a = bh:a=b, and pa:P  a\mathit{pa} : P\;apa:Pa. Choosing the motive M=PM = PM=P gives

Eq.ndrec1,0  Nat  a  P  pa  b  h  :  P  b.\EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;a\;P\;\mathit{pa}\;b\;h \;:\; P\;b.Eq.ndrec1,0​NataPpabh:Pb.

This one line is the logical content of rewriting: a fact about aaa becomes a fact about bbb. The rw tactic of Chapter 10 builds such terms automatically.

In Lean, the type argument of Eq is implicit, written {A} in the declaration, and the elaborator fills it in, so users write Eq a b or a = b. Our kernel sees only fully explicit terms, so we write every argument; filling them in is the job of the layer above the kernel. In the script language the constants are Eq, Eq.refl, and the dependent recursors Eq.rec0 and Eq.rec1; the non-dependent Eq.ndrec\EqRec{}Eq.ndrec​ is not predeclared, but it is a two-line definition, shown in the playground below. Since there is no universe polymorphism, the kernel declares Eq once, at A:Sort 1A : \Sort{1}A:Sort1, which covers Nat\NatNat and every user-declared data type; equality between proofs is not available.

Definitional versus propositional equality

There are now two notions of equality, and keeping them apart is essential to understanding how a proof assistant behaves.

  • Definitional equality ≡\conv≡ is decided by the kernel, by computation. It is a judgment about terms, not a type; no proof object is involved.
  • Propositional equality Eq\Eq{}Eq​ is a type. Its proofs are terms, and finding one may require real reasoning, such as induction.

The constructor refl\refl{}refl​ connects them: by T-Conv, reflu  A  a:Equ  A  a  b\refl{u}\;A\;a : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;breflu​Aa:Equ​Aab whenever a≡ba \conv ba≡b. So every definitional equality yields a propositional one for free. The converse fails, and the standard example is the two halves of n+0=nn + 0 = nn+0=n and 0+n=n0 + n = n0+n=n. With the definition of add\addadd from Chapter 7 and sss its step function,

n+0  →δβ  Nat.rec1  (λ(_:Nat). Nat)  n  s  zero  →ι  n,n + 0 \;\to_{\delta\beta}\; \NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{\Nat})\;n\;s\;\zero \;\iotared\; n,n+0→δβ​Nat.rec1​(λ(_:Nat).Nat)nszero→ι​n,

so refl1  Nat  n:n+0=n\refl{1}\;\Nat\;n : n + 0 = nrefl1​Natn:n+0=n, and Lean proves this by rfl. In contrast,

0+n  →δβ  Nat.rec1  (λ(_:Nat). Nat)  0  s  n0 + n \;\to_{\delta\beta}\; \NatRec{1}\;(\tLam{\_}{\Nat}{\Nat})\;0\;s\;n0+n→δβ​Nat.rec1​(λ(_:Nat).Nat)0sn

is stuck: nnn is a variable, and the iota-rules fire only on zero\zerozero and succ\sucsucc. So 0+n=n0 + n = n0+n=n is not provable by refl\refl{}refl​ and needs induction.

The reduction explorer shows both computations with nnn as a variable in the context. The first reaches nnn; the second stops with the recursor waiting for a constructor it will never get.

def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n
def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n
def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n

# n + 0 = n holds by computation: the recursor sees the constructor zero.
goal forall (n : Nat), Eq Nat (add n Nat.zero) n
intro n
rfl
qed

# 0 + n = n does not: the recursor is stuck on the variable n.
goal forall (n : Nat), Eq Nat (add Nat.zero n) n
intro n
rfl

Which equations hold by rfl depends on how a function was defined, not on what it computes. Addition by recursion on the second argument makes n+0=nn + 0 = nn+0=n definitional and 0+n=n0 + n = n0+n=n propositional; recursion on the first argument would swap them. Lean users meet this constantly: rfl closes a goal or does not depending on the direction of recursion in the definitions involved.

Example: proving 0 + n = n

We prove Π(n:Nat). 0+n=n\tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}Π(n:Nat).0+n=n by induction, using Nat.rec0\NatRec{0}Nat.rec0​ with the motive M0=λ(n:Nat). 0+n=nM_0 = \tLam{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}M0​=λ(n:Nat).0+n=n.

Base. We need M0  0M_0\;0M0​0, which is convertible to 0+0=00 + 0 = 00+0=0. Since 0+00 + 00+0 computes to 000, the term refl1  Nat  0\refl{1}\;\Nat\;0refl1​Nat0 works.

Step. Given k:Natk : \Natk:Nat and ih:0+k=k\mathit{ih} : 0 + k = kih:0+k=k, we need M0  (succ  k)M_0\;(\suc\;k)M0​(succk), that is, 0+succ  k=succ  k0 + \suc\;k = \suc\;k0+succk=succk. By the second iota-rule, 0+succ  k0 + \suc\;k0+succk computes to succ  (0+k)\suc\;(0 + k)succ(0+k), so it suffices to prove succ  (0+k)=succ  k\suc\;(0 + k) = \suc\;ksucc(0+k)=succk. We start from refl1  Nat  (succ  (0+k))\refl{1}\;\Nat\;(\suc\;(0 + k))refl1​Nat(succ(0+k)), a proof of succ  (0+k)=succ  (0+k)\suc\;(0+k) = \suc\;(0+k)succ(0+k)=succ(0+k), and transport it along ih\mathit{ih}ih with the motive N=λ(b:Nat). succ  (0+k)=succ  bN = \tLam{b}{\Nat}{\suc\;(0 + k) = \suc\;b}N=λ(b:Nat).succ(0+k)=succb, which replaces the second 0+k0 + k0+k by kkk:

step=λ(k:Nat). λ(ih:0+k=k). Eq.ndrec1,0  Nat  (0+k)  N  (refl1  Nat  (succ  (0+k)))  k  ih.\mathit{step} = \tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{\mathit{ih}}{0 + k = k}{ \EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;(0 + k)\;N\;(\refl{1}\;\Nat\;(\suc\;(0 + k)))\;k\;\mathit{ih}}}.step=λ(k:Nat).λ(ih:0+k=k).Eq.ndrec1,0​Nat(0+k)N(refl1​Nat(succ(0+k)))kih.

The proof is

zero_add=Nat.rec0  M0  (refl1  Nat  0)  step  :  Π(n:Nat). 0+n=n.\mathit{zero\_add} = \NatRec{0}\;M_0\;(\refl{1}\;\Nat\;0)\;\mathit{step} \;:\; \tPi{n}{\Nat}{0 + n = n}.zero_add=Nat.rec0​M0​(refl1​Nat0)step:Π(n:Nat).0+n=n.

The kernel checks it with Algorithm 5.1. Each argument is checked against the corresponding part of the type of Nat.rec0\NatRec{0}Nat.rec0​, instantiated with M0M_0M0​, and every comparison succeeds after normalization. Here is the complete term, submitted to the kernel in one piece. The non-dependent recursor is defined first, exactly as in Figure 9.1.

def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n

# Eq.ndrec at levels (1, 0): transport a proof of M a along a = b to M b.
def ndrec : forall (A : Sort 1), forall (a : A), forall (M : A -> Sort 0), M a -> forall (b : A), Eq A a b -> M b := fun (A : Sort 1) => fun (a : A) => fun (M : A -> Sort 0) => fun (m : M a) => fun (b : A) => fun (h : Eq A a b) => Eq.rec0 A a (fun (b' : A) => fun (_h : Eq A a b') => M b') m b h

goal forall (n : Nat), Eq Nat (add Nat.zero n) n
exact Nat.rec0 (fun (n : Nat) => Eq Nat (add Nat.zero n) n) (Eq.refl Nat Nat.zero) (fun (k : Nat) => fun (ih : Eq Nat (add Nat.zero k) k) => ndrec Nat (add Nat.zero k) (fun (b : Nat) => Eq Nat (Nat.succ (add Nat.zero k)) (Nat.succ b)) (Eq.refl Nat (Nat.succ (add Nat.zero k))) k ih)
qed

Writing such terms by hand is tedious, and finding the right motive is the hard part: the motive NNN had to mention bbb in exactly one of the two places where 0+k0 + k0+k occurs. Tactics (Chapter 10) automate both the bookkeeping and the choice of motive.

Changes to the kernel

Surprisingly little changed to get from propositional logic to arithmetic with equality. Infer\InferInfer gained a case for constants, which looks up the type in Σ\SigmaΣ (T-Const). Check\CheckCheck is unchanged. Only Whnf\WhnfWhnf, and through it IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq, learned the new delta- and iota-steps. Chapter 12 shows how a single Whnf\WhnfWhnf handles every inductive type, and Chapter 14 discusses what inductive types change in the metatheory.

Exercises

Prove symmetry of equality: build a term of type Π(a:Nat). Π(b:Nat). a=b→b=a\tPi{a}{\Nat}{\tPi{b}{\Nat}{a = b \to b = a}}Π(a:Nat).Π(b:Nat).a=b→b=a using Eq.ndrec\EqRec{}Eq.ndrec​.

Solution

Transport the proof refl  a:a=a\refl{}\;a : a = arefl​a:a=a along h:a=bh : a = bh:a=b with the motive λ(x:Nat). x=a\tLam{x}{\Nat}{x = a}λ(x:Nat).x=a, which turns a=aa = aa=a into b=ab = ab=a: λ(a:Nat). λ(b:Nat). λ(h:a=b). Eq.ndrec1,0  Nat  a  (λ(x:Nat). x=a)  (refl1  Nat  a)  b  h\tLam{a}{\Nat}{\tLam{b}{\Nat}{\tLam{h}{a = b}{\EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;a\;(\tLam{x}{\Nat}{x = a})\;(\refl{1}\;\Nat\;a)\;b\;h}}}λ(a:Nat).λ(b:Nat).λ(h:a=b).Eq.ndrec1,0​Nata(λ(x:Nat).x=a)(refl1​Nata)bh.

goal forall (a : Nat), forall (b : Nat), Eq Nat a b -> Eq Nat b a
exact fun (a : Nat) => fun (b : Nat) => fun (h : Eq Nat a b) => ndrec Nat a (fun (x : Nat) => Eq Nat x a) (Eq.refl Nat a) b h
qed

(with ndrec defined as in the playground above).

Explain why Eq\Eq{}Eq​ eliminates into every universe although it is a proposition, but a type Or with two constructors does not.

Solution

Eq\Eq{}Eq​ is a subsingleton: one constructor with no fields. A function defined by its recursor cannot distinguish two proofs of a=ba = ba=b, because there is only one way to build any such proof. Or has two constructors, so its recursor into Nat\NatNat could return different numbers for the two injections, making the value of a program depend on which proof was supplied. Chapter 8 states the rule precisely.

What to remember

  • Eq\Eq{}Eq​ is an inductive family with parameters AAA and aaa, index bbb, and one constructor refl\refl{}refl​ with no fields.
  • Its recursor transports a fact about aaa to a fact about bbb along a proof of a=ba = ba=b, and does nothing on refl\refl{}refl​. This is rewriting.
  • Definitional equality is decided by computation; propositional equality is a type whose proofs may need induction. refl\refl{}refl​ turns the former into the latter.
  • n+0=nn + 0 = nn+0=n is definitional and 0+n=n0 + n = n0+n=n is not, because addition recurses on its second argument.

Chapter 10

Tactics: Building Proof Terms Interactively

Lean users rarely write terms like the one at the end of Chapter 9 by hand. They write a tactic script, a sequence of commands that build the term step by step while the system displays what remains to be proved. This chapter shows how the common tactics construct terms in our system, and why none of them needs to be trusted.

In Lean, the theorem of Chapter 9 is proved like this:

theorem zero_add (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih => rw [Nat.add_succ, ih]

Each tactic is a small program that builds part of the proof term. Tactics run outside the kernel. Their output is an ordinary term, which the kernel checks with Algorithm 5.1 like any other term.

Goals and proof states

A goal ⟨Γ⊢?m:T⟩\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{T}⟨Γ⊢?m​:T⟩ asks for a term of type TTT in the context Γ\GammaΓ. The hole ?m\hole{m}?m​ stands for the term still to be found; Lean calls it a metavariable. A proof state is a list of goals together with a partial proof term, a term that may contain holes.

To prove TTT, we start from the partial term ?0\hole{0}?0​ and the single goal ⟨⋅⊢?0:T⟩\goal{\cdot}{\hole{0}}{T}⟨⋅⊢?0​:T⟩. A tactic works on the first goal ⟨Γ⊢?m:T⟩\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{T}⟨Γ⊢?m​:T⟩. It assigns to ?m\hole{m}?m​ a term that may contain fresh holes, and replaces the goal by one new goal for each fresh hole. When no goals remain, the partial term contains no holes, and the kernel checks it against TTT. A hole may sit under binders, as ?1\hole{1}?1​ does in λ(x:A). ?1\tLam{x}{A}{\hole{1}}λ(x:A).?1​, and the term that fills it may use those bound variables. That is why each goal carries its own context.

Each tactic must make sure that its assignment has type TTT in Γ\GammaΓ, assuming each fresh hole is later filled with a term of the type its goal states. We write ⟨Γ⊢?m:T⟩⇝new goals\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{T} \leadsto \text{new goals}⟨Γ⊢?m​:T⟩⇝new goals, followed by the assignment.

A first example

The script examples/identity.leanmini proves the opening example of Chapter 1. The explorer below runs it one command at a time.

goal forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P
intro P
intro p
exact p
qed

Step through it with the buttons or the arrow keys. The middle panel is the list of goals after each command, and the right panel is the partial proof term, with the hole for the current goal highlighted. The three panels always agree: a tactic changes the goals because it assigns a term to a hole.

A list of goals alone would not be enough: after intro p, the goal PPP does not remember that its solution must be wrapped in two λ\lambdaλs. The partial term records exactly that.

Basic tactics

intro x. If TTT normalizes to a Π\PiΠ-type, the tactic moves its argument into the context:

⟨Γ⊢?m:Π(y:A). B⟩  ⇝  ⟨Γ,x:A⊢?1:B[y↦x]⟩,?m:=λ(x:A). ?1.\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{\tPi{y}{A}{B}} \;\leadsto\; \goal{\Gamma, x : A}{\hole{1}}{\subst{B}{y}{x}}, \qquad \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \tLam{x}{A}{\hole{1}}.⟨Γ⊢?m​:Π(y:A).B⟩⇝⟨Γ,x:A⊢?1​:B[y↦x]⟩,?m​:=λ(x:A).?1​.

The assignment has the right type by T-Lam. The name xxx must not be in dom(Γ)\dom(\Gamma)dom(Γ); otherwise the new assumption would shadow an existing one, which makes the kernel unsound (Chapter 11). Our intro refuses such a name with the message "binder name already in context"; Lean renames it.

exact t. The tactic closes the goal with a given term:

⟨Γ⊢?m:T⟩  ⇝  no goals,?m:=t,\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{T} \;\leadsto\; \text{no goals}, \qquad \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} t,⟨Γ⊢?m​:T⟩⇝no goals,?m​:=t,

after running Check(Γ,t,T)\Check(\Gamma, t, T)Check(Γ,t,T) itself. The kernel would reject an ill-typed ttt at the end anyway; checking early only gives a better error message.

apply f. If fff has type A1→⋯→An→BA_1 \to \cdots \to A_n \to BA1​→⋯→An​→B with B≡TB \conv TB≡T, the tactic leaves the arguments as new goals:

⟨Γ⊢?m:T⟩  ⇝  ⟨Γ⊢?1:A1⟩,…,⟨Γ⊢?n:An⟩,?m:=f  ?1⋯?n.\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{T} \;\leadsto\; \goal{\Gamma}{\hole{1}}{A_1}, \ldots, \goal{\Gamma}{\hole{n}}{A_n}, \qquad \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} f\;\hole{1} \cdots \hole{n}.⟨Γ⊢?m​:T⟩⇝⟨Γ⊢?1​:A1​⟩,…,⟨Γ⊢?n​:An​⟩,?m​:=f?1​⋯?n​.

The assignment has type BBB by nnn uses of T-App, and type TTT by T-Conv. When the type of fff is a dependent Π\PiΠ, later AiA_iAi​ and BBB mention earlier arguments, and the tactic must find those arguments by matching BBB against TTT. Lean does this by unification, solving for metavariables. Our restricted version handles only non-dependent arrows, and reports "dependent apply requires elaboration/unification" otherwise. (With n=0n = 0n=0, that is, when the type of fff is already convertible to TTT, apply f behaves like exact f.)

For example, transitivity of implication, the second exercise of Chapter 6, works backwards from the conclusion:

goal forall (P : Sort 0), forall (Q : Sort 0), forall (R : Sort 0), (P -> Q) -> (Q -> R) -> P -> R
intro P
intro Q
intro R
intro f
intro g
intro p
apply g
apply f
exact p
qed

After the six intros the goal is ⟨Γ⊢?6:R⟩\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{6}}{R}⟨Γ⊢?6​:R⟩ with Γ=P,Q,R:Sort 0,  f:P→Q,  g:Q→R,  p:P\Gamma = P, Q, R : \Sort{0},\; f : P \to Q,\; g : Q \to R,\; p : PΓ=P,Q,R:Sort0,f:P→Q,g:Q→R,p:P. No hypothesis has type RRR, so exact cannot close it, but ggg ends in RRR: apply g assigns ?6:=g  ?7\hole{6} \mathrel{:=} g\;\hole{7}?6​:=g?7​ and leaves ?7:Q\hole{7} : Q?7​:Q. Likewise apply f assigns ?7:=f  ?8\hole{7} \mathrel{:=} f\;\hole{8}?7​:=f?8​ and leaves ?8:P\hole{8} : P?8​:P, which exact p closes. The body of the resulting term is g  (f  p)g\;(f\;p)g(fp). Note the difference between the two tactics: exact g fails, because ggg has type Q→RQ \to RQ→R, not RRR, whereas apply g turns the missing argument of ggg into a new goal.

change T'. The tactic replaces the goal by a definitionally equal one:

⟨Γ⊢?m:T⟩  ⇝  ⟨Γ⊢?1:T′⟩,?m:=?1,\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{T} \;\leadsto\; \goal{\Gamma}{\hole{1}}{T'}, \qquad \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \hole{1},⟨Γ⊢?m​:T⟩⇝⟨Γ⊢?1​:T′⟩,?m​:=?1​,

provided T′T'T′ is a type and T′≡TT' \conv TT′≡T. It adds nothing to the term; it only changes how the goal is displayed, and T-Conv justifies it. change is needed because rw (below) finds subterms only up to alpha-equivalence: a subterm that appears only after computation must first be exposed with change, as in the example at the end of this chapter.

rfl. If TTT normalizes to Equ  A  a  b\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;bEqu​Aab with a≡ba \conv ba≡b, the tactic closes the goal:

⟨Γ⊢?m:Equ  A  a  b⟩  ⇝  no goals,?m:=reflu  A  a.\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;b} \;\leadsto\; \text{no goals}, \qquad \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \refl{u}\;A\;a.⟨Γ⊢?m​:Equ​Aab⟩⇝no goals,?m​:=reflu​Aa.

The assignment has type Equ  A  a  a\Eq{u}\;A\;a\;aEqu​Aaa, which is convertible to the goal. So rfl proves exactly the equations that hold by definitional equality (Chapter 9).

Induction

Let n:Natn : \Natn:Nat be a variable in Γ\GammaΓ, and let Γ⊢T:Sort u\Gamma \vdash T : \Sort{u}Γ⊢T:Sortu. The tactic induction n abstracts nnn in the goal to form the motive, and produces one goal per constructor:

⟨Γ⊢?m:T⟩  ⇝  ⟨Γ⊢?z:T[n↦zero]⟩,  ⟨Γ,k:Nat,ih:T[n↦k]⊢?s:T[n↦succ  k]⟩,?m:=Nat.recu  (λ(z:Nat). T[n↦z])  ?z  (λ(k:Nat). λ(ih:T[n↦k]). ?s)  n.\begin{array}{l} \goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{T} \;\leadsto\; \goal{\Gamma}{\hole{z}}{\subst{T}{n}{\zero}},\; \goal{\Gamma, k : \Nat, \mathit{ih} : \subst{T}{n}{k}}{\hole{s}}{\subst{T}{n}{\suc\;k}}, \\[4pt] \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \NatRec{u}\;(\tLam{z}{\Nat}{\subst{T}{n}{z}})\;\hole{z}\;(\tLam{k}{\Nat}{\tLam{\mathit{ih}}{\subst{T}{n}{k}}{\hole{s}}})\;n. \end{array}⟨Γ⊢?m​:T⟩⇝⟨Γ⊢?z​:T[n↦zero]⟩,⟨Γ,k:Nat,ih:T[n↦k]⊢?s​:T[n↦succk]⟩,?m​:=Nat.recu​(λ(z:Nat).T[n↦z])?z​(λ(k:Nat).λ(ih:T[n↦k]).?s​)n.​

With the motive M=λ(z:Nat). T[n↦z]M = \tLam{z}{\Nat}{\subst{T}{n}{z}}M=λ(z:Nat).T[n↦z], the type of Nat.recu  M\NatRec{u}\;MNat.recu​M asks for M  zeroM\;\zeroMzero and Π(k:Nat). M  k→M  (succ  k)\tPi{k}{\Nat}{M\;k \to M\;(\suc\;k)}Π(k:Nat).Mk→M(succk), and the result has type M  nM\;nMn. These are convertible to the types of the two goals and to TTT, by beta. The construction is correct only if the names are fresh, the level uuu is right, and no other hypothesis mentions nnn.

  • The motive binds a fresh name zzz, not nnn: since nnn is already in Γ\GammaΓ, writing λ(n:Nat). T\tLam{n}{\Nat}{T}λ(n:Nat).T would shadow it, which is the pitfall of Chapter 11. Likewise kkk and ih\mathit{ih}ih must be fresh. (Our implementation names the motive's variable ind_x, the successor's field k when n is taken, and the hypothesis ih.)
  • The level uuu of the motive comes from the type of the goal, found by InferSort\InferSortInferSort. For a proposition it is 000, and Nat.rec0\NatRec{0}Nat.rec0​ is induction.
  • If another hypothesis mentions nnn, for example h:n=2h : n = 2h:n=2, the new goals still contain hhh about the original nnn, and ih\mathit{ih}ih says nothing about it. The goals are then correct but may be unprovable. Lean's induction first moves such hypotheses into the goal (it reverts them), so that they become part of the motive. Our version requires that no later hypothesis mentions nnn, and says "induction: revert dependent hypotheses first" otherwise.

The implementation is not specific to Nat\NatNat. It works for any inductive type without indices: it reads the recursor's type from the signature, peels one minor premise per constructor, and turns each into a goal whose context contains the constructor's fields and induction hypotheses. The script examples/generic-list.leanmini uses it on a user-declared list type.

Rewriting

Let h:Equ  A  a  bh : \Eq{u}\;A\;a\;bh:Equ​Aab, and let the goal TTT be a proposition. The tactic rw h replaces aaa by bbb in the goal in three steps.

  1. Abstract. Choose a fresh xxx and let CCC be TTT with every occurrence of aaa replaced by xxx. Occurrences are found up to alpha-equivalence, not up to conversion, and an occurrence under a binder that binds a free variable of aaa is skipped, since there it denotes something else.
  2. Check the motive. Check that Γ,x:A⊢C:Sort 0\Gamma, x : A \vdash C : \Sort{0}Γ,x:A⊢C:Sort0. This can fail, as shown below.
  3. Build the term. The new goal is C[x↦b]\subst{C}{x}{b}C[x↦b], the goal with aaa replaced by bbb:
    ⟨Γ⊢?m:T⟩  ⇝  ⟨Γ⊢?1:C[x↦b]⟩,?m:=Eq.ndrecu,0  A  a  (λ(x:A). C→T)  (λ(p:T). p)  b  h  ?1.\goal{\Gamma}{\hole{m}}{T} \;\leadsto\; \goal{\Gamma}{\hole{1}}{\subst{C}{x}{b}}, \qquad \hole{m} \mathrel{:=} \EqRec{u,0}\;A\;a\;(\tLam{x}{A}{C \to T})\;(\tLam{p}{T}{p})\;b\;h\;\hole{1}.⟨Γ⊢?m​:T⟩⇝⟨Γ⊢?1​:C[x↦b]⟩,?m​:=Eq.ndrecu,0​Aa(λ(x:A).C→T)(λ(p:T).p)bh?1​.

To see that the assignment has type TTT, write N=λ(x:A). C→TN = \tLam{x}{A}{C \to T}N=λ(x:A).C→T for the motive. Since C[x↦a]=T\subst{C}{x}{a} = TC[x↦a]=T, the term N  aN\;aNa is convertible to T→TT \to TT→T, which the identity λ(p:T). p\tLam{p}{T}{p}λ(p:T).p inhabits. Transport along hhh then gives N  bN\;bNb, which is convertible to C[x↦b]→T\subst{C}{x}{b} \to TC[x↦b]→T, and applying it to ?1\hole{1}?1​ gives TTT. Lean builds a different term, Eq.mpr (congrArg (fun x => C) h), from the same idea, and additionally tries to close the new goal with rfl; ours leaves that to an explicit rfl, so the two steps are visible in the script.

When the motive is ill typed. Abstracting aaa can break the goal. Let Γ=n:Nat,  h:n=2,  q:n=0\Gamma = n : \Nat,\; h : n = 2,\; q : n = 0Γ=n:Nat,h:n=2,q:n=0, and suppose we run rw h on the goal Eq0  (n=0)  q  q\Eq{0}\;(n = 0)\;q\;qEq0​(n=0)qq, a statement about the proof qqq. Abstracting nnn gives C=Eq0  (x=0)  q  qC = \Eq{0}\;(x = 0)\;q\;qC=Eq0​(x=0)qq, which is ill typed: qqq has type n=0n = 0n=0, not x=0x = 0x=0, and qqq itself cannot be abstracted. Step 2 fails, and Lean reports the same situation as "motive is not type correct". Without step 2 the tactic would produce a term that the kernel rejects, which is harmless for soundness but unhelpful for the user.

Tactics are methods of ProofState in src/proof.rs. The partial proof term is a Template (src/template.rs), a term with Hole(i) nodes; materialize substitutes the solutions and fails if any hole is unsolved. ProofState::replace performs an assignment: it records the solution for the current goal and splices the new goals in at the front. intro, exact, apply, change, rfl, induction, and rw each follow the description above; rw uses replace_exact for step 1 and check_transport for step 2, and finish is qed: it materializes the term and calls Kernel::check against the original goal.

Example: 0 + n = n with tactics

In our system the proof of Chapter 9 becomes the following script, which is examples/zero-add.leanmini with the definition of add\addadd included (the script writes add Nat.zero n for 0+n0 + n0+n).

def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n
goal forall (n : Nat), Eq Nat (add Nat.zero n) n
intro n
induction n
rfl
change Eq Nat (Nat.succ (add Nat.zero k)) (Nat.succ k)
rw ih
rfl
qed

Watch the partial term grow: induction n inserts Nat.rec0\NatRec{0}Nat.rec0​ with two holes, rfl fills the first, change leaves the term alone and only rewrites the goal, and rw ih inserts the transport with one hole left for the final rfl. Delete the change line and apply the script to see rw fail to find its left-hand side.

# Addition by recursion on the second argument:
#   add m zero     = m
#   add m (succ k) = succ (add m k)
def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n

# add zero n = n is not definitional, so it needs induction on n.
goal forall (n : Nat), Eq Nat (add Nat.zero n) n
intro n
induction n
# Base case: add zero zero reduces to zero.
rfl
# Step case: unfold add zero (succ k) to succ (add zero k), then use ih.
change Eq Nat (Nat.succ (add Nat.zero k)) (Nat.succ k)
rw ih
rfl
qed

The term differs from the hand-written one of Chapter 9 in two places: it starts with λ(n:Nat). …  n\tLam{n}{\Nat}{\ldots\;n}λ(n:Nat).…n because of intro, and its step uses the motive built by rw. Both are proofs of the same proposition, and the kernel does not care which one it receives. Try deleting the change line in the playground and read the error rw gives.

Why tactics need not be trusted

The kernel checks the final term, so tactics do not have to be correct for the system to be sound. A buggy tactic can fail, or it can produce an ill-typed term, which the kernel rejects; it cannot make the kernel accept a false theorem. The checks that tactics perform themselves, such as Check\CheckCheck in exact or the motive check in rw, exist only to report errors early and clearly.

The trusted part of the system is therefore small: Algorithm 5.1, the reduction and comparison functions of Part III, and the signature-building procedure of Chapter 8. Everything in src/proof.rs and src/syntax.rs is outside it.

Lean's tactic framework is far richer than the one sketched here. It has metavariables solved by unification, an elaborator that fills in implicit arguments and expands notation such as 0 + n, an induction that reverts dependent hypotheses and handles indexed families, and automation such as simp. All of this lives on the untrusted side: Lean's kernel, like ours, only ever sees complete terms [de Moura and Ullrich 2021].

Exercises

Prove Π(n:Nat). n=n\tPi{n}{\Nat}{n = n}Π(n:Nat).n=n with tactics, by induction, and explain why rfl closes both cases.

Solution

This is examples/nat-reflexivity.leanmini: intro n, induction n, rfl, rfl, qed. The base goal is 0=00 = 00=0 and the step goal is succ  k=succ  k\suc\;k = \suc\;ksucck=succk; both sides are syntactically identical, so definitional equality holds trivially. The induction is unnecessary here (a single rfl after intro n would do) but shows the shape of the goals.

Write the term that rw produces when the goal is Eq  Nat  a  c\Eq{}\;\Nat\;a\;cEq​Natac, the hypothesis is h:a=bh : a = bh:a=b, and the context is a,b,c:Nata, b, c : \Nata,b,c:Nat.

Solution

Abstracting aaa gives C=(x=c)C = (x = c)C=(x=c) and the new goal b=cb = cb=c. The assignment is Eq.ndrec1,0  Nat  a  (λ(x:Nat). (x=c)→(a=c))  (λ(p:a=c). p)  b  h  ?1\EqRec{1,0}\;\Nat\;a\;(\tLam{x}{\Nat}{(x = c) \to (a = c)})\;(\tLam{p}{a = c}{p})\;b\;h\;\hole{1}Eq.ndrec1,0​Nata(λ(x:Nat).(x=c)→(a=c))(λ(p:a=c).p)bh?1​ with ?1:b=c\hole{1} : b = c?1​:b=c.

What to remember

  • A proof state is a list of goals plus a partial term with holes. A tactic assigns a term to the first hole and opens one new goal per fresh hole.
  • intro builds a λ\lambdaλ, exact plugs in a term, apply builds an application with holes for the arguments, change uses T-Conv, rfl uses refl\refl{}refl​.
  • induction abstracts the variable into a motive and applies the recursor; rw abstracts the left side into a motive and applies transport.
  • The kernel re-checks the complete term, so tactics are outside the trusted base.

Chapter 11

Substitution, Capture, and Alpha-Equivalence

The previous chapters treated three operations on terms as black boxes: substitution, used by T-App, by Freshen, and by every computation step; weak head normalization, used to expose a Π\PiΠ or a universe; and definitional equality, used by Check. These operations are part of the trusted kernel, and most kernel bugs hide in them, because they must handle the names of bound variables correctly. This chapter opens the first box, substitution, shows the same naming problem in contexts, and then defines when two terms are equal up to the names of their bound variables.

Free variables and substitution

Π\PiΠ and λ\lambdaλ bind their variable: in λ(x:A). t\tLam{x}{A}{t}λ(x:A).t, occurrences of xxx inside ttt refer to the argument. The binder's scope is the body only; xxx is not bound in the annotation AAA. A variable occurrence that is not bound by an enclosing Π\PiΠ or λ\lambdaλ is free.

Definition 11.1 (Free variables).

FV(Sort u)=∅FV(Π(x:A). B)=FV(A)∪(FV(B)∖{x})FV(x)={x}FV(λ(x:A). t)=FV(A)∪(FV(t)∖{x})FV(t  s)=FV(t)∪FV(s)FV(c)=∅\begin{array}{rclcrcl} \FV(\Sort{u}) &=& \emptyset &\qquad& \FV(\tPi{x}{A}{B}) &=& \FV(A) \cup (\FV(B) \setminus \{x\}) \\[2pt] \FV(x) &=& \{x\} && \FV(\tLam{x}{A}{t}) &=& \FV(A) \cup (\FV(t) \setminus \{x\}) \\[2pt] \FV(t\;s) &=& \FV(t) \cup \FV(s) && \FV(c) &=& \emptyset \end{array}FV(Sortu)FV(x)FV(ts)​===​∅{x}FV(t)∪FV(s)​​FV(Π(x:A).B)FV(λ(x:A).t)FV(c)​===​FV(A)∪(FV(B)∖{x})FV(A)∪(FV(t)∖{x})∅​

For example, FV(λ(x:P). f  x  y)={P,f,y}\FV(\tLam{x}{P}{f\;x\;y}) = \{P, f, y\}FV(λ(x:P).fxy)={P,f,y}, and FV(Π(P:Sort 0). P→P)=∅\FV(\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}) = \emptysetFV(Π(P:Sort0).P→P)=∅, so the latter is a closed term. Constants are never bound, so they contribute nothing.

The explorer colours each bound variable like its binder and underlines free ones; hover a variable to see its binder. Try a term with shadowing, such as fun (x : A) => fun (x : A) => x.

We write t[x↦s]\subst{t}{x}{s}t[x↦s] for the result of replacing the free occurrences of xxx in ttt with sss. The only subtle case is a binder. Consider (λ(y:A). x)[x↦y]\subst{(\tLam{y}{A}{x})}{x}{y}(λ(y:A).x)[x↦y]. The body says "ignore the argument and return the outer xxx". Replacing xxx by yyy naively gives λ(y:A). y\tLam{y}{A}{y}λ(y:A).y, the identity function, which means something else: the free yyy has been captured by the binder. Substitution must avoid this by renaming the binder first.

Definition 11.2 (Capture-avoiding substitution). For □∈{Π,λ}\square \in \{\Pi, \lambda\}□∈{Π,λ}:

In the last example, the free yyy of the replacement still refers to the outer yyy, and the bound variable, now zzz, still refers to the argument. Without the renaming, the result would be λ(y:A). f  y  y\tLam{y}{A}{f\;y\;y}λ(y:A).fyy, which passes its argument twice. The explorer performs both substitutions side by side; the colours show whether the yyy in the result is the free one from the replacement or the one the binder captured.

Definitions 11.1 and 11.2 are fv and subst in src/substitution.rs. The binder case of subst is below. It has one extra shortcut compared with the definition: if xxx does not occur free in the body at all, the body is returned unchanged, which saves a traversal and never changes the result.

Term::Pi(y, domain, body) | Term::Lam(y, domain, body) => {
    let substituted_domain = subst(domain, x, replacement);
    let (renamed_binder, substituted_body) = if y == x || !fv(body).contains(x) {
        (y.clone(), (**body).clone())                       // shadowed, or nothing to do
    } else if !fv(replacement).contains(y) {
        (y.clone(), subst(body, x, replacement))            // no capture possible
    } else {
        let mut avoid = all_names(body);                    // capture: rename y to a fresh z
        avoid.extend(all_names(domain));
        avoid.extend(all_names(replacement));
        avoid.insert(x.to_string());
        let z = fresh(y, &avoid);
        let body_with_z = subst(body, y, &var(&z));
        (z, subst(&body_with_z, x, replacement))
    };
    // ... rebuild the Pi or Lam with renamed_binder, substituted_domain, substituted_body
}

The fresh function appends primes to the hint until the name is unused. The avoid set is all_names, every name in the terms involved rather than just the free ones, which is more than the definition requires but makes the output easier to read.

Variable capture in contexts

It is tempting to drop the side condition x∉dom(Γ)x \notin \dom(\Gamma)x∈/dom(Γ) of C-Ext and let a new assumption simply shadow an old one, as most programming languages do. Doing so makes the kernel unsound. Consider

t=λ(x:Sort 0). λ(y:x). λ(x:Sort 0). y.t = \tLam{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{y}{x}{\tLam{x}{\Sort{0}}{y}}}.t=λ(x:Sort0).λ(y:x).λ(x:Sort0).y.

The variable yyy has the outer xxx as its type, and the innermost λ\lambdaλ ignores its argument. So the correct type of ttt is

Π(x:Sort 0). Π(y:x). Π(x′:Sort 0). x.\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{y}{x}{\tPi{x'}{\Sort{0}}{x}}}.Π(x:Sort0).Π(y:x).Π(x′:Sort0).x.

A checker without Freshen\FreshenFreshen looks up yyy in the context x:Sort 0,  y:x,  x:Sort 0x : \Sort{0},\; y : x,\; x : \Sort{0}x:Sort0,y:x,x:Sort0 and returns its type, the bare name xxx. At that point xxx refers to the inner binder, and the checker returns

Π(x:Sort 0). Π(y:x). Π(x:Sort 0). x,\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{y}{x}{\tPi{x}{\Sort{0}}{x}}},Π(x:Sort0).Π(y:x).Π(x:Sort0).x,

which says "from any element of any type, produce an element of every type". Given A:Sort 0A : \Sort{0}A:Sort0 and a:Aa : Aa:A, the term t  A  at\;A\;atAa then has type Π(B:Sort 0). B\tPi{B}{\Sort{0}}{B}Π(B:Sort0).B, a proof of False. Such AAA and aaa exist even in the empty context: A=Π(P:Sort 0). P→PA = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}A=Π(P:Sort0).P→P is itself a proposition, and the identity function a=λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:P). ha = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}a=λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:P).h proves it.

With Freshen\FreshenFreshen, the innermost binder is renamed to x′x'x′ before it enters the context, so the context becomes x:Sort 0,  y:x,  x′:Sort 0x : \Sort{0},\; y : x,\; x' : \Sort{0}x:Sort0,y:x,x′:Sort0, the lookup of yyy returns xxx, which still refers to the outer binder, and Infer\InferInfer returns the correct type above. The derivation explorer shows the renaming happen: the note on the innermost T-Lam node reports it, and the context of the leaf contains x′x'x′.

# The kernel renames the inner x to x' and infers the correct type.
# A kernel that let the inner x shadow the outer one would accept this
# as a proof of the second statement, which is false.
goal forall (x : Sort 0), forall (y : x), forall (x' : Sort 0), x
exact fun (x : Sort 0) => fun (y : x) => fun (x : Sort 0) => y
qed
goal forall (x : Sort 0), forall (y : x), forall (x' : Sort 0), x'
exact fun (x : Sort 0) => fun (y : x) => fun (x : Sort 0) => y
qed

The problem is the same as in substitution: a name is moved into a scope where it means something else. It affects any representation that identifies variables by name, whether the context is a list or a hash map. There are three common remedies.

  1. Reject shadowing outright. This is the simplest option, but the reserved name _ used by A→BA \to BA→B must be exempt and never added to the context.
  2. Rename on entry, as Freshen\FreshenFreshen does. This is our choice.
  3. Represent bound variables by position (de Bruijn indices [de Bruijn 1972]) or use the locally nameless style, in which bound variables are indices and free variables carry unique identifiers. Lean 4 takes the latter approach.

A test suite should include ttt above and check that the kernel either rejects it or assigns it the correct type.

This bug is easy to write and hard to notice, because every ordinary proof still checks. Only a term that deliberately reuses a name in a nested binder exposes it. A kernel's test suite needs adversarial terms, not just correct proofs.

Alpha-equivalence

The names of bound variables carry no meaning. λ(x:A). x\tLam{x}{A}{x}λ(x:A).x and λ(y:A). y\tLam{y}{A}{y}λ(y:A).y are the same function, and Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P and Π(Q:Sort 0). Q→Q\tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{Q \to Q}Π(Q:Sort0).Q→Q are the same proposition. Terms that differ only in the names of bound variables are called alpha-equivalent. A kernel cannot compare types with plain syntactic equality, which would reject the second pair.

Definition 11.3 (Alpha-equivalence). =α\alphaeq=α​ is the smallest congruence on terms containing, for □∈{Π,λ}\square \in \{\Pi, \lambda\}□∈{Π,λ},

□(x:A). B  =α  □(y:A). B[x↦y]whenever y∉FV(B).\square(x{:}A).\,B \;\alphaeq\; \square(y{:}A).\,\subst{B}{x}{y} \qquad \text{whenever } y \notin \FV(B).□(x:A).B=α​□(y:A).B[x↦y]whenever y∈/FV(B).

(A congruence is an equivalence relation that is preserved by every term constructor: if the parts are related, so are the wholes.) This definition is easy to state but not directly executable, since it does not say which names to choose. An implementation instead walks both terms in lockstep and remembers, for each side, the list of binders passed so far. A bound variable is then identified by which binder it refers to, not by its name.

To describe this walk, we use a judgment of the form E1;E2⊢s=αtE_1; E_2 \vdash s \alphaeq tE1​;E2​⊢s=α​t, where E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​ are lists of names. The list E1E_1E1​ records the binders that enclose sss, from the outermost to the innermost, and E2E_2E2​ records those that enclose ttt. The judgment reads: "sss, placed inside the binders E1E_1E1​, and ttt, placed inside the binders E2E_2E2​, are the same term up to the names of bound variables". Two lists are needed because the two terms may use different names for corresponding binders. For example, comparing λ(x:A). λ(y:B). x\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{y}{B}{x}}λ(x:A).λ(y:B).x with λ(a:A). λ(b:B). a\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{B}{a}}λ(a:A).λ(b:B).a passes two binders on each side and arrives at

x,y;  a,b⊢x=αa,x, y;\; a, b \vdash x \alphaeq a,x,y;a,b⊢x=α​a,

which holds because xxx and aaa both refer to the outer of the two binders. Comparing two whole terms starts from empty lists, ⋅ ;⋅⊢s=αt\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t⋅;⋅⊢s=α​t.

To say "the same binder" precisely, let idx(E,x)\mathrm{idx}(E, x)idx(E,x) be the position of the last occurrence of xxx in EEE, counted from the right starting at 000, or undefined if x∉Ex \notin Ex∈/E. In the example, idx((x,y),x)=idx((a,b),a)=1\mathrm{idx}((x, y), x) = \mathrm{idx}((a, b), a) = 1idx((x,y),x)=idx((a,b),a)=1. Taking the last occurrence handles shadowing: in λ(x:A). λ(x:B). x\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{x}{B}{x}}λ(x:A).λ(x:B).x the body refers to the inner xxx.

Free variables are compared by name (α\alphaα-Free), bound variables by position (α\alphaα-Bound), and constants by name (α\alphaα-Const). A variable that is bound on one side and free on the other is never equal to anything, which is why there is no rule for that case. Because both sides descend through binders together, E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​ always have the same length. So comparing positions counted from the right is the same as comparing positions counted from the left, and an implementation may store each list as a map from names to binding depths, provided it restores the previous entry when it leaves a binder. Using positions instead of names everywhere gives the de Bruijn representation, in which alpha-equivalent terms are syntactically identical.

Examples

The first example of Chapter 6 ended by comparing the inferred type with the stated one, where P→PP \to PP→P abbreviates Π(_:P). P\tPi{\_}{P}{P}Π(_:P).P:

  • ⋅ ;⋅⊢Π(P:Sort 0). Π(h:P). Sort 0=αΠ(P:Sort 0). Π(_:P). P\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}}} \alphaeq \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tPi{\_}{P}{P}}⋅;⋅⊢Π(P:Sort0).Π(h:P).Sort0=α​Π(P:Sort0).Π(_:P).P α\alphaα-Pi

    • P; P⊢Π(h:P). Sort 0=αΠ(_:P). PP;\, P \vdash \tPi{h}{P}{\Sort{0}} \alphaeq \tPi{\_}{P}{P}P;P⊢Π(h:P).Sort0=α​Π(_:P).P α\alphaα-Pi

      • P,h;  P,_⊢Sort 0=αPP, h;\; P, \_ \vdash \Sort{0} \alphaeq PP,h;P,_⊢Sort0=α​P: no rule applies

Positions also tell apart terms that a careless comparison of names would confuse. λ(x:A). λ(y:A). x\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{y}{A}{x}}λ(x:A).λ(y:A).x and λ(a:A). λ(b:A). b\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{A}{b}}λ(a:A).λ(b:A).b are not alpha-equivalent: the bodies reach x,y; a,b⊢x=αbx, y;\, a, b \vdash x \alphaeq bx,y;a,b⊢x=α​b, and idx\mathrm{idx}idx gives 111 for xxx but 000 for bbb. Conversely, λ(x:A). λ(x:A). x\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{x}{A}{x}}λ(x:A).λ(x:A).x and λ(a:A). λ(b:A). b\tLam{a}{A}{\tLam{b}{A}{b}}λ(a:A).λ(b:A).b are alpha-equivalent, because the last occurrence of xxx in (x,x)(x, x)(x,x) has index 000, the same as bbb in (a,b)(a, b)(a,b).

The rules of Figure 11.1 are a different definition from Definition 11.3, so we must check that they agree.

Theorem 11.4 (Correctness of algorithmic alpha-equivalence). For all terms sss and ttt, s=αts \alphaeq ts=α​t in the sense of Definition 11.3 if and only if ⋅ ;⋅⊢s=αt\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t⋅;⋅⊢s=α​t is derivable by the rules of Figure 11.1.

The idea of the proof is that both sides say the same thing: sss and ttt have the same de Bruijn representation. For the algorithm this is almost immediate, since its rules compare positions exactly as de Bruijn indices do. For Definition 11.3, the key fact is that renaming a bound variable does not change the de Bruijn representation. Appendix B gives the full proof.

Figure 11.1 is the function alpha in src/substitution.rs. The two binder lists are Vec<String>s pushed and popped around the recursive call on bodies, and binder_distance is idx\mathrm{idx}idx: it searches the list from the end, so the distance to the nearest enclosing binder of that name is found first.

(Term::Var(x), Term::Var(y)) => {
    match (binder_distance(bound_a, x), binder_distance(bound_b, y)) {
        (Some(i), Some(j)) => i == j,     // alpha-Bound
        (None, None) => x == y,           // alpha-Free
        _ => false,                       // bound on one side only
    }
}

Exercises

Compute (λ(y:A). λ(x:B). x  y)[x↦y]\subst{(\tLam{y}{A}{\tLam{x}{B}{x\;y}})}{x}{y}(λ(y:A).λ(x:B).xy)[x↦y] step by step.

Solution

The outer binder is yyy, which is free in the replacement yyy, so the capture case applies: rename yyy to a fresh zzz, giving body λ(x:B). x  z\tLam{x}{B}{x\;z}λ(x:B).xz, then substitute. The inner binder is xxx, the variable being replaced, so the inner body is untouched. Result: λ(z:A). λ(x:B). x  z\tLam{z}{A}{\tLam{x}{B}{x\;z}}λ(z:A).λ(x:B).xz. Note that the inner xxx was never a free occurrence, so nothing was replaced at all; the only effect was the renaming forced by capture avoidance.

Decide whether λ(x:A). λ(y:A). y  x\tLam{x}{A}{\tLam{y}{A}{y\;x}}λ(x:A).λ(y:A).yx and λ(y:A). λ(x:A). x  y\tLam{y}{A}{\tLam{x}{A}{x\;y}}λ(y:A).λ(x:A).xy are alpha-equivalent by running Figure 11.1.

Solution

Yes. After two α\alphaα-Lam steps the lists are x,yx, yx,y and y,xy, xy,x, and the bodies are y  xy\;xyx and x  yx\;yxy. α\alphaα-App compares yyy with xxx: indices 000 and 000. Then xxx with yyy: indices 111 and 111. Both hold. Names are swapped, positions agree.

What to remember

  • Substitution replaces free occurrences only, and must rename a binder when the replacement mentions the binder's name (capture).
  • The same capture problem arises in contexts. A kernel that lets a binder shadow a context entry can prove False; Freshen prevents it.
  • Alpha-equivalence compares bound variables by the position of their binder and free variables by name. Figure 11.1 is the algorithm; Theorem 11.4 says it matches the definition.
  • All three live in src/substitution.rs: subst, fv, and alpha.

Chapter 12

Reduction and Conversion

Chapter 11 handled names. This chapter handles computation: the three kinds of reduction step, the definition of definitional equality, and the algorithms Whnf, Normalize, and IsDefEq that Algorithm 5.1 left open. The main design point is that the computation rules of inductive types are stored as data in the signature, so one reduction function serves every inductive type ever declared.

Reduction

Applying a λ\lambdaλ-abstraction to an argument is computed by substituting the argument for the bound variable:

(λ(x:A). t)  s  →β  t[x↦s].(\tLam{x}{A}{t})\;s \;\betared\; \subst{t}{x}{s}.(λ(x:A).t)s→β​t[x↦s].

This step is beta-reduction, and a subterm of the form (λ(x:A). t)  s(\tLam{x}{A}{t})\;s(λ(x:A).t)s is a beta-redex. Part II added two more kinds of step: delta-reduction, which unfolds a definition (Chapter 7), and iota-reduction, which runs a recursor on a constructor (Figures 7.1 and 9.1, and the general rule of Chapter 8). We allow each step anywhere inside a term, and write →\to→ for a single step of any kind. A term in which no step applies is in normal form. For example, with Id=λ(X:Sort 0). X\mathit{Id} = \tLam{X}{\Sort{0}}{X}Id=λ(X:Sort0).X,

λ(h:Id  P). (λ(y:P). y)  h  →β  λ(h:P). (λ(y:P). y)  h  →β  λ(h:P). h,\tLam{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{(\tLam{y}{P}{y})\;h} \;\betared\; \tLam{h}{P}{(\tLam{y}{P}{y})\;h} \;\betared\; \tLam{h}{P}{h},λ(h:IdP).(λ(y:P).y)h→β​λ(h:P).(λ(y:P).y)h→β​λ(h:P).h,

and the last term is in normal form. Reducing the inner redex first leads to the same result.

Conversion

Definitional equality, also called conversion, identifies terms that compute to the same result, up to the names of bound variables.

Definition 12.1 (Conversion). s≡ts \conv ts≡t is the smallest equivalence relation that contains =α\alphaeq=α​ and →\to→ and is closed under all term constructors.

To decide s≡ts \conv ts≡t, the kernel normalizes both terms and compares the results with =α\alphaeq=α​. This procedure relies on two facts.

  • Reduction is confluent: different reduction orders cannot lead to different normal forms. So s≡ts \conv ts≡t holds exactly when the normal forms of sss and ttt are alpha-equivalent; there is no need to search for a clever sequence of steps.
  • Every well-typed term has a normal form, so normalization terminates. This holds for our system, but it is a deep theorem (strong normalization, Chapter 14) [Barendregt 1992].

A practical kernel also caps the number of reduction steps, so that a bug cannot make it loop forever; our implementation stops after 20,000 steps with the error "reduction fuel exhausted".

Why decide equality by normalizing rather than by searching for a chain of steps? Because confluence turns an existence question ("is there some way to make these equal?") into a canonical-form question ("do they have the same normal form?"), which has a direct algorithm. The price is that normalization can be expensive: a definition that unfolds into a large term is fully expanded even if the two sides differ in their first symbol. Production kernels avoid this with lazy comparison, discussed at the end of the chapter.

Computation rules as data

Figures 7.1 and 9.1 write each iota-rule as a separate equation, which suggests that every new inductive type needs new reduction code in the kernel. It does not. A kernel stores the iota-rules as data in the signature, next to the recursor, and a single piece of code applies them for every inductive type.

Each recursor entry records the position of its major premise, the argument whose constructor decides which rule applies, and the constructors of its inductive type. For each constructor the kernel knows how many leading arguments are parameters (which the rule ignores) and how many are fields (which the rule passes on), and which fields are recursive. For three of our recursors, the data and the resulting right-hand sides are as follows; type annotations on λ\lambdaλ are omitted.

RecursorMajorConstructorParams, fieldsRight-hand sideNat.recu4thzero0,  0λM z s.  zsucc0,  1λM z s n.  s  n  (Nat.recu  M  z  s  n)Eq.recu,v6threflu2,  0λA a M m b.  mTree.recv5thleaf0,  0λM m1 m2 m3.  m1node0,  1λM m1 m2 m3 t.  m2  t  (Tree.recv  M m1 m2 m3  t)branch0,  2λM m1 m2 m3 l r.  m3  l  r  (Tree.recv  M m1 m2 m3  l)  (⋯  r)\begin{array}{llcll} \textbf{Recursor} & \textbf{Major} & \textbf{Constructor} & \textbf{Params, fields} & \textbf{Right-hand side} \\[2pt] \NatRec{u} & \text{4th} & \zero & 0,\;0 & \lambda M\,z\,s.\; z \\[2pt] & & \suc & 0,\;1 & \lambda M\,z\,s\,n.\; s\;n\;(\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;n) \\[2pt] \EqRecDep{u,v} & \text{6th} & \refl{u} & 2,\;0 & \lambda A\,a\,M\,m\,b.\; m \\[2pt] \mathsf{Tree.rec}_v & \text{5th} & \mathsf{leaf} & 0,\;0 & \lambda M\,m_1\,m_2\,m_3.\; m_1 \\[2pt] & & \mathsf{node} & 0,\;1 & \lambda M\,m_1\,m_2\,m_3\,t.\; m_2\;t\;(\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v\;M\,m_1\,m_2\,m_3\;t) \\[2pt] & & \mathsf{branch} & 0,\;2 & \lambda M\,m_1\,m_2\,m_3\,l\,r.\; m_3\;l\;r\;(\mathsf{Tree.rec}_v\;M\,m_1\,m_2\,m_3\;l)\;(\cdots\;r) \end{array}RecursorNat.recu​Eq.recu,v​Tree.recv​​Major4th6th5th​Constructorzerosuccreflu​leafnodebranch​Params, fields0,00,12,00,00,10,2​Right-hand sideλMzs.zλMzsn.sn(Nat.recu​Mzsn)λAaMmb.mλMm1​m2​m3​.m1​λMm1​m2​m3​t.m2​t(Tree.recv​Mm1​m2​m3​t)λMm1​m2​m3​lr.m3​lr(Tree.recv​Mm1​m2​m3​l)(⋯r)​

Weak head normal form and normalization

Algorithm 12.1 defines the three functions that Algorithm 5.1 left open. Both Whnf\WhnfWhnf and Normalize\NormalizeNormalize view a term as a spine h  a1⋯anh\;a_1 \cdots a_nha1​⋯an​: a head hhh that is not an application, applied to n≥0n \ge 0n≥0 arguments (Chapter 2). Every term has exactly one such decomposition.

Algorithm 12.1. Weak head normalization with beta, delta, and iota; full normalization; and definitional equality.

Whnf(t):
  loop:
    write t as a spine h a_1 ... a_n
    if h = λ(x : A). b and n ≥ 1:                               -- beta
        t ← (b[x ↦ a_1]) a_2 ... a_n
    else if h = c and (c : C := d) ∈ Σ:                         -- delta
        t ← d a_1 ... a_n
    else if h = c is a recursor with major position p ≤ n:      -- iota
        k b_1 ... b_j ← Whnf(a_p)
        if k is a constructor of c's inductive type with q parameters:
            t ← rhs_k a_1 ... a_{p-1} b_{q+1} ... b_j a_{p+1} ... a_n
        else return t                                           -- stuck, e.g. on a variable
    else return t

Normalize(t):
  t ← Whnf(t)
  if t = Π(x : A). B:  return Π(x : Normalize(A)). Normalize(B)
  if t = λ(x : A). b:  return λ(x : Normalize(A)). Normalize(b)
  else write t as a spine h a_1 ... a_n and return h Normalize(a_1) ... Normalize(a_n)

IsDefEq(s, t):
  return  · ; · ⊢ Normalize(s) =α Normalize(t)                  -- Figure 11.1

Whnf\WhnfWhnf reduces only at the head of a term, until no rule applies there; the result is the weak head normal form. It never looks inside a λ\lambdaλ, a Π\PiΠ, or the arguments of a stuck head. This is enough when a caller only needs the outermost shape of a type, such as a Π\PiΠ in the application case of Infer\InferInfer, and it is cheaper than full normalization. Normalize\NormalizeNormalize first computes the weak head normal form and then normalizes every immediate subterm. For example, with t=λ(h:Id  P). ht = \tLam{h}{\mathit{Id}\;P}{h}t=λ(h:IdP).h and Id\mathit{Id}Id as above,

Whnf(t)=t,Normalize(t)=λ(h:P). h,\Whnf(t) = t, \qquad \Normalize(t) = \tLam{h}{P}{h},Whnf(t)=t,Normalize(t)=λ(h:P).h,

because the head of ttt is a λ\lambdaλ with no arguments, while Normalize\NormalizeNormalize continues into the annotation Id  P\mathit{Id}\;PIdP. Likewise, Whnf(Id  (Id  P→P))=Id  P→P\Whnf(\mathit{Id}\;(\mathit{Id}\;P \to P)) = \mathit{Id}\;P \to PWhnf(Id(IdP→P))=IdP→P, which already shows a Π\PiΠ although its domain is not yet normal. Both are visible below: no head step applies, yet the normal form differs.

The three cases of Whnf\WhnfWhnf have the following properties.

  • The iota case contains no reference to Nat\NatNat, Eq\Eq{}Eq​, or Tree\mathsf{Tree}Tree. It reads the major position and the constructor data from the signature. It is written once; after that, each new inductive type adds rows of data, not code.
  • The major premise is put in weak head normal form before the rules are consulted, because it may become a constructor only after computation. For 2+12 + 12+1 in Chapter 7, the major premise is the numeral 1=succ  zero1 = \suc\;\zero1=succzero, already a constructor; for double  (1+1)\mathit{double}\;(1 + 1)double(1+1), it is 1+11 + 11+1, which Whnf\WhnfWhnf turns into succ  (1+0)\suc\;(1 + 0)succ(1+0) first.
  • If the major premise does not become a constructor, for instance because it is a variable, the term is stuck and stays as it is; this is why 0+n0 + n0+n does not reduce (Chapter 9).

Here is Whnf\WhnfWhnf at work on double  (1+1)\mathit{double}\;(1 + 1)double(1+1), with double\mathit{double}double as in Chapter 7, computed live. Only the head is ever reduced, but reducing the major premise forces an inner computation.

def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n
def double : Nat -> Nat := fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) Nat.zero (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ (Nat.succ r)) n

The step marked whnf is the inner computation: the recursor needs its major premise to be a constructor, so 1+11 + 11+1 is reduced at its head first. The final weak head normal form still contains a stuck inner recursor; the normal form below it is what Normalize\NormalizeNormalize produces by continuing inside.

IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq normalizes fully for simplicity, and our implementation does the same. Practical kernels compare lazily instead: they reduce both sides to weak head normal form, compare the heads, and recurse into the arguments only when needed, which avoids normalizing large terms that differ at the head. Termination of all three functions for well-typed terms is strong normalization.

In the code

Algorithm 12.1 is src/reduction.rs. whnf, normalize, and is_def_eq are thin wrappers that allocate the fuel budget (REDUCTION_FUEL = 20000) and call whnf_with_fuel, normalize_with_fuel, and is_def_eq_with_fuel. The loop in whnf_with_fuel is a direct transcription:

let (head, args) = spine(&t);
let reduced = match head {
    // beta: (fun x. b) a_1 a_2 ... a_n  ~>  b[x := a_1] a_2 ... a_n
    Term::Lam(x, _, body) if !args.is_empty() => Some(apps(
        subst(&body, &x, &args[0]),
        args[1..].iter().cloned(),
    )),
    Term::Const(c) => match self.decls.get(&c) {
        // delta: c as  ~>  d as   where (c := d) in Sigma
        Some(Decl { kind: DeclKind::Definition(body), .. }) => Some(apps(body.clone(), args)),
        // iota: I.rec ps M ms is (c_j ps' as)  ~>  m_j as hs
        Some(Decl { kind: DeclKind::Recursor(recursor), .. }) => {
            self.iota_reduce(&c, recursor, &args, fuel)?
        }
        _ => None,
    },
    _ => None,
};
match reduced {
    Some(next) => t = next,
    None => return Ok(t),
}

iota_reduce finds the major premise at recursor.major_argument_index, puts it in weak head normal form, checks that its head is a constructor of the right inductive type applied to all of its parameters and fields, checks that the constructor's parameters are convertible to the recursor's (a well-typed redex guarantees this, but the kernel verifies rather than assumes), and then builds mj  a⃗  h⃗m_j\;\vec{a}\;\vec{h}mj​ah followed by any extra arguments. The induction hypotheses h⃗\vec{h}h are built by induction_hypothesis, which instantiates the stored y⃗:B⃗\vec{y} : \vec{B}y​:B and s⃗\vec{s}s of each recursive field with the actual parameters and field values and wraps a recursive call in the corresponding λ\lambdaλs.

Rather than storing a right-hand-side term per rule as in the table above, the implementation computes the right-hand side from the InductiveInfo each time. The two are equivalent; computing on the fly avoids keeping a second copy of the constructor data in sync.

One subtlety in normalize_with_fuel deserves mention. After normalizing the function and argument of an application, it calls whnf on the rebuilt term once more. Normalizing an argument can expose a new redex at the head: for a stuck recursor application whose major premise becomes a constructor only after its own arguments are normalized, the head must be reduced again. Without this re-check, is_def_eq would miss some equalities, and the test conversion_renormalizes_exposed_redex in src/proof.rs guards it.

Exercises

Give the weak head normal form and the normal form of (λ(f:Nat→Nat). f)  (λ(x:Nat). x)  zero(\tLam{f}{\Nat \to \Nat}{f})\;(\tLam{x}{\Nat}{x})\;\zero(λ(f:Nat→Nat).f)(λ(x:Nat).x)zero.

Solution

The spine has head λ(f:Nat→Nat). f\tLam{f}{\Nat \to \Nat}{f}λ(f:Nat→Nat).f with two arguments. Beta on the first argument gives (λ(x:Nat). x)  zero(\tLam{x}{\Nat}{x})\;\zero(λ(x:Nat).x)zero, which is again a beta-redex at the head and reduces to zero\zerozero. So both the weak head normal form and the normal form are zero\zerozero. (This is the term in the test conversion_renormalizes_exposed_redex.)

Why does Whnf\WhnfWhnf not reduce under a λ\lambdaλ? What would go wrong in Infer\InferInfer if Whnf\WhnfWhnf returned λ(x:A). b\tLam{x}{A}{b}λ(x:A).b with bbb normalized?

Solution

Nothing would be wrong: the result would still be convertible to the input. But it would be wasted work. Infer\InferInfer calls Whnf\WhnfWhnf only to learn the outermost shape, which is already visible once the head is a λ\lambdaλ. Reducing inside could be arbitrarily expensive, for instance in an annotation that is never compared with anything. Keeping Whnf\WhnfWhnf shallow is what makes type inference cheap on large terms.

What to remember

  • Three reduction steps: beta (apply a λ\lambdaλ), delta (unfold a definition), iota (run a recursor on a constructor). Conversion is the equivalence they generate together with alpha-equivalence.
  • Conversion is decided by normalizing both sides and comparing up to alpha, which is correct by confluence and terminates by strong normalization.
  • Iota-rules are data: the major premise position plus constructor metadata. One whnf serves every inductive type.
  • Whnf reduces only at the head and is what Infer needs; Normalize goes everywhere and is what IsDefEq uses. A step budget guards against bugs.

Chapter 13

Universes: Why Sort u?

Chapter 4 showed that the typing rules implement a logic, and that the system is acceptable only if it is consistent. This chapter asks a question that has been deferred since Chapter 2: what is the type of Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0? The simplest answer, a single universe that contains itself, makes the system inconsistent. Lean's answer, a hierarchy Sort 0:Sort 1:Sort 2:⋯\Sort{0} : \Sort{1} : \Sort{2} : \cdotsSort0:Sort1:Sort2:⋯ with an impredicative bottom universe, does not. Along the way the chapter explains the one odd-looking piece of T-Pi, the function imax\imaximax.

What is the type of Sort 0?

A proposition variable appears in the type theory as an assumption P:Sort 0P : \Sort{0}P:Sort0. It can occur in two places: in a context, as in the left judgment below, or bound by λ\lambdaλ or Π\PiΠ, as in the right one:

P:Sort 0⊢λ(h:P). h:P→Pversus⊢λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:P). h:Π(P:Sort 0). P→P.P : \Sort{0} \vdash \tLam{h}{P}{h} : P \to P \qquad\text{versus}\qquad \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}.P:Sort0⊢λ(h:P).h:P→Pversus⊢λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:P).h:Π(P:Sort0).P→P.

The left judgment proves P→PP \to PP→P for one fixed PPP supplied from outside. The right one is a single closed term that proves it for every PPP, and it can be applied later to any particular proposition; this is what the ∀\forall∀ rows of Figure 4.1 need.

Both forms require Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 to be a type. C-Ext, which adds P:Sort 0P : \Sort{0}P:Sort0 to a context, and T-Lam and T-Pi, which bind P:Sort 0P : \Sort{0}P:Sort0, all have the premise Γ⊢A:Sort u\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u}Γ⊢A:Sortu for the type AAA of the new variable. With A=Sort 0A = \Sort{0}A=Sort0, this premise reads Γ⊢Sort 0:Sort u\Gamma \vdash \Sort{0} : \Sort{u}Γ⊢Sort0:Sortu for some uuu: the universe of propositions must itself have a type. The question is which.

Type is not a type

Suppose we replace all universes by a single universe Type\mathsf{Type}Type that contains itself:

⊢Γ;okΓ⊢Type:TypeΓ⊢A:TypeΓ,x:A⊢B:TypeΓ⊢Π(x:A). B:Type\dfrac{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}} \qquad \dfrac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathsf{Type} \qquad \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \mathsf{Type}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \mathsf{Type}}Γ⊢Type:Type⊢Γ;ok​Γ⊢Π(x:A).B:TypeΓ⊢A:TypeΓ,x:A⊢B:Type​

Translate ∀P. φ\forall P.\,\varphi∀P.φ as Π(P:Type). φ∗\tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{\varphi^\ast}Π(P:Type).φ∗. Then PPP ranges over a collection that contains Type\mathsf{Type}Type itself and every type built from it. Such a collection is the type-theoretic analogue of the set of all sets, and naive set theory shows that such collections lead to contradictions. The best-known example is Russell's paradox: for R={ x∣x∉x }R = \{\, x \mid x \notin x \,\}R={x∣x∈/x}, both R∈RR \in RR∈R and R∉RR \notin RR∈/R lead to a contradiction.

Type theory has no membership test like x∉xx \notin xx∈/x, so Russell's argument does not carry over word for word. Girard instead adapted a related paradox about the collection of all well-orderings, due to Burali-Forti [Girard 1972], and Hurkens simplified the resulting term [Hurkens 1995]. The result is a closed term tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ with

⊢tH:Π(P:Type). P,\vdash t_{\mathrm{H}} : \tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{P},⊢tH​:Π(P:Type).P,

so the system is inconsistent: ⊥\bot⊥ has no proof, yet ⊥∗\bot^\ast⊥∗ has a term, and a kernel built on these rules accepts a proof of every statement. The essential ingredient is a type UUU that quantifies over all of Type\mathsf{Type}Type while being a member of Type\mathsf{Type}Type, which lets UUU contain a copy of its own double power set, something no set can do. Appendix C gives tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ in full, explains how it works, and shows how to reproduce the result by changing one line of the kernel.

The damage reaches the algorithm as well. Subject reduction still holds, so if tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ had a normal form, it would be a normal closed term of type Π(p:Type). p\tPi{p}{\mathsf{Type}}{p}Π(p:Type).p. The part of the consistency proof in Appendix D that analyses normal terms does not use strong normalization and carries over to Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type; it shows that no such normal term exists. Hence tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ has no normal form, strong normalization fails, and Normalize\NormalizeNormalize runs forever on it. A kernel with Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type is not only unsound but also, on some inputs, non-terminating.

Martin-Löf's first type theory of 1971 had exactly this rule, and Girard's paradox was discovered against it the following year. Every dependent type theory since then has had either a hierarchy of universes or some other device to break the self-reference. The paradox is not a curiosity: the self-containing universe is the obvious design, and the obvious design is wrong.

A hierarchy with an impredicative bottom

The second answer is that Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 lives in a larger universe, which lives in a larger one still:

⊢Γ;okΓ⊢Sort u:Sort (u+1);(T-Sort)soSort 0:Sort 1:Sort 2:⋯ .\dfrac{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}}\rulename{T-Sort} \qquad\text{so}\qquad \Sort{0} : \Sort{1} : \Sort{2} : \cdots.Γ⊢Sortu:Sort(u+1)⊢Γ;ok​;(T-Sort)soSort0:Sort1:Sort2:⋯.

No universe contains itself. A Π\PiΠ-type takes an argument from one universe and returns a type in another, so T-Pi must also say which universe the Π\PiΠ-type itself belongs to. Lean's answer uses the function imax\imaximax:

Γ⊢A:Sort uΓ,x:A⊢B:Sort vΓ⊢Π(x:A). B:Sort imax(u,v);(T-Pi)imax(u,v)={0if v=0,max⁡(u,v)otherwise.\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u} \qquad \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \Sort{v}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \Sort{\imax(u, v)}}\rulename{T-Pi} \qquad \imax(u, v) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } v = 0, \\ \max(u, v) & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}Γ⊢Π(x:A).B:Sortimax(u,v)Γ⊢A:SortuΓ,x:A⊢B:Sortv​;(T-Pi)imax(u,v)={0max(u,v)​if v=0,otherwise.​

The case split in imax\imaximax makes a Π\PiΠ-type impredicative when its body is a proposition, and predicative otherwise. Pick the universes of AAA and BBB below and watch where the Π\PiΠ-type lands.

Propositions are impredicative. If the body BBB is a proposition (v=0v = 0v=0), the whole Π\PiΠ is a proposition, whatever it quantifies over. In particular (∀P. φ)∗=Π(P:Sort 0). φ∗(\forall P.\,\varphi)^\ast = \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}(∀P.φ)∗=Π(P:Sort0).φ∗ is in Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0, although it quantifies over all of Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0. A universe that contains types quantifying over itself is called impredicative. Because every translated formula lies in Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0, the premise ψ∗:Sort 0\psi^\ast : \Sort{0}ψ∗:Sort0 of ∀\forall∀-elim always holds, so a universal statement can be instantiated with any proposition, even with itself. For example, with id=λ(P:Sort 0). λ(h:P). h\mathit{id} = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{\tLam{h}{P}{h}}id=λ(P:Sort0).λ(h:P).h,

id:Π(P:Sort 0). P→PandΠ(P:Sort 0). P→P:Sort 0,\mathit{id} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P} : \Sort{0},id:Π(P:Sort0).P→PandΠ(P:Sort0).P→P:Sort0,

so id  (Π(P:Sort 0). P→P)  id\mathit{id}\;(\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P})\;\mathit{id}id(Π(P:Sort0).P→P)id is well typed, with type Π(P:Sort 0). P→P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P \to P}Π(P:Sort0).P→P. The same case makes ∀n:Nat, n+0=n\forall n : \Nat,\, n + 0 = n∀n:Nat,n+0=n a proposition, even though Nat\NatNat lives in Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1; Chapter 7 relied on this for induction.

# "Every proposition implies itself" is itself a proposition,
# so it can be instantiated with itself.
def id : forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P := fun (P : Sort 0) => fun (h : P) => h
def self : forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P := id (forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P) id

# The analogous statement one level up is NOT its own instance:
# forall (A : Sort 1), A -> A lives in Sort 2, not Sort 1.
def idT : forall (A : Sort 1), A -> A := fun (A : Sort 1) => fun (a : A) => a
def selfT : forall (A : Sort 1), A -> A := idT (forall (A : Sort 1), A -> A) idT

Types are predicative. If the body is not a proposition (v≥1v \ge 1v≥1), the Π\PiΠ lives in the larger of the two universes. A type that quantifies over Sort u\Sort{u}Sortu then lives in Sort (max⁡(u+1,v))\Sort{(\max(u+1, v))}Sort(max(u+1,v)), which is never Sort u\Sort{u}Sortu:

Γ⊢Sort u:Sort (u+1);(T-Sort)Γ,x:Sort u⊢B:Sort vΓ⊢Π(x:Sort u). B:Sort (max⁡(u+1,v));(T-Pi)\dfrac{ \dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}}\rulename{T-Sort} \qquad \Gamma, x : \Sort{u} \vdash B : \Sort{v} }{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{\Sort{u}}{B} : \Sort{(\max(u+1, v))}}\rulename{T-Pi}Γ⊢Π(x:Sortu).B:Sort(max(u+1,v))Γ⊢Sortu:Sort(u+1)​;(T-Sort)Γ,x:Sortu⊢B:Sortv​;(T-Pi)

This property is called predicativity. For example, the identity on types λ(A:Sort 1). λ(a:A). a\tLam{A}{\Sort{1}}{\tLam{a}{A}{a}}λ(A:Sort1).λ(a:A).a has type Π(A:Sort 1). A→A\tPi{A}{\Sort{1}}{A \to A}Π(A:Sort1).A→A, which lives in Sort 2\Sort{2}Sort2, so it cannot be applied to its own type; a copy at Sort 2\Sort{2}Sort2 can. Each level holds the level beneath it, and in practice a few levels suffice; higher levels appear when one quantifies over large collections, such as the category of all small categories.

Why this is safe. Impredicativity looks like the self-reference that the previous section warned against, but it is confined: Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 contains types that quantify over Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0, yet Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 is not a member of itself. Coquand showed that one impredicative universe at the bottom is consistent [Coquand 1988], whereas Girard's paradox can already be derived once two levels are impredicative [Hurkens 1995]. With these rules the system is consistent and strongly normalizing (Chapter 14).

Why may propositions be impredicative when types may not? Because a proof of a proposition carries no data that a program could extract (this is exactly what the elimination restriction of Chapter 8 enforces). Quantifying over all propositions to define a proposition is like defining a set by a property that mentions all sets: dangerous when the result is itself an object that the quantifier ranges over and can be inspected, harmless when all one can do with it is use it as a hypothesis. The paradox needs to inspect the thing it builds; propositions cannot be inspected.

Comparison with Lean

In Lean [de Moura and Ullrich 2021], Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 is Prop, Sort (u+1)\Sort{(u+1)}Sort(u+1) is Type u, and Π\PiΠ-types are assigned universes with imax\imaximax exactly as above. Two differences remain.

First, Prop in Lean has definitional proof irrelevance: any two proofs of the same proposition are definitionally equal. Our conversion does not identify proofs; adding this would make conversion depend on types, so the simple "normalize and compare" check of Chapter 12 would no longer suffice.

Second, Lean has universe polymorphism, so definitions can be stated once for all levels uuu, and imax\imaximax then matters for level variables as well, with constraints such as imax(u,v)≤w\imax(u, v) \le wimax(u,v)≤w solved symbolically. In our system every level is a concrete number.

Two sorts ∗:□\ast : \square∗:□ ∗\ast∗ only □\square□ itself has no type

Sort u:Sort (u+1)\Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}Sortu:Sort(u+1) with imax\imaximax (Lean) any level normalization is harder to prove

The whole of this chapter is two lines of infer in src/typecheck.rs: the Sort(u) case returns Sort(u + 1), and the Pi case returns Sort(0) when the body's level is 0 and the maximum otherwise. Appendix C shows that changing the first line to return Sort(u) makes the kernel accept Hurkens' term.

idT expects an argument A:Sort 1A : \Sort{1}A:Sort1.
