What to remember

  • Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 needs a type, because proposition variables are bound by λ\lambdaλ and Π\PiΠ.
  • A universe containing itself is inconsistent (Girard, Hurkens) and breaks normalization.
  • The hierarchy Sort u:Sort (u+1)\Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)}Sortu:Sort(u+1) avoids self-containment; imax\imaximax makes propositions impredicative and everything else predicative.
  • One impredicative universe at the bottom is safe; two are not. Lean adds proof irrelevance and universe polymorphism on top of the same design.

Chapter 14

Properties of the System

The chapters so far have made two kinds of claim about the kernel: that its algorithm terminates, and that it never accepts a proof of False. Both rest on theorems about the type system that are much harder than anything the kernel itself does. This chapter states those theorems, explains what each one buys, and sketches how consistency follows from them. The full proof of consistency is in Appendix D.

The core system

The theorems below concern the core system: the rules of Figure 3.1, with the universes of Chapter 13 and without the constants of Part II. This is a Pure Type System in the sense of Barendregt: the Calculus of Constructions [Coquand 1988] with a hierarchy of predicative universes above its impredicative Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0, close to Luo's Extended Calculus of Constructions [Luo 1990]. The first three properties hold for every functional Pure Type System [Barendregt 1992]. Strong normalization is much harder in the presence of impredicativity and needs Girard's method of reducibility candidates [Girard 1972; Coquand 1988; Luo 1990]. The end of the chapter says what changes with inductive types.

Four properties

Theorem 14.1 (Uniqueness of types). If Γ⊢t:A\Gamma \vdash t : AΓ⊢t:A and Γ⊢t:B\Gamma \vdash t : BΓ⊢t:B, then A≡BA \conv BA≡B.

A term has, up to conversion, one type. This is what makes Infer\InferInfer meaningful: there is a single answer for it to compute, and Check\CheckCheck can compare against it without worrying that some other derivation would have produced a different, non-convertible type.

Theorem 14.2 (Type correctness). If Γ⊢t:A\Gamma \vdash t : AΓ⊢t:A, then either A=Sort uA = \Sort{u}A=Sortu for some uuu, or Γ⊢A:Sort u\Gamma \vdash A : \Sort{u}Γ⊢A:Sortu for some uuu.

The type of a well-typed term is itself a type (or is a universe, which has a type by T-Sort but need not be written as one). So the result of Infer\InferInfer can always be fed back into InferSort\InferSortInferSort, and contexts built by the algorithm stay well formed.

Theorem 14.3 (Subject reduction). If Γ⊢t:A\Gamma \vdash t : AΓ⊢t:A and t→βt′t \betared t't→β​t′, then Γ⊢t′:A\Gamma \vdash t' : AΓ⊢t′:A.

Computation preserves types. This is what justifies T-Conv and the whole strategy of deciding equality by normalization: reducing a term never takes it out of its type, so comparing normal forms compares the right things.

Theorem 14.4 (Strong normalization). If Γ⊢t:A\Gamma \vdash t : AΓ⊢t:A, then every sequence of beta-reductions starting from ttt is finite.

Every well-typed term reaches a normal form, whatever order reductions are performed in. This is the deep one. It is what makes Whnf\WhnfWhnf, Normalize\NormalizeNormalize, and therefore IsDefEq\IsDefEqIsDefEq and Infer\InferInfer terminate on well-typed input, and, as the next section shows, it is the key to consistency.

The four properties support the two guarantees in a definite pattern, drawn below: the arrows read "is needed for".

Figure 14.1. How the metatheory fits together.

Together these give the two guarantees we want from a kernel.

  • Decidability. Algorithm 5.1 terminates on every input, so whether a proof is correct can always be determined.
  • Consistency. No closed term proves False.

Strong normalization is stated for well-typed terms only. The kernel can receive ill-typed terms, and Whnf\WhnfWhnf is called during inference before typing is established. That is why the implementation has a step budget: it is the engineering substitute for the theorem on inputs the theorem does not cover.

Consistency

Theorem 14.5 (Consistency). There is no closed term ttt with ⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort 0). P\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort0).P.

The argument has two halves, and it is worth seeing their shape even without the details.

Reduce to normal forms. By strong normalization, such a term ttt would have a normal form nnn, and by subject reduction, nnn would have the same type. So it suffices to show that no normal closed term has type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P. This step is where all the difficulty lies, because it uses Theorem 14.4.

Analyse normal forms. A normal term is a universe, a Π\PiΠ, a λ\lambdaλ, or a variable applied to some arguments (a neutral term). A closed normal term whose type is a Π\PiΠ must be a λ\lambdaλ: it cannot be neutral, since no variable is in scope, and universes and Π\PiΠ-types have a universe as their type, not a Π\PiΠ. So n=λ(P:Sort 0). sn = \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{s}n=λ(P:Sort0).s with P:Sort 0⊢s:PP : \Sort{0} \vdash s : PP:Sort0⊢s:P and sss normal. Now ask what sss can be. A universe, a Π\PiΠ, or a λ\lambdaλ would have a universe or a Π\PiΠ as its type, not the variable PPP. A neutral term would have to start with a variable in scope, and the only one is PPP itself, whose type is Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0: it is not PPP, so sss cannot be PPP; and it is not a function type, so PPP cannot be applied to anything. Every case is impossible.

Appendix D carries this out carefully, including the standard facts about typing and conversion (generation, confluence, substitution) that the case analysis silently uses.

In words: to prove Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P you would have to produce a proof of an arbitrary proposition PPP with nothing to work from but the name PPP. Normal forms make "nothing to work from" literal: a normal proof cannot hide a computation that would conjure something up, so it must be built directly from what is in scope, and nothing in scope has type PPP. Strong normalization is what guarantees that every proof can be put in this honest form.

With inductive types

The iota-rules of Part II do not overlap with each other or with beta, so reduction remains confluent. Subject reduction, strong normalization, and consistency are known for the Calculus of Inductive Constructions [Werner 1994], of which our system with inductive types is a small fragment. The short consistency argument above no longer suffices by itself, because normal forms now include stuck recursor applications such as Nat.rec0  M  z  s  n\NatRec{0}\;M\;z\;s\;nNat.rec0​Mzsn with nnn a variable; consistency follows from strong normalization by a more careful analysis of normal forms, in which a neutral term may also be headed by a constant.

Each of the acceptance conditions of Chapter 8 corresponds to a way this analysis could fail: without positivity, iota-reduction can loop and strong normalization is lost; without the universe condition, a type could contain its own universe and the paradox of Chapter 13 returns; without the elimination restriction on propositions, proof irrelevance (which Lean assumes) would be refuted.

Lean's full theory, with definitional proof irrelevance, universe polymorphism, quotient types, and general nested and mutual inductive types, has subtler metatheory; Carneiro's thesis [Carneiro 2019] is the reference. The central structure, strong normalization plus an analysis of normal forms, is the same.

Lean's kernel, like ours, does not prove any of this; it assumes it. The theorems are about the type system, not about the code, and they are established once, on paper, for the system as designed. What the code must do is implement that system faithfully. The compact kernel of this book, and the even more compact description of it in Figure 3.1, Chapter 8, and Algorithm 12.1, is what makes "faithfully" checkable by a human reader.

Exercises

Which of the four properties does a kernel with Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type lose, according to Chapter 13?

Solution

Strong normalization (Hurkens' term has no normal form) and consistency (it has type Π(P:Type). P\tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{P}Π(P:Type).P). Uniqueness of types and subject reduction still hold; they are properties of the rule shapes, not of the universe structure.

The consistency argument says a closed normal term of Π\PiΠ-type must be a λ\lambdaλ. Why does this fail once constants are added, and what replaces it?

Solution

A constant such as succ\sucsucc or Nat.rec0\NatRec{0}Nat.rec0​ is closed and can head a normal term, so a closed normal term of Π\PiΠ-type may be, for instance, succ\sucsucc itself or a stuck recursor application. The analysis must then also consider neutral terms headed by constants and show, using the specific types the schema assigns to constructors and recursors, that none of them can inhabit Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P. Werner's thesis does this for the Calculus of Inductive Constructions.

What to remember

  • Uniqueness of types and type correctness make Infer\InferInfer well defined; subject reduction justifies deciding equality by normalization; strong normalization makes everything terminate.
  • Consistency follows from strong normalization plus a case analysis of normal forms: nothing in scope can prove an arbitrary PPP.
  • Inductive types preserve all four properties provided the acceptance conditions hold; each condition blocks a specific failure.
  • The kernel assumes these theorems rather than proving them. Its job is to implement the system they are about, faithfully and legibly.

Appendix A

Proof that Proofs Are Terms

Chapter 4 claimed that every proof in second-order propositional logic can be turned into a term that the kernel accepts (Theorem 4.1). This appendix makes the statement precise and proves it in full. The proof is short once the right bookkeeping is in place: it is an induction on the derivation of the logical judgment, and each case is one row of the table in Chapter 4 read from left to right.

The idea

A derivation in the logic is a tree of rule applications. The translation in Chapter 4 pairs each logical rule with a typing rule. So the natural plan is: walk the derivation from the leaves up, and at each node build the typing derivation that the paired typing rule gives. A hypothesis becomes a variable lookup, an implication introduction becomes a λ\lambdaλ, an implication elimination becomes an application, and the two quantifier rules become a λ\lambdaλ over Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 and an application to a type.

Two details need care, and both are about contexts.

  • The logical rules do not say which proposition variables are in scope. The typing side needs to know, because a proposition variable PPP is only usable after the assumption P:Sort 0P : \Sort{0}P:Sort0 is in the context. The precise statement therefore carries an explicit list Θ\ThetaΘ of proposition variables.
  • The typing rules extend contexts on the right, but the translation Δ∗\Delta^\astΔ∗ of Chapter 4 puts all proposition variables before all hypotheses. The proof is easier if any interleaving is allowed, so we prove the theorem for every context that represents the logical judgment, in a sense defined below.

The precise statement

Theorem 4.1 leaves implicit which proposition variables are in scope. For the proof we make them explicit and write

Θ;Δ⊢φ,\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi,Θ;Δ⊢φ,

where Θ\ThetaΘ is a list of distinct proposition variables, and every proposition variable free in Δ\DeltaΔ or in φ\varphiφ belongs to Θ\ThetaΘ. With this bookkeeping the rules of Chapter 4 read as follows.

φ∈ΔΘ;Δ⊢φ;(Hyp)Θ;Δ,φ⊢ψΘ;Δ⊢φ→ψ;(→-intro)Θ;Δ⊢φ→ψΘ;Δ⊢φΘ;Δ⊢ψ;(→-elim)\dfrac{\varphi \in \Delta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi}\rulename{Hyp} \qquad \dfrac{\Theta; \Delta, \varphi \vdash \psi}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi}\rulename{$\to$-intro} \qquad \dfrac{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psi \qquad \Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \psi}\rulename{$\to$-elim}Θ;Δ⊢φφ∈Δ​;(Hyp)Θ;Δ⊢φ→ψΘ;Δ,φ⊢ψ​;(→-intro)Θ;Δ⊢ψΘ;Δ⊢φ→ψΘ;Δ⊢φ​;(→-elim)
Θ,P;Δ⊢φP∉ΘΘ;Δ⊢∀P. φ;(∀-intro)Θ;Δ⊢∀P. φFV(ψ)⊆ΘΘ;Δ⊢φ[P↦ψ];(∀-elim)\dfrac{\Theta, P; \Delta \vdash \varphi \qquad P \notin \Theta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi}\rulename{$\forall$-intro} \qquad \dfrac{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphi \qquad \FV(\psi) \subseteq \Theta}{\Theta; \Delta \vdash \subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi}}\rulename{$\forall$-elim}Θ;Δ⊢∀P.φΘ,P;Δ⊢φP∈/Θ​;(∀-intro)Θ;Δ⊢φ[P↦ψ]Θ;Δ⊢∀P.φFV(ψ)⊆Θ​;(∀-elim)

The side condition P∉FV(Δ)P \notin \FV(\Delta)P∈/FV(Δ) of Chapter 4 is now implied by P∉ΘP \notin \ThetaP∈/Θ: every proposition variable free in Δ\DeltaΔ is in Θ\ThetaΘ, and PPP is not. Formulas are taken up to α\alphaα-equivalence, so a bound PPP can always be renamed to satisfy the side condition. As in Chapter 4, φ∗→ψ∗\varphi^\ast \to \psi^\astφ∗→ψ∗ stands for Π(x:φ∗). ψ∗\tPi{x}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}Π(x:φ∗).ψ∗ with xxx fresh.

The context Δ∗\Delta^\astΔ∗ of Chapter 4 lists the proposition variables first and the hypotheses after them. The proof has to extend contexts on the right, so it is convenient to allow any order.

Definition A.1 (Representation). A context Γ\GammaΓ represents (Θ;Δ)(\Theta; \Delta)(Θ;Δ) if ⊢Γ;ok\ctxok{\Gamma}⊢Γ;ok and Γ\GammaΓ consists of one assumption P:Sort 0P : \Sort{0}P:Sort0 for each P∈ΘP \in \ThetaP∈Θ and one assumption h:χ∗h : \chi^\asth:χ∗ for each χ∈Δ\chi \in \Deltaχ∈Δ, in some order.

Theorem A.2 (Theorem 4.1, precise form). If Θ;Δ⊢φ\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphiΘ;Δ⊢φ and Γ\GammaΓ represents (Θ;Δ)(\Theta; \Delta)(Θ;Δ), then Γ⊢t:φ∗\Gamma \vdash t : \varphi^\astΓ⊢t:φ∗ for some term ttt.

Theorem 4.1 is the special case Γ=Δ∗\Gamma = \Delta^\astΓ=Δ∗. Indeed, when Θ\ThetaΘ lists the free proposition variables, the context Δ∗\Delta^\astΔ∗ contains exactly the required assumptions; it is well formed by Lemma A.3 below together with the rule C-Ext, since each hypothesis type χ∗\chi^\astχ∗ is a proposition once the proposition variables are in scope.

Facts about the translation

The translation φ↦φ∗\varphi \mapsto \varphi^\astφ↦φ∗ commutes with substitution:

(φ[P↦ψ])∗=φ∗[P↦ψ∗].(\subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi})^\ast = \subst{\varphi^\ast}{P}{\psi^\ast}.(φ[P↦ψ])∗=φ∗[P↦ψ∗].

This is a routine induction on φ\varphiφ: both sides replace the free occurrences of PPP by ψ∗\psi^\astψ∗, and the translation does nothing to a proposition variable except keep its name. The ∀\forall∀-elim case of the main proof depends on this equation.

The next lemma is the one place where the universe structure of Chapter 13 enters. It says that every translated formula is a proposition, that is, has type Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0. Without it, the typing rule T-Lam could not be applied to a hypothesis, and the ∀\forall∀-elim case could not instantiate a quantifier with an arbitrary formula.

Lemma A.3 (Formulas are propositions). If ⊢Γ;ok\ctxok{\Gamma}⊢Γ;ok and (P:Sort 0)∈Γ(P : \Sort{0}) \in \Gamma(P:Sort0)∈Γ for every P∈FV(φ)P \in \FV(\varphi)P∈FV(φ), then Γ⊢φ∗:Sort 0\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}Γ⊢φ∗:Sort0.

By induction on φ\varphiφ.

For a proposition variable PPP, the assumption gives (P:Sort 0)∈Γ(P : \Sort{0}) \in \Gamma(P:Sort0)∈Γ, so Γ⊢P:Sort 0\Gamma \vdash P : \Sort{0}Γ⊢P:Sort0 by T-Var.

For φ→ψ\varphi \to \psiφ→ψ, the induction hypothesis gives Γ⊢φ∗:Sort 0\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}Γ⊢φ∗:Sort0, so Γ,x:φ∗\Gamma, x : \varphi^\astΓ,x:φ∗ is well formed by C-Ext for a fresh xxx. The induction hypothesis for ψ\psiψ in that extended context gives Γ,x:φ∗⊢ψ∗:Sort 0\Gamma, x : \varphi^\ast \vdash \psi^\ast : \Sort{0}Γ,x:φ∗⊢ψ∗:Sort0, and T-Pi gives Γ⊢Π(x:φ∗). ψ∗:Sort imax(0,0)=Sort 0\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast} : \Sort{\imax(0, 0)} = \Sort{0}Γ⊢Π(x:φ∗).ψ∗:Sortimax(0,0)=Sort0.

For ∀Q. χ\forall Q.\,\chi∀Q.χ, rename QQQ so that Q∉dom(Γ)Q \notin \dom(\Gamma)Q∈/dom(Γ). T-Sort gives Γ⊢Sort 0:Sort 1\Gamma \vdash \Sort{0} : \Sort{1}Γ⊢Sort0:Sort1, so Γ,Q:Sort 0\Gamma, Q : \Sort{0}Γ,Q:Sort0 is well formed by C-Ext. The induction hypothesis for χ\chiχ in that context gives Γ,Q:Sort 0⊢χ∗:Sort 0\Gamma, Q : \Sort{0} \vdash \chi^\ast : \Sort{0}Γ,Q:Sort0⊢χ∗:Sort0, and T-Pi gives Γ⊢Π(Q:Sort 0). χ∗:Sort imax(1,0)=Sort 0\Gamma \vdash \tPi{Q}{\Sort{0}}{\chi^\ast} : \Sort{\imax(1, 0)} = \Sort{0}Γ⊢Π(Q:Sort0).χ∗:Sortimax(1,0)=Sort0.

The last case is where impredicativity is used. The domain Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 lives in Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1, so with max⁡\maxmax in place of imax\imaximax the type (∀Q. χ)∗(\forall Q.\,\chi)^\ast(∀Q.χ)∗ would land in Sort 1\Sort{1}Sort1 rather than Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0. Then the ∀\forall∀-elim case below would hold only for formulas ψ\psiψ without ∀\forall∀, because only those would have type Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 and be allowed as arguments. Chapter 13 discusses this design choice.

The proof

We prove Theorem A.2 by induction on the derivation of Θ;Δ⊢φ\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphiΘ;Δ⊢φ, for all representing contexts Γ\GammaΓ at once. Each case builds the typing derivation shown in the right column of the table in Chapter 4.

Hypothesis. The rule concludes Θ;Δ⊢φ\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphiΘ;Δ⊢φ from φ∈Δ\varphi \in \Deltaφ∈Δ. Since Γ\GammaΓ represents (Θ;Δ)(\Theta; \Delta)(Θ;Δ), it contains an assumption h:φ∗h : \varphi^\asth:φ∗, so Γ⊢h:φ∗\Gamma \vdash h : \varphi^\astΓ⊢h:φ∗ by T-Var.

→\to→-intro. The premise is Θ;Δ,φ⊢ψ\Theta; \Delta, \varphi \vdash \psiΘ;Δ,φ⊢ψ and the conclusion is Θ;Δ⊢φ→ψ\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psiΘ;Δ⊢φ→ψ. By Lemma A.3, Γ⊢φ∗:Sort 0\Gamma \vdash \varphi^\ast : \Sort{0}Γ⊢φ∗:Sort0. For a fresh hhh, the context Γ,h:φ∗\Gamma, h : \varphi^\astΓ,h:φ∗ is therefore well formed by C-Ext, and it represents (Θ;Δ,φ)(\Theta; \Delta, \varphi)(Θ;Δ,φ). The induction hypothesis, applied to the premise and this context, gives Γ,h:φ∗⊢t:ψ∗\Gamma, h : \varphi^\ast \vdash t : \psi^\astΓ,h:φ∗⊢t:ψ∗ for some ttt, and T-Lam gives

Γ⊢λ(h:φ∗). t:Π(h:φ∗). ψ∗.\Gamma \vdash \tLam{h}{\varphi^\ast}{t} : \tPi{h}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}.Γ⊢λ(h:φ∗).t:Π(h:φ∗).ψ∗.

This type is φ∗→ψ∗\varphi^\ast \to \psi^\astφ∗→ψ∗: the free variables of ψ∗\psi^\astψ∗ are proposition variables, and hhh is not one of them, so hhh does not occur in ψ∗\psi^\astψ∗ and the Π\PiΠ is non-dependent.

→\to→-elim. The premises are Θ;Δ⊢φ→ψ\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphi \to \psiΘ;Δ⊢φ→ψ and Θ;Δ⊢φ\Theta; \Delta \vdash \varphiΘ;Δ⊢φ. The induction hypotheses give Γ⊢f:Π(x:φ∗). ψ∗\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{x}{\varphi^\ast}{\psi^\ast}Γ⊢f:Π(x:φ∗).ψ∗ with x∉FV(ψ∗)x \notin \FV(\psi^\ast)x∈/FV(ψ∗), and Γ⊢a:φ∗\Gamma \vdash a : \varphi^\astΓ⊢a:φ∗. T-App gives Γ⊢f  a:ψ∗[x↦a]\Gamma \vdash f\;a : \subst{\psi^\ast}{x}{a}Γ⊢fa:ψ∗[x↦a], and since xxx does not occur in ψ∗\psi^\astψ∗ the substitution does nothing: ψ∗[x↦a]=ψ∗\subst{\psi^\ast}{x}{a} = \psi^\astψ∗[x↦a]=ψ∗.

∀\forall∀-intro. The premise is Θ,P;Δ⊢φ\Theta, P; \Delta \vdash \varphiΘ,P;Δ⊢φ with P∉ΘP \notin \ThetaP∈/Θ, and the conclusion is Θ;Δ⊢∀P. φ\Theta; \Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphiΘ;Δ⊢∀P.φ. Renaming PPP if necessary, assume P∉dom(Γ)P \notin \dom(\Gamma)P∈/dom(Γ); a routine induction shows that renaming a variable of Θ\ThetaΘ to a fresh one preserves derivations. By T-Sort and C-Ext, Γ,P:Sort 0\Gamma, P : \Sort{0}Γ,P:Sort0 is well formed, and it represents (Θ,P;Δ)(\Theta, P; \Delta)(Θ,P;Δ). The induction hypothesis gives Γ,P:Sort 0⊢t:φ∗\Gamma, P : \Sort{0} \vdash t : \varphi^\astΓ,P:Sort0⊢t:φ∗, and T-Lam gives

Γ⊢λ(P:Sort 0). t:Π(P:Sort 0). φ∗,\Gamma \vdash \tLam{P}{\Sort{0}}{t} : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast},Γ⊢λ(P:Sort0).t:Π(P:Sort0).φ∗,

which is the translation of ∀P. φ\forall P.\,\varphi∀P.φ.

∀\forall∀-elim. The premise is Θ;Δ⊢∀P. φ\Theta; \Delta \vdash \forall P.\,\varphiΘ;Δ⊢∀P.φ with FV(ψ)⊆Θ\FV(\psi) \subseteq \ThetaFV(ψ)⊆Θ, and the conclusion is Θ;Δ⊢φ[P↦ψ]\Theta; \Delta \vdash \subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi}Θ;Δ⊢φ[P↦ψ]. The induction hypothesis gives Γ⊢f:Π(P:Sort 0). φ∗\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{\varphi^\ast}Γ⊢f:Π(P:Sort0).φ∗. Since every proposition variable of ψ\psiψ is in Θ\ThetaΘ and hence has an assumption Q:Sort 0Q : \Sort{0}Q:Sort0 in Γ\GammaΓ, Lemma A.3 gives Γ⊢ψ∗:Sort 0\Gamma \vdash \psi^\ast : \Sort{0}Γ⊢ψ∗:Sort0. T-App gives

Γ⊢f  ψ∗:φ∗[P↦ψ∗]=(φ[P↦ψ])∗,\Gamma \vdash f\;\psi^\ast : \subst{\varphi^\ast}{P}{\psi^\ast} = (\subst{\varphi}{P}{\psi})^\ast,Γ⊢fψ∗:φ∗[P↦ψ∗]=(φ[P↦ψ])∗,

where the last step is the substitution equation from the previous section.

Every rule of the logic has been covered, so the theorem holds for every derivation.

The proof never needs T-Conv. Every typing derivation it builds compares types only syntactically, up to the names of bound variables. Conversion becomes necessary only when the logic is extended with computation, as the inductive types of Part II do.

The converse direction, that every term of type φ∗\varphi^\astφ∗ comes from a proof of φ\varphiφ, is called conservativity. As Chapter 4 notes, it is harder, because Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 contains types that are not translations of formulas, and a term may pass through them. The book does not need it: what the kernel must guarantee is consistency, which is proved in Appendix D.

What to remember

  • The precise form of the theorem carries an explicit list Θ\ThetaΘ of proposition variables, and proves the claim for every context that represents (Θ;Δ)(\Theta; \Delta)(Θ;Δ), in any order.
  • Every translated formula lives in Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 (Lemma A.3). This uses impredicativity in the ∀\forall∀ case, and it is what lets ∀\forall∀-elim instantiate a quantifier with any formula.
  • The proof is an induction on the derivation; each logical rule maps to exactly one typing rule: Hyp to T-Var, the two introductions to T-Lam, the two eliminations to T-App.
  • T-Conv is never used, because the logic has no computation.

Appendix B

Correctness of Alpha-Equivalence

Chapter 11 gave two definitions of alpha-equivalence: a mathematical one (the smallest congruence that allows renaming a bound variable) and an algorithmic one (the rules of Figure 11.1, which walk two terms in lockstep and compare bound variables by position). Theorem 11.1 says that they agree. This appendix proves it.

The idea

Both definitions turn out to say the same thing: the two terms have the same de Bruijn representation, that is, the same shape once every bound variable is replaced by the distance to its binder. So the proof goes through a third, nameless representation of terms.

  • Lemma B.1 shows that the algorithm compares nameless forms. This is almost immediate, because the rules of Figure 11.1 compare positions exactly as de Bruijn indices do.
  • Lemmas B.2 and B.3 establish two facts about how nameless forms behave under renaming. The key one is that renaming a bound variable does not change the nameless form.
  • Lemma B.4 shows that the mathematical definition also compares nameless forms, using those two facts.
  • Theorem 11.1 then follows by chaining the two lemmas through the nameless form.

The proofs are inductions on terms, with one subtlety: substitution may rename a binder, so some inductions must be on the size of a term rather than on its structure.

Nameless terms

A nameless term is built like a term, except that binders carry no names and a bound variable is written as a number #i\#i#i:

d::=Sort u∣#i∣x∣Π d. d∣λ d. d∣d  dd ::= \Sort{u} \mid \#i \mid x \mid \Pi\,d.\,d \mid \lambda\,d.\,d \mid d\;dd::=Sortu∣#i∣x∣Πd.d∣λd.d∣dd

Free variables keep their names. The number #i\#i#i means "the variable bound by the iii-th enclosing binder, counting from the innermost at 000". Recall from Chapter 11 that for a list of names EEE, idx(E,x)\mathrm{idx}(E, x)idx(E,x) is the position of the last occurrence of xxx in EEE, counted from the right starting at 000, and is undefined if x∉Ex \notin Ex∈/E.

For a list of names EEE, the nameless form ⌊t⌋E\db{t}{E}⌊t⌋E​ of a term ttt that occurs under the binders EEE is defined by

⌊Sort u⌋E=Sort u⌊x⌋E={#idx(E,x)if x∈E,xotherwise,⌊Π(x:A). B⌋E=Π ⌊A⌋E. ⌊B⌋E,x⌊λ(x:A). t⌋E=λ ⌊A⌋E. ⌊t⌋E,x⌊t1  t2⌋E=⌊t1⌋E  ⌊t2⌋E.\begin{array}{rlrl} \db{\Sort{u}}{E} &= \Sort{u} & \qquad \db{x}{E} &= \begin{cases} \#\mathrm{idx}(E, x) & \text{if } x \in E, \\ x & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \\[12pt] \db{\tPi{x}{A}{B}}{E} &= \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{B}{E, x} & \qquad \db{\tLam{x}{A}{t}}{E} &= \lambda\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{t}{E, x} \\[4pt] \db{t_1\;t_2}{E} &= \db{t_1}{E}\;\db{t_2}{E}. & & \end{array}⌊Sortu⌋E​⌊Π(x:A).B⌋E​⌊t1​t2​⌋E​​=Sortu=Π⌊A⌋E​.⌊B⌋E,x​=⌊t1​⌋E​⌊t2​⌋E​.​⌊x⌋E​⌊λ(x:A).t⌋E​​={#idx(E,x)x​if x∈E,otherwise,​=λ⌊A⌋E​.⌊t⌋E,x​​

Equality of nameless terms is plain syntactic equality. Note that ⌊t⌋E\db{t}{E}⌊t⌋E​ has the same outermost shape as ttt, except that a variable may become either a number or a name. Constants, introduced in Chapter 7, are left unchanged like universes and are compared by name; they add only trivial cases below and are omitted.

Writing ⌊t⌋E\db{t}{E}⌊t⌋E​ with a nonempty EEE describes ttt as a subterm, sitting under the binders listed in EEE. The whole-term case is ⌊t⌋⋅\db{t}{\cdot}⌊t⌋⋅​, with no enclosing binders. The reason to keep EEE general is that every induction below has to pass through binders, and under a binder the subterm has one more enclosing binder than the term it came from.

The algorithm computes nameless forms

The first lemma relates the rules of Figure 11.1 to nameless forms. Its role is to replace the algorithmic judgment, which is defined by rules, by an equation between two terms, which is easier to reason about.

Lemma B.1 (The algorithm compares nameless forms). For all E1E_1E1​, E2E_2E2​, sss, and ttt: the judgment E1;E2⊢s=αtE_1; E_2 \vdash s \alphaeq tE1​;E2​⊢s=α​t is derivable if and only if ⌊s⌋E1=⌊t⌋E2\db{s}{E_1} = \db{t}{E_2}⌊s⌋E1​​=⌊t⌋E2​​.

By induction on sss, for all ttt, E1E_1E1​, and E2E_2E2​. For each shape of sss, exactly one rule of Figure 11.1 can conclude the judgment, and its premises match the equations for ⌊⋅⌋\db{\cdot}{}⌊⋅⌋​.

If x∈E1x \in E_1x∈E1​, then ⌊x⌋E1=#idx(E1,x)\db{x}{E_1} = \#\mathrm{idx}(E_1, x)⌊x⌋E1​​=#idx(E1​,x), and equality holds exactly when y∈E2y \in E_2y∈E2​ and idx(E2,y)=idx(E1,x)\mathrm{idx}(E_2, y) = \mathrm{idx}(E_1, x)idx(E2​,y)=idx(E1​,x), which is the premise of α\alphaα-Bound. If s=Π(x:A). Bs = \tPi{x}{A}{B}s=Π(x:A).B, equality holds exactly when t=Π(y:A′). B′t = \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}t=Π(y:A′).B′ with ⌊A⌋E1=⌊A′⌋E2\db{A}{E_1} = \db{A'}{E_2}⌊A⌋E1​​=⌊A′⌋E2​​ and ⌊B⌋E1,x=⌊B′⌋E2,y\db{B}{E_1, x} = \db{B'}{E_2, y}⌊B⌋E1​,x​=⌊B′⌋E2​,y​. Two facts about renaming

The definition of =α\alphaeq=α​ in Chapter 11 involves substitution: it allows replacing Π(x:A). B\tPi{x}{A}{B}Π(x:A).B by Π(y:A). B[x↦y]\tPi{y}{A}{\subst{B}{x}{y}}Π(y:A).B[x↦y] when y∉FV(B)y \notin \FV(B)y∈/FV(B). To relate it to nameless forms we need to know how ⌊⋅⌋\db{\cdot}{}⌊⋅⌋​ behaves when a bound variable is renamed. Two lemmas supply this.

The first says that ⌊t⌋E\db{t}{E}⌊t⌋E​ depends on EEE only through the free variables of ttt. Its role is technical: it lets us swap one binder list for another as long as they agree on the variables that matter.

Lemma B.2 (Agreement). If idx(E1,v)=idx(E2,v)\mathrm{idx}(E_1, v) = \mathrm{idx}(E_2, v)idx(E1​,v)=idx(E2​,v) for every v∈FV(t)v \in \FV(t)v∈FV(t), with both sides possibly undefined, then ⌊t⌋E1=⌊t⌋E2\db{t}{E_1} = \db{t}{E_2}⌊t⌋E1​​=⌊t⌋E2​​.

By induction on ttt, for all E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​. The variable case is exactly the assumption: a free variable vvv becomes the same number, or stays the same name, on both sides. Universes are unaffected by EEE, and applications follow from the induction hypothesis for both parts.

Under a binder xxx, the lists E1,xE_1, xE1​,x and E2,xE_2, xE2​,x again agree on the free variables of the body. The variable xxx has position 000 in both. Any other free variable vvv of the body is a free variable of ttt, so by assumption its position is the same in E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​; appending xxx increases that position by one on both sides, or leaves it undefined on both sides. The induction hypothesis for the body then applies, and the annotation is handled by the induction hypothesis with the original lists.

The second lemma is the heart of the appendix: renaming a binder does not change the nameless form. It is stated for a binder sitting at an arbitrary depth, with binder lists EEE before it and E′E'E′ after it, because the induction has to go under further binders.

We use that substituting a variable for a variable preserves the size of a term, even when binders are renamed along the way; this is a routine induction on the definition of substitution.

Lemma B.3 (Renaming). Let y≠xy \neq xy=x, y∉FV(B)y \notin \FV(B)y∈/FV(B), and x,y∉E′x, y \notin E'x,y∈/E′. Then ⌊B⌋E,x,E′=⌊B[x↦y]⌋E,y,E′\db{B}{E, x, E'} = \db{\subst{B}{x}{y}}{E, y, E'}⌊B⌋E,x,E′​=⌊B[x↦y]⌋E,y,E′​ for every list EEE.

By induction on the size of BBB, for all EEE and E′E'E′. Write Lx=E,x,E′L_x = E, x, E'Lx​=E,x,E′ and Ly=E,y,E′L_y = E, y, E'Ly​=E,y,E′; they differ in exactly one entry, at the same position.

If B=xB = xB=x, then B[x↦y]=y\subst{B}{x}{y} = yB[x↦y]=y. Since x,y∉E′x, y \notin E'x,y∈/E′, the last occurrence of xxx in LxL_xLx​ and the last occurrence of yyy in LyL_yLy​ are both the distinguished entry, so idx(Lx,x)\mathrm{idx}(L_x, x)idx(Lx​,x) and idx(Ly,y)\mathrm{idx}(L_y, y)idx(Ly​,y) both equal the length of E′E'E′, and the nameless forms are the same number.

Let B=Π(w:C). DB = \tPi{w}{C}{D}B=Π(w:C).D; the case of λ\lambdaλ is the same. The annotation CCC is handled by the induction hypothesis in each case below, so we consider only the body. There are three cases, following the definition of substitution in Chapter 11.

Case w=xw = xw=x. Second, the induction hypothesis for D[y↦z]\subst{D}{y}{z}D[y↦z], which has the size of DDD and has no free yyy, with E′E'E′ extended by zzz, gives ⌊D[y↦z]⌋Lx,z=⌊(D[y↦z])[x↦y]⌋Ly,z\db{\subst{D}{y}{z}}{L_x, z} = \db{\subst{(\subst{D}{y}{z})}{x}{y}}{L_y, z}⌊D[y↦z]⌋Lx​,z​=⌊(D[y↦z])[x↦y]⌋Ly​,z​. Chaining the two equations gives the claim.

The induction in Lemma B.3 is on size rather than on structure because the third case applies the induction hypothesis to D[y↦z]\subst{D}{y}{z}D[y↦z], which is not a subterm of BBB. It has the same size as DDD, which is smaller than the size of BBB, so the induction is well founded.

The definition computes nameless forms

With the two renaming facts in hand, we can show that the mathematical definition of =α\alphaeq=α​ also amounts to equality of nameless forms. The two directions are proved differently: one by the minimality of =α\alphaeq=α​ as a congruence, the other by induction on size.

Lemma B.4 (The definition compares nameless forms). If s=αts \alphaeq ts=α​t in the sense of the definition in Chapter 11, then ⌊s⌋E=⌊t⌋E\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}⌊s⌋E​=⌊t⌋E​ for every EEE. Conversely, if ⌊s⌋E=⌊t⌋E\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}⌊s⌋E​=⌊t⌋E​ for some EEE, then s=αts \alphaeq ts=α​t.

First part. Let s∼ts \sim ts∼t mean that ⌊s⌋E=⌊t⌋E\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}⌊s⌋E​=⌊t⌋E​ for every EEE. This relation is an equivalence, since equality is. It is a congruence, because ⌊⋅⌋\db{\cdot}{}⌊⋅⌋​ is defined constructor by constructor: if the parts of two terms have equal nameless forms under the appropriate lists, so do the terms. Finally, ∼\sim∼ contains the defining equation of =α\alphaeq=α​: if y∉FV(B)y \notin \FV(B)y∈/FV(B), then

⌊Π(x:A). B⌋E=Π ⌊A⌋E. ⌊B⌋E,xand⌊Π(y:A). B[x↦y]⌋E=Π ⌊A⌋E. ⌊B[x↦y]⌋E,y,\db{\tPi{x}{A}{B}}{E} = \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{B}{E, x} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \db{\tPi{y}{A}{\subst{B}{x}{y}}}{E} = \Pi\,\db{A}{E}.\,\db{\subst{B}{x}{y}}{E, y},⌊Π(x:A).B⌋E​=Π⌊A⌋E​.⌊B⌋E,x​and⌊Π(y:A).B[x↦y]⌋E​=Π⌊A⌋E​.⌊B[x↦y]⌋E,y​,

and the bodies are equal by Lemma B.3 with E′E'E′ empty; the case y=xy = xy=x is trivial, since then the two terms are identical. The same holds for λ\lambdaλ. Since =α\alphaeq=α​ is the smallest congruence containing that equation, and ∼\sim∼ is a congruence containing it, s=αts \alphaeq ts=α​t implies s∼ts \sim ts∼t.

Second part. We use induction on the size of sss, for all ttt and EEE, assuming ⌊s⌋E=⌊t⌋E\db{s}{E} = \db{t}{E}⌊s⌋E​=⌊t⌋E​.

If sss is a variable, so is ttt, since nameless forms of other shapes are never a number or a name. If both nameless forms are the number #i\#i#i, both variables are the entry at position iii of EEE, so s=ts = ts=t. If both are names, then s=ts = ts=t directly. In either case s=αts \alphaeq ts=α​t by reflexivity.

Universes are equal outright. For applications, the nameless forms of the two parts agree, so the induction hypothesis gives =α\alphaeq=α​ for each part, and the congruence property of =α\alphaeq=α​ gives it for the whole.

Let s=Π(x:A). Bs = \tPi{x}{A}{B}s=Π(x:A).B, so that t=Π(y:A′). B′t = \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}t=Π(y:A′).B′ with ⌊A⌋E=⌊A′⌋E\db{A}{E} = \db{A'}{E}⌊A⌋E​=⌊A′⌋E​ and ⌊B⌋E,x=⌊B′⌋E,y\db{B}{E, x} = \db{B'}{E, y}⌊B⌋E,x​=⌊B′⌋E,y​. The induction hypothesis gives A=αA′A \alphaeq A'A=α​A′. For the bodies, choose z∉FV(B)∪FV(B′)∪{x,y}z \notin \FV(B) \cup \FV(B') \cup \{x, y\}z∈/FV(B)∪FV(B′)∪{x,y}. Lemma B.3 with E′E'E′ empty gives ⌊B⌋E,x=⌊B[x↦z]⌋E,z\db{B}{E, x} = \db{\subst{B}{x}{z}}{E, z}⌊B⌋E,x​=⌊B[x↦z]⌋E,z​ and ⌊B′⌋E,y=⌊B′[y↦z]⌋E,z\db{B'}{E, y} = \db{\subst{B'}{y}{z}}{E, z}⌊B′⌋E,y​=⌊B′[y↦z]⌋E,z​, so

⌊B[x↦z]⌋E,z=⌊B′[y↦z]⌋E,z.\db{\subst{B}{x}{z}}{E, z} = \db{\subst{B'}{y}{z}}{E, z}.⌊B[x↦z]⌋E,z​=⌊B′[y↦z]⌋E,z​.

Π(x:A). B  =α  Π(z:A). B[x↦z]  =α  Π(z:A′). B′[y↦z]  =α  Π(y:A′). B′,\tPi{x}{A}{B} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{z}{A}{\subst{B}{x}{z}} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{z}{A'}{\subst{B'}{y}{z}} \;\alphaeq\; \tPi{y}{A'}{B'},Π(x:A).B=α​Π(z:A).B[x↦z]=α​Π(z:A′).B′[y↦z]=α​Π(y:A′).B′,

by the defining equation (valid since z∉FV(B)z \notin \FV(B)z∈/FV(B)), by congruence, and by the defining equation read backwards (valid since z∉FV(B′)z \notin \FV(B')z∈/FV(B′)). The case of λ\lambdaλ is the same.

Proof of Theorem 11.1

Theorem 11.1 (Correctness of algorithmic alpha-equivalence). For all terms sss and ttt, s=αts \alphaeq ts=α​t in the sense of the definition in Chapter 11 if and only if ⋅ ;⋅⊢s=αt\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t⋅;⋅⊢s=α​t is derivable by the rules of Figure 11.1.

If s=αts \alphaeq ts=α​t, then ⌊s⌋⋅=⌊t⌋⋅\db{s}{\cdot} = \db{t}{\cdot}⌊s⌋⋅​=⌊t⌋⋅​ by the first part of Lemma B.4 (taking EEE empty), and then ⋅ ;⋅⊢s=αt\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t⋅;⋅⊢s=α​t by Lemma B.1.

Conversely, if ⋅ ;⋅⊢s=αt\cdot\,;\cdot \vdash s \alphaeq t⋅;⋅⊢s=α​t, then ⌊s⌋⋅=⌊t⌋⋅\db{s}{\cdot} = \db{t}{\cdot}⌊s⌋⋅​=⌊t⌋⋅​ by Lemma B.1, and then s=αts \alphaeq ts=α​t by the second part of Lemma B.4.

The theorem is stated for whole terms, with empty binder lists, because that is how the kernel calls the comparison. Lemma B.1 is more general and describes what the algorithm computes at every recursive call, which is what one needs when reading the implementation of alpha in src/substitution.rs: the two vectors of bound names it carries are E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​, and binder_distance computes idx\mathrm{idx}idx.

What to remember

  • Both definitions of alpha-equivalence compute the same thing: equality of de Bruijn (nameless) forms. The nameless form is the bridge between them.
  • The algorithm matches nameless forms directly (Lemma B.1), rule by rule.
  • The key fact about the mathematical definition is that renaming a bound variable does not change the nameless form (Lemma B.3), which needs an induction on size because substitution can itself rename binders.
  • A kernel that uses de Bruijn indices gets this theorem for free: alpha-equivalent terms are syntactically identical.

Appendix C

Hurkens' Paradox

Chapter 13 claimed that a single universe containing itself makes the type theory inconsistent: there is a closed term of type Π(p:Type). p\tPi{p}{\mathsf{Type}}{p}Π(p:Type).p, a proof of everything. This appendix gives that term in full, explains the idea behind it, and shows exactly where the rule Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type is used, so that you can see why the universe hierarchy blocks it.

The setting

Throughout this appendix the universes of the kernel are replaced by one universe Type\mathsf{Type}Type with the two rules

⊢Γ;okΓ⊢Type:TypeΓ⊢A:TypeΓ,x:A⊢B:TypeΓ⊢Π(x:A). B:Type\dfrac{\ctxok{\Gamma}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}} \qquad \dfrac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathsf{Type} \qquad \Gamma, x : A \vdash B : \mathsf{Type}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{x}{A}{B} : \mathsf{Type}}Γ⊢Type:Type⊢Γ;ok​Γ⊢Π(x:A).B:TypeΓ⊢A:TypeΓ,x:A⊢B:Type​

in place of T-Sort and T-Pi. Everything else, including T-Lam, T-App, T-Conv, substitution, and β\betaβ-reduction, is unchanged. The goal is a closed term tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ with

⊢tH:⊥,⊥=Π(p:Type). p.\vdash t_{\mathrm{H}} : \bot, \qquad \bot = \tPi{p}{\mathsf{Type}}{p}.⊢tH​:⊥,⊥=Π(p:Type).p.

Such a term proves every proposition CCC, because tH  C:Ct_{\mathrm{H}}\;C : CtH​C:C.

The construction is due to Girard, who adapted the Burali-Forti paradox of set theory to the type theory with Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type [Girard 1972]. The term below is Hurkens' simplification [Hurkens 1995], which fits on one page and uses nothing beyond Π\PiΠ, λ\lambdaλ, and application.

Power sets in type theory

Read a function p:S→Typep : S \to \mathsf{Type}p:S→Type as a predicate on SSS, or equivalently as a subset of SSS: the elements xxx for which p  xp\;xpx has a proof are the members. The type of all such predicates is the power set of SSS:

℘S  =  S→Type.\wp S \;=\; S \to \mathsf{Type}.℘S=S→Type.

Applying this twice, ℘℘S=(S→Type)→Type\wp\wp S = (S \to \mathsf{Type}) \to \mathsf{Type}℘℘S=(S→Type)→Type is the type of families of subsets of SSS.

In set theory, Cantor's theorem says that no set contains a copy of its own power set, let alone of its double power set: ℘S\wp S℘S is always strictly larger than SSS. The paradox is built on a type UUU that violates this. It contains a copy of ℘℘U\wp\wp U℘℘U, with a function τ:℘℘U→U\tau : \wp\wp U \to Uτ:℘℘U→U that packs a family of subsets of UUU into a single element of UUU, and a function σ:U→℘℘U\sigma : U \to \wp\wp Uσ:U→℘℘U that unpacks it again. The type

U  =  Π(X:Type). ((℘℘X→X)→℘℘X)U \;=\; \tPi{X}{\mathsf{Type}}{\bigl((\wp\wp X \to X) \to \wp\wp X\bigr)}U=Π(X:Type).((℘℘X→X)→℘℘X)

achieves this by quantifying over all of Type\mathsf{Type}Type. For UUU to be a member of Type\mathsf{Type}Type while quantifying over Type\mathsf{Type}Type is exactly what Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type permits and the hierarchy of Chapter 13 forbids.

The term

The following abbreviations are expanded in place; the kernel sees only Π\PiΠ, λ\lambdaλ, variables, and application. We write ¬φ\neg\varphi¬φ for φ→⊥\varphi \to \botφ→⊥.

⊥=Π(p:Type). p℘S=S→TypeU=Π(X:Type). ((℘℘X→X)→℘℘X)τ=λ(t:℘℘U). λ(X:Type). λ(f:℘℘X→X). λ(p:℘X). t  (λ(x:U). p  (f  (x  X  f)))σ=λ(s:U). s  U  τΔ=λ(y:U). ¬ (Π(p:℘U). σ  y  p→p  (τ  (σ  y)))Ω=τ  (λ(p:℘U). Π(x:U). σ  x  p→p  x)\begin{array}{rcl} \bot &=& \tPi{p}{\mathsf{Type}}{p} \\[4pt] \wp S &=& S \to \mathsf{Type} \\[4pt] U &=& \tPi{X}{\mathsf{Type}}{((\wp\wp X \to X) \to \wp\wp X)} \\[4pt] \tau &=& \tLam{t}{\wp\wp U}{\tLam{X}{\mathsf{Type}}{\tLam{f}{\wp\wp X \to X}{\tLam{p}{\wp X}{t\;(\tLam{x}{U}{p\;(f\;(x\;X\;f))})}}}} \\[4pt] \sigma &=& \tLam{s}{U}{s\;U\;\tau} \\[4pt] \Delta &=& \tLam{y}{U}{\neg\,(\tPi{p}{\wp U}{\sigma\;y\;p \to p\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;y))})} \\[4pt] \Omega &=& \tau\;(\tLam{p}{\wp U}{\tPi{x}{U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;x}}) \end{array}⊥℘SUτσΔΩ​=======​Π(p:Type).pS→TypeΠ(X:Type).((℘℘X→X)→℘℘X)λ(t:℘℘U).λ(X:Type).λ(f:℘℘X→X).λ(p:℘X).t(λ(x:U).p(f(xXf)))λ(s:U).sUτλ(y:U).¬(Π(p:℘U).σyp→p(τ(σy)))τ(λ(p:℘U).Π(x:U).σxp→px)​

The shape is an application: a λ\lambdaλ binding h0h_0h0​, applied (on the last line) to an argument of the type that h0h_0h0​ expects. Inside, h0h_0h0​ is applied to two arguments, Δ\DeltaΔ and a proof about Δ\DeltaΔ, and the result is applied to one more argument. Everything is explained below.

How the term works

Packing and unpacking. The two functions τ:℘℘U→U\tau : \wp\wp U \to Uτ:℘℘U→U and σ:U→℘℘U\sigma : U \to \wp\wp Uσ:U→℘℘U are inverse enough for the argument. Unfolding the definitions and β\betaβ-reducing gives, for every t:℘℘Ut : \wp\wp Ut:℘℘U and p:℘Up : \wp Up:℘U,

σ  (τ  t)  p  ≡  t  (λ(x:U). p  (τ  (σ  x))).\sigma\;(\tau\;t)\;p \;\conv\; t\;(\tLam{x}{U}{p\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;x))}).σ(τt)p≡t(λ(x:U).p(τ(σx))).

This equation is used by the kernel through T-Conv at several points in tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​; it is a computation, not an axiom.

An ordering on UUU. Read σ  x  p\sigma\;x\;pσxp as "the predicate ppp holds of everything below xxx". This gives UUU something like an order, and lets us say two things about predicates and elements.

  • A predicate p:℘Up : \wp Up:℘U is inductive if whenever it holds of everything below xxx, it holds of xxx: that is, Π(x:U). σ  x  p→p  x\tPi{x}{U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;x}Π(x:U).σxp→px.
  • An element x:Ux : Ux:U is well-founded if every inductive predicate holds of xxx: that is, Π(p:℘U). (Π(x:U). σ  x  p→p  x)→p  x\tPi{p}{\wp U}{(\tPi{x}{U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;x}) \to p\;x}Π(p:℘U).(Π(x:U).σxp→px)→px.

The element Ω\OmegaΩ is built to play the part of "the collection of all well-founded elements": it packs the family consisting of all inductive predicates. In Burali-Forti's paradox this is the set of all ordinals, which is itself an ordinal, hence a member of itself, hence not well-founded although all ordinals are.

The three ingredients. Reading tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ from the bottom up:

  1. The last line, λ(p:℘U). λ(h1:⋯ ). h1  Ω  (λ(x:U). h1  (τ  (σ  x)))\tLam{p}{\wp U}{\tLam{h_1}{\cdots}{h_1\;\Omega\;(\tLam{x}{U}{h_1\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;x))})}}λ(p:℘U).λ(h1​:⋯).h1​Ω(λ(x:U).h1​(τ(σx))), proves that Ω\OmegaΩ is well-founded. Its type is Π(p:℘U). (Π(x:U). σ  x  p→p  x)→p  Ω\tPi{p}{\wp U}{(\tPi{x}{U}{\sigma\;x\;p \to p\;x}) \to p\;\Omega}Π(p:℘U).(Π(x:U).σxp→px)→pΩ, which is the type of h0h_0h0​. So h0h_0h0​ stands for "Ω\OmegaΩ is well-founded".
  2. The predicate Δ  y\Delta\;yΔy says "yyy is not below itself" (strictly, it speaks of τ  (σ  y)\tau\;(\sigma\;y)τ(σy), which behaves like yyy by the equation above). The second argument of h0h_0h0​, the long λ\lambdaλ beginning λ(x:U). λ(h2:⋯ ). ⋯\tLam{x}{U}{\tLam{h_2}{\cdots}{\cdots}}λ(x:U).λ(h2​:⋯).⋯, proves that Δ\DeltaΔ is inductive. Hence h0  Δ  (⋯ ):Δ  Ωh_0\;\Delta\;(\cdots) : \Delta\;\Omegah0​Δ(⋯):ΔΩ, that is, Ω\OmegaΩ is not below itself.
  3. The remaining argument, λ(p:℘U). h0  (λ(y:U). p  (τ  (σ  y)))\tLam{p}{\wp U}{h_0\;(\tLam{y}{U}{p\;(\tau\;(\sigma\;y))})}λ(p:℘U).h0​(λ(y:U).p(τ(σy))), proves that Ω\OmegaΩ is below itself, by applying the well-foundedness of Ω\OmegaΩ to a predicate transformed through the packing equation.

Since Δ  Ω\Delta\;\OmegaΔΩ is the negation of "Ω\OmegaΩ is below itself", applying the result of step 2 to the result of step 3 yields a term of type ⊥\bot⊥.

The argument is Burali-Forti's in disguise. Ordinals are well-founded; the collection Ω\OmegaΩ of all ordinals is an ordinal, so it is a member of itself; but no well-founded thing is a member of itself. Set theory escapes by refusing to let the collection of all ordinals be a set. The type theory with Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type has no such refusal, because UUU can quantify over everything, including itself.

Where Type : Type is used

Every typing step in tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ is ordinary except one. In σ=λ(s:U). s  U  τ\sigma = \tLam{s}{U}{s\;U\;\tau}σ=λ(s:U).sUτ, the variable s:Us : Us:U is applied to the type UUU itself. The type of sss begins Π(X:Type). ⋯\tPi{X}{\mathsf{Type}}{\cdots}Π(X:Type).⋯, so T-App requires U:TypeU : \mathsf{Type}U:Type. But UUU is a Π\PiΠ type that quantifies over Type\mathsf{Type}Type, and in a system with a universe hierarchy such a type lives one level above the universe it quantifies over:

Γ⊢Sort u:Sort (u+1)Γ,X:Sort u⊢B:Sort vΓ⊢Π(X:Sort u). B:Sort max⁡(u+1,v)\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash \Sort{u} : \Sort{(u+1)} \qquad \Gamma, X : \Sort{u} \vdash B : \Sort{v}}{\Gamma \vdash \tPi{X}{\Sort{u}}{B} : \Sort{\max(u+1, v)}}Γ⊢Π(X:Sortu).B:Sortmax(u+1,v)Γ⊢Sortu:Sort(u+1)Γ,X:Sortu⊢B:Sortv​

With the T-Pi rule of Chapter 13, UUU is in Sort (u+1)\Sort{(u+1)}Sort(u+1) at best, never in Sort u\Sort{u}Sortu, so s  Us\;UsU is ill typed and σ\sigmaσ cannot be written. The whole construction collapses at this one application. Impredicativity of Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 does not reopen the door: UUU has body (℘℘X→X)→℘℘X(\wp\wp X \to X) \to \wp\wp X(℘℘X→X)→℘℘X, whose result ℘℘X\wp\wp X℘℘X is a function type into a universe and therefore is not a proposition, so imax\mathrm{imax}imax does not place UUU in Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0. Coquand showed that one impredicative universe at the bottom is consistent [Coquand 1988]; Hurkens' term shows that two impredicative levels are already too many [Hurkens 1995].

Reproducing it with the kernel

You can watch the kernel accept and reject this term. The only rule to change is T-Sort, implemented by the Term::Sort(u) case of infer in src/typecheck.rs:

// T-Sort, as shipped: every universe lives in the next one.
Term::Sort(u) => Ok(Term::Sort(u.checked_add(1).ok_or("universe overflow")?)),

Replace the right-hand side by Ok(Term::Sort(*u)), so that Sort 0:Sort 0\Sort{0} : \Sort{0}Sort0:Sort0, and use Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 as Type\mathsf{Type}Type throughout. Nothing else needs to change: with every type in Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0, the T-Pi rule with imax\mathrm{imax}imax already assigns Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 to every Π\PiΠ type, which is the second rule of this appendix. With that one-line change, infer returns exactly Π(p:Sort 0). p\tPi{p}{\Sort{0}}{p}Π(p:Sort0).p for tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​. The unmodified kernel rejects the term with a type mismatch at the application s  Us\;UsU inside σ\sigmaσ, as predicted above.

Do not leave the modification in. Besides making the kernel inconsistent, it breaks termination: as Chapter 13 explains, tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ has no normal form, so asking the modified kernel to normalize it runs until the reduction fuel of Chapter 12 is exhausted.

Why there is no normal form

Chapter 14 proves consistency of the real system by showing that no normal closed term has type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P. The part of that proof that analyses the shapes of normal terms does not use strong normalization and goes through unchanged for Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type. So if tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ had a normal form, that normal form would be a closed normal term of type ⊥\bot⊥, which cannot exist. Subject reduction still holds, so reduction cannot escape the type ⊥\bot⊥ either. The only remaining possibility is that tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ reduces forever: strong normalization fails, and with it the termination of the type checker. Girard's paradox is therefore not only a logical defect but a computational one, and it is the reason the design of universes in Chapter 13 matters for the algorithm as much as for the logic.

What to remember

  • With Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type, the type UUU quantifies over all types while being one of them, so it contains a copy of its own double power set, which no set can do.
  • Hurkens' term tHt_{\mathrm{H}}tH​ turns this into Burali-Forti's paradox: Ω\OmegaΩ, the packed family of all inductive predicates, is both well-founded and below itself.
  • The rule Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type is used in exactly one place, the application s  Us\;UsU in σ\sigmaσ; a universe hierarchy makes that application ill typed.
  • The term has no normal form, so the paradox breaks termination of the kernel as well as consistency.

Appendix D

Proof of Consistency

Chapter 14 states that the core system is consistent: no closed term has type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P (Theorem 14.5). This appendix gives the full proof, including the standard facts about typing and conversion that the argument uses. It concerns the core system: the rules of Figure 3.1 with the universes of Chapter 13, without the constants of Part II.

The idea

The proof combines a deep theorem with an elementary argument. The deep theorem is strong normalization: every well-typed term reduces to a normal form. Together with subject reduction, it means that if any closed term had type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P, a normal closed term would too. The elementary argument is a case analysis showing that no normal closed term can have that type.

The case analysis runs in two rounds. First, the normal form must be a λ\lambdaλ, because nothing else closed and normal can have a Π\PiΠ type. Second, its body must be a term of type PPP in the context P:Sort 0P : \Sort{0}P:Sort0, and no normal term can be, because the only variable in scope has type Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0, which is neither PPP nor a function type.

To make the case analysis rigorous, we need to know what the type of a term of each shape looks like (the generation lemma), and that terms of different shapes are never convertible (a consequence of confluence). Those facts are collected first.

Facts about the type system

Besides subject reduction and strong normalization from Chapter 14, the proof uses the following standard properties of Pure Type Systems [Barendregt 1992]. Subject reduction extends from one step to any number of steps by induction on the number of steps.

Lemma D.1 (Standard properties).

(a) Generation. If Γ⊢t:T\Gamma \vdash t : TΓ⊢t:T, then, depending on the shape of ttt:

  • if t=xt = xt=x, then (x:A)∈Γ(x : A) \in \Gamma(x:A)∈Γ and T≡AT \conv AT≡A for some AAA;
  • if t=Sort ut = \Sort{u}t=Sortu, then T≡Sort (u+1)T \conv \Sort{(u+1)}T≡Sort(u+1);
  • if t=Π(x:A). Bt = \tPi{x}{A}{B}t=Π(x:A).B, then T≡Sort wT \conv \Sort{w}T≡Sortw for some www;
  • if t=λ(x:A). st = \tLam{x}{A}{s}t=λ(x:A).s, then Γ,x:A⊢s:B\Gamma, x : A \vdash s : BΓ,x:A⊢s:B and T≡Π(x:A). BT \conv \tPi{x}{A}{B}T≡Π(x:A).B for some BBB;
  • if t=f  at = f\;at=fa, then Γ⊢f:Π(x:A). B\Gamma \vdash f : \tPi{x}{A}{B}Γ⊢f:Π(x:A).B and Γ⊢a:A\Gamma \vdash a : AΓ⊢a:A for some xxx, AAA, and BBB.

(b) Confluence. If s≡ts \conv ts≡t, then sss and ttt reduce to a common term. Consequently: Π(x:A). B≡Π(y:A′). B′\tPi{x}{A}{B} \conv \tPi{y}{A'}{B'}Π(x:A).B≡Π(y:A′).B′ implies A≡A′A \conv A'A≡A′ and B[x↦z]≡B′[y↦z]\subst{B}{x}{z} \conv \subst{B'}{y}{z}B[x↦z]≡B′[y↦z] for a fresh zzz; and no two of a variable, a universe, and a Π\PiΠ are convertible.

(c) Substitution. If s≡ts \conv ts≡t, then s[z↦a]≡t[z↦a]\subst{s}{z}{a} \conv \subst{t}{z}{a}s[z↦a]≡t[z↦a].

Generation is the typing rules read backwards: it says that the only way to type a term of a given shape is the rule for that shape, possibly followed by uses of T-Conv. That is why each case says "T≡…T \conv \ldotsT≡…" rather than "T=…T = \ldotsT=…".

The consequences in (b) hold because a variable and a universe do not reduce at all, a Π\PiΠ reduces only to a Π\PiΠ (reduction happens inside its annotation or body, never at its root), and two terms with a common reduct must therefore have the same outermost shape.

Shapes of normal terms

Recall from Chapter 12 that every term is a spine h  a1⋯anh\;a_1 \cdots a_nha1​⋯an​ whose head hhh is not an application. The next lemma classifies normal terms by their head. Its role is to leave only four possibilities for the normal form in the main proof, each of which can then be ruled out.

Lemma D.2 (Normal forms). Let nnn be a normal term with Γ⊢n:T\Gamma \vdash n : TΓ⊢n:T. Then nnn is a universe, a Π\PiΠ, a λ\lambdaλ, or a neutral term x  a1⋯akx\;a_1 \cdots a_kxa1​⋯ak​ with k≥0k \ge 0k≥0 whose head xxx is a variable in dom(Γ)\dom(\Gamma)dom(Γ). Moreover, if k≥1k \ge 1k≥1, then Γ⊢x:C\Gamma \vdash x : CΓ⊢x:C for some CCC that is convertible to a Π\PiΠ.

Write n=h  a1⋯akn = h\;a_1 \cdots a_kn=ha1​⋯ak​ with hhh not an application.

If k=0k = 0k=0, then n=hn = hn=h is a universe, a Π\PiΠ, a λ\lambdaλ, or a variable, since those are the only shapes other than application. A variable is in dom(Γ)\dom(\Gamma)dom(Γ) by generation.

Let k≥1k \ge 1k≥1. Applying the generation lemma for application kkk times, from the outside in, shows that every prefix h  a1⋯aih\;a_1 \cdots a_iha1​⋯ai​ is typable, and in particular, from the innermost application h  a1h\;a_1ha1​, that Γ⊢h:Π(y:A). B\Gamma \vdash h : \tPi{y}{A}{B}Γ⊢h:Π(y:A).B for some yyy, AAA, and BBB. Now consider the shape of hhh. It is not a λ\lambdaλ, since h  a1h\;a_1ha1​ would then be a β\betaβ-redex inside the normal term nnn. It is not a universe or a Π\PiΠ either: by generation, its type would be convertible to a universe, and by confluence a universe is not convertible to Π(y:A). B\tPi{y}{A}{B}Π(y:A).B. So hhh is a variable xxx, which is in dom(Γ)\dom(\Gamma)dom(Γ) by generation, and Γ⊢x:Π(y:A). B\Gamma \vdash x : \tPi{y}{A}{B}Γ⊢x:Π(y:A).B, which is the required CCC.

Proof of Theorem 14.5

Theorem 14.5 (Consistency). There is no closed term ttt with ⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort 0). P\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort0).P.

Suppose that ⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort 0). P\cdot \vdash t : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}⋅⊢t:Π(P:Sort0).P. By strong normalization, ttt reduces to a normal term nnn, and by subject reduction, ⋅⊢n:Π(P:Sort 0). P\cdot \vdash n : \tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}⋅⊢n:Π(P:Sort0).P. We show that no such nnn exists, using Lemma D.2 twice.

The normal form is a λ\lambdaλ. By Lemma D.2, nnn is a universe, a Π\PiΠ, a λ\lambdaλ, or a neutral term.

  • It is not neutral, because its head would be a variable in the empty context, and there is none.
  • It is not a universe or a Π\PiΠ, because generation would make Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P convertible to a universe, which confluence rules out.

So n=λ(x:A). sn = \tLam{x}{A}{s}n=λ(x:A).s. By generation, x:A⊢s:Bx : A \vdash s : Bx:A⊢s:B and Π(P:Sort 0). P≡Π(x:A). B\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P} \conv \tPi{x}{A}{B}Π(P:Sort0).P≡Π(x:A).B for some BBB. By confluence, A≡Sort 0A \conv \Sort{0}A≡Sort0 and P[P↦z]≡B[x↦z]\subst{P}{P}{z} \conv \subst{B}{x}{z}P[P↦z]≡B[x↦z] for a fresh zzz, that is, z≡B[x↦z]z \conv \subst{B}{x}{z}z≡B[x↦z]. Substituting xxx for zzz on both sides, which preserves convertibility by part (c) of Lemma D.1, gives x≡Bx \conv Bx≡B. The body sss is normal, because it is a subterm of the normal term nnn. In short: x:A⊢s:Bx : A \vdash s : Bx:A⊢s:B with A≡Sort 0A \conv \Sort{0}A≡Sort0 and B≡xB \conv xB≡x.

The body cannot exist. Let Γ=x:A\Gamma = x : AΓ=x:A. By Lemma D.2, sss is a universe, a Π\PiΠ, a λ\lambdaλ, or a neutral term.

  • If sss is a universe or a Π\PiΠ, generation makes BBB convertible to a universe; if sss is a λ\lambdaλ, it makes BBB convertible to a Π\PiΠ. But B≡xB \conv xB≡x, and by confluence a variable is convertible to neither.
  • If sss is neutral, its head is a variable in dom(Γ)={x}\dom(\Gamma) = \{x\}dom(Γ)={x}, so s=x  a1⋯aks = x\;a_1 \cdots a_ks=xa1​⋯ak​. If k=0k = 0k=0, then s=xs = xs=x, and generation gives B≡AB \conv AB≡A. Then x≡B≡A≡Sort 0x \conv B \conv A \conv \Sort{0}x≡B≡A≡Sort0, but a variable is not convertible to a universe. If k≥1k \ge 1k≥1, Lemma D.2 gives Γ⊢x:C\Gamma \vdash x : CΓ⊢x:C with CCC convertible to a Π\PiΠ, and generation for the variable xxx gives C≡A≡Sort 0C \conv A \conv \Sort{0}C≡A≡Sort0. Then a Π\PiΠ is convertible to a universe, which confluence rules out.

Every case leads to a contradiction, so no closed term has type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P.

In words: the only variable available inside the λ\lambdaλ is xxx, whose type is Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0. It can neither be returned, since Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 is not xxx, nor be applied to anything, since Sort 0\Sort{0}Sort0 is not a function type. Every other normal term has a universe or a Π\PiΠ as its type, and xxx is neither. The argument relies on strong normalization to reduce the question to normal terms; that step is where all the difficulty lies.

The second half of the proof, the analysis of normal terms, does not use strong normalization and does not depend on the universe structure. It carries over unchanged to a system with Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type. That is how Chapter 13 concludes that Hurkens' term (Appendix C), which has type Π(P:Type). P\tPi{P}{\mathsf{Type}}{P}Π(P:Type).P in that system, cannot have a normal form: if it did, the analysis would rule it out. So in the inconsistent system it is strong normalization that fails, not generation or confluence.

With the inductive types of Part II, normal forms also include stuck recursor applications, such as Nat.recu  M  z  s  n\NatRec{u}\;M\;z\;s\;nNat.recu​Mzsn with nnn a variable, and the short case analysis above no longer suffices on its own. Consistency of the Calculus of Inductive Constructions, of which the extended system is a fragment, follows from strong normalization by a more careful analysis of normal forms [Werner 1994].

What to remember

  • Consistency is proved by combining strong normalization and subject reduction (to pass to a normal form) with a case analysis on the shape of normal terms.
  • The case analysis uses two standard facts: generation (the typing rules read backwards) and confluence (terms of different outermost shapes are never convertible).
  • A normal closed term of type Π(P:Sort 0). P\tPi{P}{\Sort{0}}{P}Π(P:Sort0).P would have to be a λ\lambdaλ whose body has type xxx in the context x:Sort 0x : \Sort{0}x:Sort0, and no normal term does.
  • The hard part is strong normalization; the shape analysis alone also applies to Type:Type\mathsf{Type} : \mathsf{Type}Type:Type, and shows that Hurkens' term has no normal form.

Appendix E

The leanmini Language

The scripts in this book are written in a small language called leanmini, read by the parser in src/syntax.rs and the command loop in src/main.rs. It is deliberately explicit: every binder carries its type, every argument is written out, and nothing is inferred. This appendix is the complete reference, derived line by line from the code, together with every example script of the repository in a runnable form.

Running scripts

The runner is the binary mini-lean built from src/main.rs.

cargo run -- examples/identity.leanmini    # run a script file
cargo run                                  # interactive session on stdin
cargo test                                 # the kernel's own test suite

A script is a sequence of lines. The runner processes them from top to bottom and stops at the first error, printing the message and exiting with status 1. Blank lines and lines beginning with # are comments and are skipped.

# This is a comment.
goal forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P

Without a file argument the runner reads the same commands from standard input, one per line, after printing a reminder of the available commands. Errors are reported with the prefix error: and the session continues. The command quit (or exit) ends it. One command differs between the two modes: in a file, an inductive block is the header line followed by its | lines; interactively, the block is closed by a line containing only end.

The command-line runner prints terms in Rust's Debug format, for example App(Const("Nat.succ"), Const("Nat.zero")), because the kernel has no pretty-printer. The playgrounds in this book run the same kernel compiled to WebAssembly, with a small pretty-printer added on top that writes terms back in leanmini syntax, and they echo each command before its output so that the transcript can be read on its own.

Terms

A term is written in one of the following forms. A, B, t stand for terms and x for a name.

Syntax Meaning Notation in the book
Sort 0, Sort 1, ... A universe; the number is required Sort u\Sort{u}Sortu
x A variable or a constant, depending on scope xxx or ccc
forall (x : A), B A dependent function type Π(x:A). B\tPi{x}{A}{B}Π(x:A).B
A -> B A non-dependent function type A→BA \to BA→B
fun (x : A) => t A function λ(x:A). t\tLam{x}{A}{t}λ(x:A).t
f a Application f  af\;afa
(t) Grouping

Application associates to the left and binds tightest: f a b is (f a) b. Arrows associate to the right: A -> B -> C is A -> (B -> C). A forall or fun extends as far to the right as possible, and so does the right-hand side of an arrow, so A -> forall (x : B), C needs no parentheses. A forall or fun used as an argument must be parenthesized, as in Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m. The arrow A -> B is read as forall (_ : A), B; the name _ is reserved for this purpose and may not be used as a binder in an inductive declaration.

The tokenizer splits on whitespace and on the characters (, ), ,, :, and the two-character symbols -> and =>. A name is a run of letters, digits, _, ', and ., so Nat.succ, List.rec1, and x' are single names. Three Unicode characters are accepted as aliases: → for ->, λ for fun, and ∀ for forall. Any other character is rejected with unexpected character: ....

Names are resolved when the term is parsed, not later.

  • A name bound by an enclosing fun or forall, or present in the current goal's context, is a local variable.
  • Otherwise, a name declared in the kernel (by inductive, def, axiom, or recursor, or built in) is a constant.
  • Otherwise the parse fails with unknown identifier: x. This is also the error you get for a misspelled constructor or for using a hypothesis that has not been introduced yet.

A local shadows a constant of the same name. The parser never guesses types: Sort must be followed by a numeral, and a binder must be written (x : A) with its type.

Declarations

Inductive types

inductive List (A : Sort 1) : Sort 1 where
  | nil
  | cons (head : A) (tail : List A)

The header has the form inductive Name (p : P) ... (index i : J) ... : Sort u where. Each parenthesized binder is a parameter, or an index if it starts with the word index. Parameters must come before indices (parameters must precede indices). The universe after the colon must be a literal Sort u (inductive result must be Sort u), and the line must end with where.

Each following line begins with | and declares one constructor: | ctor (field : T) ... [: Name params indices]. Field types may mention the parameters, the earlier fields, and Name itself. The result type after the optional colon must be Name applied to the parameters, in order and unchanged (constructor parameters must be uniform), followed by one index term per index. If the type has indices, every constructor must give its result type (indexed constructor requires explicit result type); if it has none, the result type may be omitted. The index keyword is not allowed on constructor fields.

inductive Vec (A : Sort 1) (index n : Nat) : Sort 1 where
  | nil : Vec A Nat.zero
  | cons (n : Nat) (head : A) (tail : Vec A n) : Vec A (Nat.succ n)

Constructors are registered under qualified names: the declaration above adds Vec.nil and Vec.cons, and the constructors of List are List.nil and List.cons. Scripts must use the qualified form.

Accepting the declaration runs the four conditions of Chapter 8: the type of Name is a type, each constructor type is a type that ends in Name applied to the parameters, every field that mentions Name is strictly positive, and no field lives in a universe above Sort u when u is at least 1. The messages for failures include non-strictly-positive / unsupported recursive field, field f lives in Sort w, exceeding inductive universe Sort u, and inductive occurrence inside result index. Binder names starting with _ or __ are refused (reserved binder name), because the kernel uses such names for the binders it generates.

On success the runner prints inductive Name registered and the kernel adds the type former, the constructors, the recursor Name.rec0, and, when large elimination is allowed, Name.rec1. A proposition (Sort 0) gets Name.rec1 only if it is a subsingleton, as Chapter 8 explains.

In a script file, the constructor lines of an inductive block must follow the header without any intervening comment line. The runner collects lines that start with | or are blank; a # line ends the block early, and the first constructor line after it is then reported as start with 'goal <type>' (or unknown command: ... if a proof is in progress).

Definitions and axioms

def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n
axiom em : forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P

def name : T := t checks that T is a type and that t : T in the empty context, then adds name with the body t; the kernel unfolds it during reduction (δ\deltaδ-reduction, Chapter 12). The runner prints defined name. A definition must fit on one line, and the first := separates type from body.

axiom name : T adds name : T without a body, after checking that T is a type. It prints added axiom name. Axioms never unfold. Nothing prevents you from assuming something false this way; the kernel checks that the type is well formed, not that it is true.

Names must be new: redeclaring one fails with duplicate declaration: name, and nothing may be declared inside the namespace Name.rec... of an existing inductive type.

Extra recursors

recursor Nat 2

recursor I v generates I.recv for the elimination universe v, if it does not exist yet, and prints generated I.recv. Levels 0 and 1 are generated automatically by inductive; use this command when a motive needs to return a type in Sort 2 or higher. It fails for a proposition that does not allow large elimination (I is not a subsingleton proposition; cannot eliminate into Sort v).

The standard kernel

Every session starts with Nat and Eq already declared, exactly as if the following declarations had been run. The generated binder names begin with __; they are shown here as M and m for readability, and renaming bound variables does not change a type.

Nat      : Sort 1
Nat.zero : Nat
Nat.succ : Nat -> Nat
Nat.rec0 : forall (M : Nat -> Sort 0), M Nat.zero -> (forall (n : Nat), M n -> M (Nat.succ n)) -> forall (x : Nat), M x
Nat.rec1 : forall (M : Nat -> Sort 1), M Nat.zero -> (forall (n : Nat), M n -> M (Nat.succ n)) -> forall (x : Nat), M x

Eq       : forall (A : Sort 1), A -> A -> Sort 0
Eq.refl  : forall (A : Sort 1), forall (a : A), Eq A a a
Eq.rec0  : forall (A : Sort 1), forall (a : A), forall (M : forall (b : A), Eq A a b -> Sort 0), M a (Eq.refl A a) -> forall (b : A), forall (h : Eq A a b), M b h
Eq.rec1  : forall (A : Sort 1), forall (a : A), forall (M : forall (b : A), Eq A a b -> Sort 1), M a (Eq.refl A a) -> forall (b : A), forall (h : Eq A a b), M b h

Nat.rec1 is recursion into types and Nat.rec0 is induction into propositions (Chapter 7). Eq takes its type argument A explicitly, so the equation a=ba = ba=b in Nat\NatNat is written Eq Nat a b, and its proof by reflexivity is Eq.refl Nat a (Chapter 9). Because Eq is declared with A : Sort 1, equality is available for types in Sort 1 such as Nat and List Nat, not for propositions.

In general the recursor of an inductive type I into Sort v is named I.recv: List.rec0, List.rec1, Vec.rec1, and so on. Its argument order is parameters, motive, one minor premise per constructor in declaration order, indices, and finally the major premise (Chapter 8).

Proofs

Starting a goal

goal forall (n : Nat), Eq Nat n n

goal T checks that T is a type in the empty context and starts a proof with the single goal ?0 : T. It prints nothing in the command-line runner (the playgrounds print the goal). Any tactic given before a goal fails with start with 'goal <type>'. Starting a new goal abandons an unfinished proof.

After every tactic, the runner prints the remaining goals, each as its number, its hypotheses, and its target after a turnstile:

?3:
  n : Nat
  k : Nat
  ih : Eq Nat (add Nat.zero k) k
  ⊢ Eq Nat (add Nat.zero (Nat.succ k)) (Nat.succ k)

When no goals are left it prints No goals. Run 'qed' to kernel-check. The command show prints the goals without changing anything.

Tactics always act on the first goal. Terms given to tactics are parsed in that goal's context, so hypothesis names are in scope. Chapter 10 explains what each tactic does to the partial proof term; this section states the interface.

Tactics

intro x requires the target to reduce to a forall or an arrow. It adds x : A to the context, where A is the domain, and makes the body the new target. The name must not already be in the context (binder name already in context); otherwise the message is intro expects a Pi/arrow goal.

exact t closes the goal with t, after checking t against the target. A mismatch is reported by the kernel as type mismatch: actual ..., expected ....

apply f infers the type of f and peels off non-dependent arrows until the result is definitionally equal to the target; each peeled domain becomes a new goal, in order. If the type of f already matches the target, apply f behaves like exact f. Dependent binders are refused with dependent apply requires elaboration/unification, and a result that never matches gives apply result does not match the goal.

change T replaces the target by T, which must be a type definitionally equal to it (change expects definitionally equal target). It is used to expose a subterm that only appears after computation, before rw.

rfl requires the target to reduce to Eq A a b (rfl expects Eq A lhs rhs) with a and b definitionally equal (rfl: sides are not definitionally equal), and closes it with Eq.refl A a.

rw h requires h to have a type that reduces to Eq A a b (rw expects proof of equality). It replaces every occurrence of a in the target by b and leaves the rewritten target as the new goal. Occurrences are found syntactically, up to the names of bound variables; a term that is only equal after computation is not found, which gives rw: no syntactic occurrence of lhs in goal; use change first. Unlike Lean's rw, it does not try rfl afterwards, so a goal of the form Eq A x x must still be closed explicitly. If abstracting a produces an ill-typed motive, the kernel's type error is reported before the proof state changes.

induction x requires x to be a hypothesis whose type reduces to an inductive type without indices, and no later hypothesis may mention x (induction: revert dependent hypotheses first). It creates one goal per constructor, in declaration order. Each goal's context gains the constructor's fields, under their declared names, and one induction hypothesis per recursive field, named ih (with primes appended if ih is taken). The field named n of Nat.succ is renamed to k when n is already in use, which is why the goals of the examples below mention k and ih. The recursor used is I.recv, where v is the universe of the target; if that recursor does not exist, the message is no elimination recursor at target universe. Indexed families are not supported (indexed induction requires motive/index elaboration (not implemented)).

qed fails if goals remain (N goals remain). Otherwise it assembles the proof term from the tactic steps, sends it to the kernel to be checked against the original goal, prints QED. Kernel checked proof: followed by the term, and ends the proof. This final check is the only step that the soundness of the system depends on.

Any other line gives unknown command: ....

Errors from the kernel

Some messages come from the kernel rather than from the tactic layer, and can appear under any command.

Message Meaning
unbound local: x A variable is used outside its binder; this cannot be produced by the parser, only by a term built incorrectly.
unknown constant: c A constant was removed or never declared.
application of non-function: ... The function position of an application does not have a forall type.
expected a type, got ... A binder annotation, goal, or declared type is not a type.
type mismatch: actual ..., expected ... The inferred type is not definitionally equal to the required one.
universe overflow The universe level does not fit in 64 bits.
reduction fuel exhausted A single reduction exceeded 20,000 steps; this happens for very large computations such as adding big numerals.

The example scripts

Every script of the examples/ directory follows, as a playground. Each one has been checked by the kernel; edit it and press run to see what changes.

identity.leanmini

# The polymorphic identity on propositions: for every P, P -> P.
goal forall (P : Sort 0), P -> P
intro P
intro p
exact p
qed

nat-reflexivity.leanmini

# Every natural number equals itself, proved by induction on Nat.
# Each case closes by rfl because both sides are syntactically the same.
goal forall (n : Nat), Eq Nat n n
intro n
induction n
rfl
rfl
qed

zero-add.leanmini

# Addition by recursion on the second argument:
#   add m zero     = m
#   add m (succ k) = succ (add m k)
def add : Nat -> Nat -> Nat := fun (m : Nat) => fun (n : Nat) => Nat.rec1 (fun (_n : Nat) => Nat) m (fun (k : Nat) => fun (r : Nat) => Nat.succ r) n

# add zero n = n is not definitional, so it needs induction on n.
goal forall (n : Nat), Eq Nat (add Nat.zero n) n
intro n
induction n
# Base case: add zero zero reduces to zero.
rfl
# Step case: unfold add zero (succ k) to succ (add zero k), then use ih.
change Eq Nat (Nat.succ (add Nat.zero k)) (Nat.succ k)
rw ih
rfl
qed

generic-list.leanmini

# A user-declared polymorphic list. Declaring it generates List.rec0, List.rec1, ...
inductive List (A : Sort 1) : Sort 1 where
  | nil
  | cons (head : A) (tail : List A)

# induction works for any non-indexed inductive, not only Nat.
goal forall (xs : List Nat), Eq (List Nat) xs xs
intro xs
induction xs
rfl
rfl
qed

generic-vec.leanmini

# Length-indexed vectors. The index n varies between constructors,
# so it is declared with the `index` keyword in the header.
inductive Vec (A : Sort 1) (index n : Nat) : Sort 1 where
  | nil : Vec A Nat.zero
  | cons (n : Nat) (head : A) (tail : Vec A n) : Vec A (Nat.succ n)

# Constructors take the parameter A explicitly.
def one : Vec Nat (Nat.succ Nat.zero) := Vec.cons Nat Nat.zero Nat.zero (Vec.nil Nat)

# The tactic `induction` does not support indexed families yet,
# but the kernel still checks terms that use Vec directly.
goal Eq (Vec Nat (Nat.succ Nat.zero)) one (Vec.cons Nat Nat.zero Nat.zero (Vec.nil Nat))
rfl
qed

What is missing compared with Lean 4

leanmini is a vehicle for understanding the kernel, not a proof assistant. The table lists what Lean's front end does for you and this language does not.

Lean 4 leanmini
Implicit arguments, filled in by the elaborator Every argument is explicit; Eq Nat a b, not a = b
Unification to solve for metavariables None; tactics work only when the term fixes everything
Universe polymorphism (Sort u with a level variable) Every level is a numeral; one recursor per level
Mutual and nested inductive types A single inductive type at a time; List Tree as a field is rejected
Definitional proof irrelevance Proofs of a proposition are compared like any terms
induction on indexed families, with reverting Non-indexed types only; dependent hypotheses must be reverted by hand (which no tactic does)
apply with dependent arguments Non-dependent arrows only
rw up to instances, with rfl afterwards Syntactic matching only; no automatic rfl
simp, omega, and other automation None
Notation, numerals, and theorem with named results Nat.succ (Nat.succ Nat.zero); a finished proof is not saved under a name

The last row has a practical consequence: a qed prints the proof term and discards it. To reuse a result, state it as a def with the term written out, or as an axiom.

Everything in the right column is work that Lean's elaborator and tactic framework perform before a term reaches the kernel. Lean's kernel, like ours, only ever sees complete terms. The limitations above are limitations of the front end in this repository, not of the type theory.

What to remember

  • A leanmini script is a list of commands: inductive, def, axiom, recursor, goal, and the tactics intro, exact, apply, change, rw, rfl, induction, closed by qed.
  • Terms are fully explicit: Sort u, forall (x : A), B, fun (x : A) => t, A -> B, and left-associative application.
  • Constructors and recursors are qualified: List.cons, List.rec1. Nat and Eq are predeclared.
  • The front end is minimal by design; only the final qed check, performed by the kernel, matters for soundness.
